[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > Nonetheless, having an alternative in a menu is neither "steering" nor
  > "promotion", because promoting an alternative needs to explicitly and
  > actively describe it in favorable terms, not just show it.

Marketing promotion typically does try to present an alternative in
terms of praise, but not necessarily.  Some promotional activities aim
only to make people aware that something exists, or lead them to dwell
on its name for a moment.  Either way, the effect is to promote the
uptake of that product, as marketers know.

What I mean by "promoting" a program or service is doing anything that
suggests (even implicitly) that we encourage people to use it -- that
it is a good thing to use.  That includes making users aware that it
exists.  If we do something that promotes an unjust program or
service, we encourage it to be used by (and to mistreat) more users
and we associate ourselves with that promotion.

We could also describe this as "mentioning to the users" that program
or service.

  > The words we use don't matter, as long as we agree that doing so does
  > not disqualify a non-GNU free program that Emacs communicates with.

You and the GNU Project very much disagree about this point.  Whether
hermes.el references the Hermes agent is out of our hands.  However,
whether GNU Emacs refers to hermes.el is the GNU Project's decision.

Including hermes.el in ELPA means Emacs refers to / promotes /
recommends / mentions hermes.el in a very strong manner.  That can't
avoid encouraging Emacs users to use the Hermes Agent and its
configuration program, because using hermes.el leads almost inevitably
to using the other two.

Given those circumstances, the GNU Coding Standards say that a
reference to something nonfree from the Hermes Agent counts as a
reference from hermes.el.

Hermes Agent refers to / promotes / recommends / mentions Nous in a
very strong manner, and Nous implies use of various nonfree and SaaSS
LLMs; I think all of them are non-free.  (Shall we call it "Noose", as
in "Not recommended to put it around your neck"?)  Anyone who starts
using hermes.el will probably be led to one of those LLMs.

The message of that chain of reference contradicts our principle
message to the public, so we should break that chain of promotion.

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > JL, Andrew's llm package supports locally run LLMs via, for example,
  > llm-ollama and llm-llamacpp, making it easy to satisfy non-SaSS
  > deployment.

Recommending/mentioning alternatives that are non-SaaSS is not enough
to satisfy the GNU Coding Standards.  The problem is
recommending/mentioning alternatives that ARE SaaSS.

  > It is up to the user to decide which models to use

That is true, but it is neither here nor there.  This issue is about
what GNU Emacs should say, not about what users do.

                                                      and to
  > determine for themselves if such models are "rms Free"

What counts for this GNU Project decision is whether it is free as
understood by the GNU Project.

We don't yet have a published criterion for that, but we should have
one soon.

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > > To adopt a philosophy of partly surrendering so that people who don't
  > > care about GNU or freedom will choose GNU for their own purely
  > > practical reasons will not inspire anyone.  It would be the sort of
  > > competition that tech businesses do.  We would not morally be better
  > > than them.

In addition, making "bets" on the future consequences of current and
likely future technology is the usual practice of venture capital.
A look at that world shows how risky these bets are.

We hear often about the few that won their bets on the future.  But
most of them bet wrong and then failed.

The entrepreneurs that do this sort of betting usually have plausible
arguments that the future will develop as they forecast.  They need
those to attract investment.  But looking back, we know most of them
failed.

For this reason, I am skeptical of pitches to sacrifice something
important for a _chance_ of winning more success and support.

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > Once again, the Hermes agent is a separate program, not part of the
  > ELPA package.

Yes, the overall description, when I saw it this morning, made that
clear.

                   The Hermes agent is installed and configured separately
  > by the user.

Thank you.  But I don't think this affects the conclusion.  The significant
point is that using hermes.el requires using the Hermes agent -- so
those two programs are morally linked.

                  The choice of 3 possible ways to configure it is
  > presented by the configuration tool that is part of the Hermes agent,

Ok.

  > and if it is invoked (it doesn't have too, because that's an optional
  > step),

I am finding that strange.  If configuring the Hermes agent is optional,
what does the Hermes agent DO if you try to use it without configuring it?

           it is done when the Hermes agent (NOT hermes.el the ELPA
  > package!) is first run by the user who installed it.  At that time,
  > the user should decide how to configure the Hermes agent (again: NOT
  > hermes.el the ELPA package).

This suggests (but I'm not sure) that invoking the Hermes agent
will tell you you must configure it to proceed.

If those are the facts, I would say that the Hermes agent _requires_
that the user configure it.  Configuring it is not optional.
(I am not sure that detail makes a difference -- either way, configuring
it makes a crucial decision between alternatives, and the Hermes agent
recommends each of the alternatives.)

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > > If the user, at per own initiative, gives a command to load a package
  > > that Emacs did not suggest, then Emacs obeys.

  > Yes.  And similarly if the user configures programs or sites which
  > Emacs uses and connects to in a way that runs or connects to non-free
  > software.

You left out "at per own initiative", and that makes the crucial difference.

If the user _at per own initiative_ configures programs or sites which
Emacs uses and connects to in a way that runs or connects to non-free
software, that is the user's responsibility and not Emacs's
responsibility.

But if Emacs (or programs Emacs recommends / promotes / suggests)
makes a suggestion to configure programs or sites in that way, and the
user accepts that suggestion, making that suggestion makes Emacs
responsible.  So Emacs should not suggest that.


--

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > > While Hermes Agent is free software, from the viewpoint of GNU free 
  > > software philosophy it is effectively shackled to a SaaSS business 
  > > model.

  > I disagree with this harsh characterization, and in any case, that's
  > not our concern here, as long as Hermes is a free program.

Eli, this is the crucial point where you have misunderstood the
GNU Project standards about referring to nonfree programs.
The misunderstanding is not about the Hermes agent in particular,
but about the standards themselves.

Given a free program P1, whether it is ok for a GNU package to
reference / recommend / promote / mention the program P1 _depends_ on
whether P1 itself references / recommends / promotes / mentions
nonfree programs in a significant way.

A few months ago I looked at contribution.html and pointed out a
paragraph about this.  I was sure it did not match the actual GNU
Project policy, but I couldn't make sense of what it did say.

I could not understand what condition it was trying to state.

Now I think I know what it was trying to say.  It was trying to state
a condition for accepting packages, something like, "As long as foo.el
offers to use at least one free alternative, it is ok, regardless of
what nonfree alternatives it may also offer."  The same thing you
were saying just now.

That crucially disagrees with the GNU Project's actual policy on
references to nonfree programs.  Our policy is stricter than that.
This misstatement needs to be clarified.

-- 
Dr Richard Stallman (https://stallman.org)
Chief GNUisance of the GNU Project (https://gnu.org)
Founder, Free Software Foundation (https://fsf.org)

> Yes, so I think we still need a flag to control this behavior. However,
> naming it is difficult.  The xxx-text-scaling-p template would be:
>
> - overline-text-scaling-p
> - strike-through-text-scaling-p
> - overline-and-strike-through-text-scaling-p

"-p" stands for "predicate", i.e. a function that returns a boolean, not
a boolean variable.  We have such mistakes already, but it's not
a reason to make it worse.

The ELisp manual recommends the "-flag" suffix for boolean variables.
I personally prefer no suffix at all since it's common enough for
boolean variables to be later extended to support more than 2 values.

>> i am considering using oauth2.el to reduce/simplify the authentication
>> code in mastodon.el, which gives me headaches, but i'm having trouble
>> understanding some basics.
>>
>> i have successfully obtained and stored a token with a registered app,
>> but i'm unclear on how to fetch the token from the store as needed.
>>
>> the main entrypoint has client-secret and client-id as mandatory
>> parameters, which seems to mean that i have to store them somewhere
>> else (presumably in a second encrypted plstore, causing more
>> headaches: client-id and client-secret should be treated like
>> passwords) in order to be able to fetch the auth token. is this
>> correct, or is a package expected to handle tokens in some other way?
>>
>> mastodon.el also supports multiple accounts, at least for saving auth
>> credentials. you set username and host to a different value,
>> reauthenticate, and mastodon.el keeps two sets of credentials, so if
>> you switch back to the first account you don't have to do the auth
>> flow again. i didn't manage to try this out due to the previous
>> hurdle, but i'm curious if this would be (easily) supported by
>> oath2.el, or does it assume 1 account per service somehow?
>>
>> finally, mastodon.el also supports storing auth tokens (but not
>> client/app data) in auth-sources. i take it oauth2.el doesn't have
>> support for storing in auth-sources?
>

I also maintain auth-source-xoauth2-plugin[1] which advices auth-source
to make use of xoauth2 handling using oauth2.el to handle low-level
details. It also requires customization to enable xoauth2 in Gnus
(documented in README.org) but smtpmail should work once the plugin is
enabled. Some users reported success on using this plugin.

So yes, oauth2.el is a low-level library that focus on the xoauth2
handling. I hope auth-source-xoauth2-plugin should work for your use
cases, but do let me know if anything is missing and I'll try to see
what I can do.

(Also thank you for maintaining mastodon.el!)

[1] https://elpa.gnu.org/packages/auth-source-xoauth2-plugin.html

> Are there other GUI editors which offer such customizations?  If not,
> it isn't urgent for us to consider such complications.

I don't use any other editor ;-)

I took a look at KWrite, the KDE editor, but found nothing regarding
text decorations.  In LibreOffice, it is possible to choose a style
(simple, double, wave, bold, ...) and a color as character attributes.

However, I found this in the CSS specification:
<https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Properties/text-decoration-thickness>

The 'text-decoration-thickness' CSS property sets the stroke thickness
of the decoration line that is used on text in an element, such as a
line-through, underline, or overline.

/* Single keyword */
text-decoration-thickness: auto;
text-decoration-thickness: from-font;

/* length */
text-decoration-thickness: 0.1em;
text-decoration-thickness: 3px;

/* percentage */
text-decoration-thickness: 10%;

auto
     The browser chooses an appropriate width for the text decoration
     line.

from-font
     If the font file includes information about a preferred thickness,
     use that value. If the font file doesn't include this information,
     behave as if auto was set, with the browser choosing an
     appropriate thickness.

<length>
     Specifies the thickness of the text decoration line as a <length>,
     overriding the font file suggestion or the browser default.

<percentage>
     Specifies the thickness of the text decoration line as a
     <percentage> of 1em in the current font. A percentage inherits as
     a relative value, and so therefore scales with changes in the
     font. The browser must use a minimum of 1 device pixel. For a
     given application of this property, the thickness is constant
     across the whole box it is applied to, even if there are child
     elements with a different font size.

Scaling, as far as I have observed elsewhere applies to the entire
text, including decorations (this is the case in LibreOffice, for
example).

>[...] "www.rendo-shrimp.de" is an
>url (even if abbreviated), so in such case why is the link (very) different? I mean if
>"www.rendo-shrimp.de" is a valid (and safe) url why using something else?

If I understand your question correctly, I have observed two cases when people do that.

One, common in publicity email, newsletters and so on, is gathering user statistics: the real url is unique per user, pointing to a tracking system which provides user statistics.  This means that the user is individually and reliably identified and tracked.

Anopther one, common in istitutional email systems, is security: when I write to some university colleague, for examples, and they reply in html to me while citing my text-only email, I  see that in the cited email all plain text links have been converted to links where the text of the link is the plain text link that I had written, while the url of the link points to a shielding service intended to prevent users from following dangerous links.

> From: Richard Stallman <rms@gnu.org>
> Cc: emacs-devel@gnu.org
> Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 00:47:51 -0400
> 
>                    The Hermes agent is installed and configured separately
>   > by the user.
> 
> Thank you.  But I don't think this affects the conclusion.  The significant
> point is that using hermes.el requires using the Hermes agent

No, it's the other way around: hermes.el is useful only to people who
already have the Hermes agent installed.  hermes.el is useless without
the Hermes agent, but the Hermes agent can be used without hermes.el.

>                   The choice of 3 possible ways to configure it is
>   > presented by the configuration tool that is part of the Hermes agent,
> 
> Ok.
> 
>   > and if it is invoked (it doesn't have too, because that's an optional
>   > step),
> 
> I am finding that strange.  If configuring the Hermes agent is optional,
> what does the Hermes agent DO if you try to use it without configuring it?

I didn't say "without configuring", I said "without invoking the
configuration tool".  The Hermes agent can be configured by other
means, bypassing the configuration "wizard".  For example, manually.
It's similar to Emacs: you can use Customize and have it update your
init files, or you can edit your init files manually (or by any other
means).

>            it is done when the Hermes agent (NOT hermes.el the ELPA
>   > package!) is first run by the user who installed it.  At that time,
>   > the user should decide how to configure the Hermes agent (again: NOT
>   > hermes.el the ELPA package).
> 
> This suggests (but I'm not sure) that invoking the Hermes agent
> will tell you you must configure it to proceed.

You should configure it, but there''s more than one way to do so.

> If those are the facts, I would say that the Hermes agent _requires_
> that the user configure it.  Configuring it is not optional.

It _is_ optional.  But if the Hermes agent is not configured to use
some LLM, it will not be useful, because the Hermes agent is a
"harness" for LLMs, a mediator between a model and the user.  It must
be told which model(s) to use, or it will not be capable of doing
anything useful.

> (I am not sure that detail makes a difference -- either way, configuring
> it makes a crucial decision between alternatives, and the Hermes agent
> recommends each of the alternatives.)

It isn't the Hermes agent that recommends alternatives, it's the
optional configuration tool.

> Cc: arne_bab@web.de, monnier@iro.umontreal.ca, bugs@gnu.support,
> 	yandros@gmail.com, emacs-devel@gnu.org
> Date: Thu, 01 Oct 2026 00:48:13 -0400
> 
>   > > If the user, at per own initiative, gives a command to load a package
>   > > that Emacs did not suggest, then Emacs obeys.
> 
>   > Yes.  And similarly if the user configures programs or sites which
>   > Emacs uses and connects to in a way that runs or connects to non-free
>   > software.
> 
> You left out "at per own initiative", and that makes the crucial difference.

No, I didn't.  Configuring a program is by definition a user's "own
initiative", because the user decides how to do that and which
alternatives to choose.

> If the user _at per own initiative_ configures programs or sites which
> Emacs uses and connects to in a way that runs or connects to non-free
> software, that is the user's responsibility and not Emacs's
> responsibility.

That's what happens in the case of hermes.el.

> But if Emacs (or programs Emacs recommends / promotes / suggests)
> makes a suggestion to configure programs or sites in that way, and the
> user accepts that suggestion, making that suggestion makes Emacs
> responsible.  So Emacs should not suggest that.

Neither Emacs nor hermes.el do that.  Not even the Hermes agent does,
although it is not a GNU program.  It is the user who configures the
Hermes agent, and at that time the user needs to decide which model(s)
to use.  Thus, the user is responsible for this configuration.

As another example, consider most modern Web browsers, both free and
nonfree.  When the user starts typing a site in the URL input box, a
typical browser will drop down a menu of suggested sites, some based
on trhe user input history, others based on popular sites.  If this
menu is also to be considered as recommendations / promotion /
suggestions, as AFAIU you are saying, then the concept of user's
choice of a site to go to should change accordingly, and this choice
can no longer be considered to be user's responsibility.  Then
invoking any such Web browser from Emacs should also be considered
problematic at best, if not downright forbidden.  If you disagree with
this logic, please explain how to distinguish between these
suggestions by Web browsers and the list of LLMs and list of sites
shown by the Hermes agent's configuration tool.  Because I don't see
the difference.

not? is "rendo-shrimp.de" also a URL, and if so, why? what about
"google" or "Wikipedia"?

textsec.el currently decides whether it's a URL by looking at the
return value of url-generic-parse-url.  If you can suggest some
heuristics to improve that which will not run a significant risk of
false positives, please do, and we can then consider installing it.
Features like this must not produce too many false positives, or else
users will disable them or stop paying attention to them.

> 
> One, common in publicity email, newsletters and so on, is gathering user statistics: the real url is unique per user, pointing to a tracking system which provides user statistics.  This means that the user is individually and reliably identified and tracked.

If we want to flag such cases, it should be a user option (and that's
besides the need to have code which detects them, see my other
message).

> Anopther one, common in istitutional email systems, is security: when I write to some university colleague, for examples, and they reply in html to me while citing my text-only email, I  see that in the cited email all plain text links have been converted to links where the text of the link is the plain text link that I had written, while the url of the link points to a shielding service intended to prevent users from following dangerous links.

Likewise here.  (And I expect these cases to be much harder to process
correctly, i.e. without too many false positives.)

> Eli, this is the crucial point where you have misunderstood the

> The misunderstanding is not about the Hermes agent in particular,

If I misunderstood the GNU standards, the standards need to be
clarified for such misunderstanding not to be possible.  My
understanding or misunderstanding is based on careful reading of
standards.texi and interpreting what it says in the context of this
and similar issues and decisions.

> Given a free program P1, whether it is ok for a GNU package to
> reference / recommend / promote / mention the program P1 _depends_ on
> whether P1 itself references / recommends / promotes / mentions
> nonfree programs in a significant way.

What if P1 communicates with or invokes or depends on a free program
P2, which in turn communicates with or invokes or depends on a free
program P3, etc. etc.?  Does this potentially unlimited chain of
dependencies also affect a GNU package that references / recommends /
promotes / mentions the program P1?  If it does, then I cannot find
any clear guidance for such cases.  All I see in the node "References"
is (1) a description if the immediate dependency on P1 (which in the
case of the Hermes agent is a free program), and (2) the following
text:

     Sometimes a program is free software in itself but depends on a
  nonfree platform in order to run.  For instance, it used to be the case
  that many Java programs depended on some nonfree Java libraries.  (See
  <https://www.gnu.org/philosophy/java-trap.html>.)  To recommend or
  promote such a program is to promote the other programs it needs;
  therefore, judge mentions of the former as if they were mentions of the
  latter.  For this reason, we were careful about listing Java programs in
  the Free Software Directory: we wanted to avoid promoting the nonfree
  Java libraries.

     Java no longer has this problem, but the general principle will
  remain the same: don't recommend, promote or legitimize programs or
  services whose use depends on running some nonfree software or
  dis-service.

This specifically talks about nonfree platforms or programs or
services, which is not the case in point: the Hermes agent is a free
program.  It also fails to mention the strict criteria for "recommend
or promote", about which you are now saying that a simple mentioning
is enough to be considered as "promotion"; the single example in the
text above says "depends", which is much stronger (the Hermes agent
does not "depend" on any of the nonfree sites or LLMs).  If the
situation with the chain of dependencies in the case of Hermes, and
any longer chain of dependencies, must be treated as forbidden, please
make sure standards.texi says that explicitly.  That is, for example,
if the case of dependencies like this:

  GNU package -> P1 -> P2 -> P3 -> P4 -> P5 -> P6 -> P7 -> nonfree

where each Pn is a free program, means such a GNU package violates the
GNU standards, please augment the text in standards.texi to make it
unequivocally clear.  Please also make very clear there that "->" in
the above diagram means _any_ reference in any part of the
corresponding program Pn or its documentation, even if there are
user-selectable alternatives which avoid ending up with "nonfree" at
the end.  Currently, such cases are left vaguely defined at best, so I
used my own understanding of the user's responsibility to configure
the dependencies so as to avoid nonfree stuff.  If this is incorrect,
it is not my fault, it's the fault of standards.texi's ambiguous and
incomplete wording.  It must be fixed ASAP.

After standards.texi is fixed, we can see what its updated guidance
means for GNU and nonGNU ELPA and for Emacs in general.

> Now I think I know what it was trying to say.  It was trying to state
> a condition for accepting packages, something like, "As long as foo.el
> offers to use at least one free alternative, it is ok, regardless of
> what nonfree alternatives it may also offer."  The same thing you
> were saying just now.

Yes, because in the absence of a specific clear guidance, this is how
we understood the policies.

> That crucially disagrees with the GNU Project's actual policy on
> references to nonfree programs.  Our policy is stricter than that.
> This misstatement needs to be clarified.

Please do, and let's take it from there.

Eli, you and the other maintainers and any circumstantial maintainer of
emacs should ask when something can be morally questionable or go against
the policies of the GNU project.

I know that sometimes your work overwhelms you and you're even capable of
changing a comma in another maintainer's package without consulting them
even though the package is tremendously active and willing to collaborate,
but as for moral issues and project policies, the most recommendable thing
is to ask, and I hope you share with me what I want to mean here with
"recommend." Cheers.

David

about every decision.  RMS appoints maintainers so that projects could
be developed without being critically dependent on asking for his

is redundant and serves no useful purpose.

> be developed without being critically dependent on asking for his
> guidance in each and every case.  We do ask when unsure, but in the
> case in point there was no such doubt.  When there's no doubt, asking
> is redundant and serves no useful purpose.

Content-Type: text/plain

Our regexp engine is using a backtracking approach, which has all kinds
of benefits but means that it does not enjoy the nice linear-time
complexity that theoretical CS says should apply to the problem of
regexp matching.

In practice this is usually not a problem: the time is almost always
linear anyway, and the backtracking approach has a fairly nice constant
factor, so all is well.  *Except* when it isn't: for those regexps that
can match the same string in many different ways (e.g. "a*a*a*" or
"(a*)*"), we hit the non-linear part of our algorithm which is typically
experienced by the end user as "Emacs froze" (because some font-lock
regexp bumped into a somewhat unusual line that hit that pathological
spot so the match takes minutes instead of a fraction of a second).

I have pushed to `scratch/regex-memoize` a patch which purports to fix
this problem by memoizing the failures during backtracking, so we get
back the linear-time complexity even for those nasty regexps.

I've been using a similar patch for a few years locally but it had
a fairly high cost in the "normal" case, so it seemed inappropriate for
`master`, but I have now refined the patch with enough "fastpath" that
the normal case is almost as fast as before in my tests:

I have found one test where I still see a 26% slowdown when running on
an ARM Cortex-A55 (a low-power in-order CPU), but in x86 CPUs the
slowdown is below 10% on all my tests (and for most tests there is
simply no measurable performance difference or a slight speed up,
except of course for those tests that bump into the pathological
behavior where the new code trounces the old one).

I'd be interested to hear feedback from people out there who may have
benchmarks of their own.  For the curious I attached the current patch.


=== Stefan

+/* **************** Memoization **********************************************
+   As we "all" known from our computation theory classes, regexps are wonderful
+   because we can convert them to NFA and then DFA to match them in O(n) using
+   a constant amount of space.  [ Where n is the size of the string.  ]
+
+   Sadly, practice is a bit different from theory:
+   - That "matching" is for the exact string, whereas here we need to see
+     if there exists a match for a prefix (re_match) or a substring (re_search)
+     of the string.
+   - We need to keep track of the match-beginning/end positions.
+   - We have backreferences.
+   - We have look ahead/behind.
+   - We need to know not just if a match exist but want to choose a paticular
+     match, according to greediness of the repetition operators and other rules.
+   - ...
+
+   Some of those aspects don't make too much difference, but some completely
+   break the implementation technique and algorithmic complexity.
+
+   Also, while converting RE->NFA is mostly O(m) [where m is the size of the
+   regexp], converting NFA->DFA is a painful O(2^m), which means that
+   matching the regexp via DFA is actually O(2^m + n) and the space needed
+   O(2^m).
+
+   Thompson's NFA simulates a DFA during the match without building the DFA
+   upfront, which gives a much better behavior: matching using the NFA that way
+   is O(m * n) in time and O(m) in space.
+
+   Of course, that's still theoretical and doesn't account for things like
+   backreferences.  In practice lots of regexp matchers, like this one
+   rely on backtracking, which tends to be fast when the first match is
+   the one we want and is easy to find, and accomodates all those regexp
+   extensions more easily.  Sadly, it's algorithmically horrible, like
+   O(2^n) in time and O(n) in space.  So here we try to recover Thompson's
+   NFA algorithmic behavior by memoization, following the same approach
+   as described in
+
+       Using Selective Memoization to Defeat Regular Expression
+       Denial of Service (ReDoS)
+       James C. Davis, Francisco Servant, and Dongyoon Lee
+       doi:10.1109/SP40001.2021.00032
+
+   on_failure_jump_smart: this one should disappear before we have to
+       worry about memoization.
+   on_failure_keep_string_jump: we don't want to memoize this one,
+       because we want it to be as fast as possible.  Sadly, this means
+       that we can still be O(n^2) in some cases where memoization would
+       reduce it to O(n), e.g. for "a*a*b".
+   on_failure_jump: currently this is used both for loops and non-loops,
+       whereas we'd ideally want to memoize only the loop ones.
+   on_failure_jump_loop:
+   on_failure_jump_nastyloop:
+   succeed_n:
+       We want to memoize those since they're part of loops by definition.  */
+
+#ifndef MEMOIZE_FAILURES
+# define MEMOIZE_FAILURES 1
+#endif
+
+#if MEMOIZE_FAILURES
+
+/* A simple type to keep a set of small integers in the form of a bitset.
+   We assume the small integers will always be positive,
+   and usually close to each other and close to 0.  */
+struct memo_bits {
+  unsigned char *bytes;
+  ptrdiff_t max;		/* In units of bytes.  */
+};
+
+static void
+memo_bits_free (struct memo_bits *bs)
+{
+  xfree (bs->bytes);
+}
+
+static bool
+memo_bits_get (struct memo_bits *bs, ptrdiff_t bit)
+{
+  ptrdiff_t byte_nb = bit / CHAR_BIT;
+  if (0 <= byte_nb && byte_nb < bs->max)
+    return bs->bytes[byte_nb] & (1 << (bit % CHAR_BIT));
+  else
+    return false;
+}
+
+static void
+memo_bits_set_noalloc (struct memo_bits *bs, ptrdiff_t bit)
+{
+  ptrdiff_t byte_nb = bit / CHAR_BIT;
+  eassert (0 <= byte_nb && byte_nb < bs->max);
+  eassert (!memo_bits_get (bs, bit));
+  unsigned char *byte = &bs->bytes[byte_nb];
+  *byte |= 1 << (bit % CHAR_BIT);
+  eassert (memo_bits_get (bs, bit));
+}
+
+#define MEMO_BITS_STEP (4 * sizeof (int))
+
+static void
+memo_bits_set (struct memo_bits *bs, ptrdiff_t bit)
+{
+  eassert (bit >= 0);
+  ptrdiff_t byte_nb = bit / CHAR_BIT;
+  if (byte_nb >= bs->max)
+    {
+      ptrdiff_t oldsize = bs->max;
+      ptrdiff_t added = max (oldsize, bs->max - byte_nb + 1);
+      bs->bytes = xrealloc (bs->bytes,
+			    oldsize + ROUNDUP (added, MEMO_BITS_STEP));
+      memset (bs->bytes + oldsize, 0, added);
+      bs->max += added;
+    }
+  memo_bits_set_noalloc (bs, bit);
+}
+
+static struct memo_bits
+memo_bits (ptrdiff_t first)
+{
+  int initial_size = 1 + first / CHAR_BIT;
+  unsigned char *bytes = xmalloc (ROUNDUP (initial_size, MEMO_BITS_STEP));
+  memset (bytes, 0, initial_size);
+  struct memo_bits bs = { bytes, initial_size };
+  memo_bits_set_noalloc (&bs, first);
+  return bs;
+}
+
+struct memo {
+  EMACS_INT past_failures;
+  ptrdiff_t max_offset;
+  struct memo_bits *fail_counters;
+  int nb_counters;
+  /* When a backref leads to failure, all the failures "sent up" while
+     backtracking (until we backtrack over the corresponding stop_memory)
+     can't be memoized because they depended on the state of register,
+     which we don't use as key to lookup the memo table.  */
+  unsigned backrefs;
+};
+
+static void
+memo_free (void *ptr)
+{
+  struct memo *memo = ptr;
+  if (memo->fail_counters)
+    {
+      for (int i = 0; i < memo->nb_counters; i++)
+	memo_bits_free (&memo->fail_counters[i]);
+      xfree (memo->fail_counters);
+    }
+  xfree (memo);
+}
+
+/* Every on_failure_jump operation occupies at least 3 bytes.  */
+#define MEMO_BYTES_PER_COUNTER 3
+
+static void
+memo_fail (struct memo *memo,
+	   struct re_pattern_buffer *bufp, re_char *pat, ptrdiff_t fail_offset)
+{
+  eassert (fail_offset >= 0);
+  if (memo->max_offset <= fail_offset)
+    memo->max_offset = fail_offset + 1;
+  if (!memo->fail_counters)
+    {
+      memo->past_failures++;
+      /* Tests suggest an "arbitrary" threshold of 2 failures per byte
+	 before deciding memoization might be worthwhile.  */
+      if ((memo->past_failures >> 1) > memo->max_offset)
+	{
+	  memo->nb_counters = bufp->used / MEMO_BYTES_PER_COUNTER;
+	  ptrdiff_t nbytes = sizeof (struct memo_bits) * memo->nb_counters;
+	  memo->fail_counters = xmalloc (nbytes);
+	  memset (memo->fail_counters, 0, nbytes);
+	  /* Setup an unwind_protect to free the memoization table.
+	     Use a copy of 'memo' so that the compiler can keep (parts
+	     of) it in registers.  */
+	  struct memo *memo_copy = xmalloc (sizeof (struct memo));
+	  *memo_copy = *memo;
+	  record_unwind_protect_ptr (memo_free, memo_copy);
+	}
+    }
+  else
+    {
+      if (memo->backrefs)
+	return;
+      ptrdiff_t bytecodepos = (pat - bufp->buffer) / MEMO_BYTES_PER_COUNTER;
+      eassert (0 <= bytecodepos && bytecodepos < memo->nb_counters);
+      struct memo_bits *counter = &memo->fail_counters[bytecodepos];
+      if (!counter->bytes)
+	{
+	  counter->max++;
+	  if (counter->max > memo->max_offset)
+	    {
+	      /* We have failed at this very same position of the
+		 pattern more times than we have visited chars, so
+		 there is room for memoization to to payoff!  */
+	      DEBUG_PRINT ("SETTING up memoization for %d!\n",
+			   bytecodepos);
+	      *counter = memo_bits (fail_offset);
+	      eassert (counter->bytes);
+	      /* FIXME: The other counters may have been inflated by the
+	         lack of memoization on the current node, so we could
+	         zero them out to avoid needlessly alllocating memo_bits
+	         for them?  */
+	    }
+	}
+      else
+	memo_bits_set (counter, fail_offset);
+    }
+}
+
+static bool
+memo_element (struct memo *memo, struct re_pattern_buffer *bufp,
+              re_char *pat, ptrdiff_t str)
+{
+  eassert (str >= 0);
+  if (memo->fail_counters)
+    {
+      ptrdiff_t bytecodepos = (pat - bufp->buffer) / MEMO_BYTES_PER_COUNTER;
+      eassert (0 <= bytecodepos && bytecodepos < memo->nb_counters);
+      struct memo_bits *counter = &memo->fail_counters[bytecodepos];
+      if (counter->bytes)
+	return memo_bits_get (counter, str);
+    }
+  return false;
+}
+#endif /* MEMOIZE_FAILURES */
+

I'd like to propose ebuild-mode for inclusion in NonGNU ELPA.

This collection of modes will help the user to efficiently write and
edit ebuilds, eclasses and other files that are specific to Gentoo,
a meta-distribution with various targets (GNU/Linux distribution,
prefixed environments in other operating systems, and integration
of other kernels and userlands like the BSDs or the GNU Hurd).

Ebuilds describe the build process and dependencies of a software
package to compile and install it automatically under the control of
a package manager.  They are simple text files based on Bash scripts.
Eclasses are comparable to libraries providing generic functions that
ebuilds can use by sourcing the eclass on request.

The package provides:
- ebuild-mode and ebuild-eclass-mode: major modes to edit the above
  two file types, with font-lock syntax highlighting, completion of
  package manager and eclass function names, KEYWORDS manipulation,
  creation of new ebuilds from a skeleton, and interfaces to Portage,
  pkgdev and pkgcheck.
- ebuild-repo-mode: minor mode for files in an ebuild repository;
  sets up some editing conventions like tab-width, fixes whitespace
  and updates copyright years on save.
- devbook-mode: editing the Gentoo Devmanual (DevBook XML).
- gentoo-newsitem-mode: editing GLEP 42 news items.
- glep-mode: editing Gentoo Linux Enhancement Proposals (GLEPs).
- ebuild-mode.texi: Texinfo manual.

Repository:
- Git clone: https://anongit.gentoo.org/git/proj/ebuild-mode.git
- Gitweb: https://gitweb.gentoo.org/proj/ebuild-mode.git/

Authors: Matthew Kennedy, Diego Petten=C3=B2, Christian Faulhammer, Ulrich =
M=C3=BCller
Maintainer: <emacs@gentoo.org>
Contents: multiple files
Version: 1.87 (tagged as ebuild-mode-1.87 in Git)
License: GNU General Public License, version 2 or any later version

Dependencies:
- GNU Emacs 26.3 or XEmacs 21.5.35
- no other dependencies on Emacs Lisp packages
- optionally uses tty-format (https://user42.tuxfamily.org/tty-format/)

The package byte-compiles without any errors or warnings and passes
all its tests on Emacs 26 to 31, Emacs from Git, and XEmacs 21.5.

ebuild-mode was first released in 2006 and is widely used by Gentoo
developers.  It is distributed in Gentoo as app-emacs/ebuild-mode
(and app-xemacs/ebuild-mode), and I have maintained it since 2007.

Any feedback about the package is welcome, in particular about any
changes necessary before inclusion in NonGNU ELPA.

Thanks in advance,
Ulrich

Hi,

Ulrich M=C3=BCller <ulm@gentoo.org> writes:

> I'd like to propose ebuild-mode for inclusion in NonGNU ELPA.
>
> This collection of modes will help the user to efficiently write and
> edit ebuilds, eclasses and other files that are specific to Gentoo,

> package to compile and install it automatically under the control of
> a package manager.  They are simple text files based on Bash scripts.
> Eclasses are comparable to libraries providing generic functions that
> ebuilds can use by sourcing the eclass on request.
>
> The package provides:
> - ebuild-mode and ebuild-eclass-mode: major modes to edit the above

> - gentoo-newsitem-mode: editing GLEP 42 news items.
> - glep-mode: editing Gentoo Linux Enhancement Proposals (GLEPs).
> - ebuild-mode.texi: Texinfo manual.

To be clear, this is supposed to be a single package including all of
these files?  I think that would be the right approach, but I just want
to be sure.

> Repository:
> - Git clone: https://anongit.gentoo.org/git/proj/ebuild-mode.git
> - Gitweb: https://gitweb.gentoo.org/proj/ebuild-mode.git/

The code looks good, my main points would be:

- In ebuild-mode.el to add an explicit an

  ;; Package-Requires: ((emacs "26.3"))

  pseudo header, so that package.el can pick up on the minimum version.

- You can drop all the :group annotations for the user options, since
  they follow a defgroup declaration.

- Some of the regular expressions seem fairly involved, I think it would
  be more readable in rx notation.  You can use the "xr" package to
  translate existing regular expressions to rx btw.

- If you don't want to write compatibility code for `static-if', you
  can also add a dependency on (compat "30").  This will only install
  the dependency if is actually necessary to do so.

- You have some trailing parentheses, like after the static-if
  definition.

- Using (kbd "C-e") instead of "\C-e" would be more conventional and
  what I think most users are used to if they read the source code.

- You have some instances where you build commands using something like

    (format "ebuild %s %s" file command)

  Shouldn't you wrap file in `shell-quote-argument', in case it includes
  spaces or some meta-charachters?

- If you want to exclude any files from the tarball, add an .elpaignore
  file that describes what files to exclude.

Other than that, I don't think there are any issues.  The package builds
cleanly (I've attached a tarball I managed to build locally), so I'll
add it to nongnu.git as soon as I am sure that you want everything in a
single package.

On Thu, Oct 1, 2026 at 12:48=E2=80=AFAM Richard Stallman <rms@gnu.org> wrot=
e:

>   > That is true, but since the Hermes agent is not part of Emacs and is
>   > not a GNU program, we cannot be held responsible for what it does.
>
> Indeed, we are not responsible for what it does.
>
> We are responsible for deciding properly whether to reference /
> promote / recommend / mention hermes.el, and what the Hermes agent
> does is part of the basis for that decision.
>

In this world, who is responsible for checking how the (non-GNU)
software package Hermes (and its documentation, which seems especially
relevant here) doesn't change over time, on any platform?

As a concrete example, it seems readily apparent that Hermes (slogan:
'The Agent That Grows With You') doesn't _today_ support every
platform Emacs does, but easily could (and probably will) support some
platforms that Emacs does (such as Android or Haiku). Taking Android
as an example, it's overwhelmingly likely that Hermes could quickly
add support for the platform without support for local models, while
support for local models on Android is being very actively pursued,
and is highly likely in the next couple years.

This example is *perhaps* a little extreme, but there are a large
variety of packages with a huge swath of such "potential transitive
responsibility' concerns. Would hermes.el become acceptible for
listing on ELPA only on some platforms? Would that change back and
forth as the capacity of Hermes itself changed? Or if the documentation
of Hermes (not hermes.el) changed? Would the creation of a fully-libre
remote-accessible LLM *somewhere* retroactively make hermes.el more
palatable to ELPA?

I suspect that I'm misunderstanding what is being proposed, but it seems
to me like I'm not the only one here with that interpretation. What am I
missing?

Thanks,
~Chad

>> Other than that, I don't think there are any issues.  The package builds

>> add it to nongnu.git as soon as I am sure that you want everything in a

The ELPA build server will look back in the history for the last commit
if can find that bumps the ";; Version:" header in the main file.  So if
you don't bump the version after pushing the changes, ELPA will not
include them in the release tarball until you do eventually cut a new
release.

I wrote as a "pitch". Even more after you first reduced it to a simple
"convenience vs freedom" argument. I'm not an english native speaker,
and I may be not getting all the information, but my feeling is real.

Also, I think we owe computers to generals and salesmen, who made
those bets and won and changed the world.

And maybe we should start to say "Software Freedom" or something like
that, now that "Unqualified Freedom" is in retreat in the whole world,
and we should avoid confusing both, because one is more important than
the other.

I've seen Firefox, one of the most important assets of Software
Freedom, go into the trash can while you watched. It has infinitesimal
presence in the biggest computer park in the hands of users:
phones. But it seems to be more important if a busy father makes his
shopping with nonfree JS to save some time.

Now AI will be the zillionth transfer of wealth from the poor to the
rich, and it will be EVEN BIGGER if the poor don't use it. Because for
$20 a month to an USA based company, you get a translator to most
languages of the world. It can of course code like a monster. It can
fix your computer (the software side) faster and better than anyone,
which is great if you don't really know how to. It can guide you to
learn about anything, at your pace, at your level. Is not just the
"programmer productivity" or the homework for the kids. All the other
things account for much more, specially for poor people. Not bad for a
bullshit generator. Now that's a pitch.

I'm sorry if this was harsh, but the fact is I feel harsh. And I will
be taking my quite small activism and contributions elsewhere, where I
see it caters to the needs of the needy.

I wrote each letter by hand in emacs, and pasted to thunderbird,
though i felt tempted to write them with Claude.

On 9/27/2026 6:47 PM, Richard Stallman wrote:
> Making our software better than "competitors" in a practical sense is
> a secondary goal for us.  Sure, we want to do that -- but that is not
> the purpose of developing GNU.

I agree wholeheartedly with this. If practicality and keeping up with 
the Joneses were my goal, I'd be using VS Code already. It too is a 
highly-extensible programming text editor available for no cost on 
multiple platforms, and it has the added benefit of its development 
being funded by one of the richest corporations in the world.

The Emacs community, and the larger GNU/FSF communities, are important. 
I credit my time as maintainer of one small corner of Emacs for showing 
me proof that a better world is possible. Even aside from the debates 
about copyright, plagiarism, and SaaSS, I'm concerned about the damage 
we could cause to the Emacs *community* by embracing LLMs. If nothing 
else, I hope Emacs, GNU, and the FSF will move carefully here to protect 
the community we've built.

Of course, since GNU Emacs is built to give users freedom to use, 
modify, and extend it as they see fit, there's nothing we could do to 
prevent someone from integrating LLMs into their Emacs. However, that 
doesn't mean we need to embrace it ourselves.

On 9/23/2026 12:54 PM, Tyler Smith wrote:
> On Sat, Sep 19, 2026, at 12:25 PM, Jim Porter wrote:
>>
>> Sorry, I got that backwards. You should *disable* 'shr-fill-text' to
>> support changing the window size, since then EWW will use
>> 'visual-line-mode' instead.
> 
> Just a quick note to let you know that I'm still interested in helping with this if I can. But I don't know enough to weigh in on best approaches for the actual solution :)

Since no one else seems to have an opinion on this, I guess I'll make a 
decision. :)

There are two things to decide on: first, how should the hook work? I 
think Stefan's suggestion is reasonable:

> Another option is to store the DOM in a var and let the hook functions
> change it by side effect.

As he mentions in his message, it's not the most pure-functionally 
elegant, but it's probably simpler. EWW already stores the DOM in the 
:dom property of 'eww-data'. Another benefit I see with this is that the 
hook can be used to do other things as well.

The second question is when the hook should run. If we go with modifying 
the DOM by overwriting :dom in 'eww-data', then we probably want to run 
the hook shortly after we parse the HTML, and (I think) also after we 
call 'eww-readable-dom'. I'd recommend doing this in 'eww-display-html' 
and 'eww-readable', since those are the places we parse the HTML. (You'd 
have to move the '(plist-put eww-data :dom document)' call in 
'eww-display-document' to those functions too, but I think that's a good 
idea because it consolidates where we write to 'eww-data'.)

It'd also be nice to call this before we display other content types. I 
think the relevant functions are 'eww-display-pdf', 'eww-display-image', 
and 'eww-display-raw'.

As for the name of the hook, I'd go with 'eww-before-render-hook' for 
symmetry with the existing 'eww-after-render-hook'.

Of course, if you or anyone else have different ideas, I'm all ears. I 
don't have a strong preference here, and am really just making a 
decision so a decision gets made. :)

dangerous links so you can't tell any more and have no other recourse

link can still be extracted from the mangled link without contacting the
"claimed to be secure" man-in-middle.

> The Emacs community, and the larger GNU/FSF communities, are important. 
> I credit my time as maintainer of one small corner of Emacs for showing 
> me proof that a better world is possible. Even aside from the debates 
> about copyright, plagiarism, and SaaSS, I'm concerned about the damage 
> we could cause to the Emacs *community* by embracing LLMs. If nothing 
> else, I hope Emacs, GNU, and the FSF will move carefully here to protect 
> the community we've built.

Those are your opinions, and we should respect them.  Other members of
the community have other opinions, and we must respect them as well.
But we cannot possibly change our actions based on what this or that
member of the community feels or believes.  We must have a policy that
is defined explicitly and unequivocally to guide our actions in cases
such as this one.  This is what this and related discussions are
about.  They are not about personal feelings of anyone.

> Of course, since GNU Emacs is built to give users freedom to use, 
> modify, and extend it as they see fit, there's nothing we could do to 
> prevent someone from integrating LLMs into their Emacs. However, that 
> doesn't mean we need to embrace it ourselves.

The issue at hand is not whether to embrace some software, it is
whether it is legitimate for an Emacs or ELPA package to allow users
to integrate LLMs into their Emacs.  That has nothing to do with
embracing, it has to do with the limits of what can be on ELPA.  Let's
not replace practical goals of these discussions with emotional ones.

> Stéphane Marks <shipmints@gmail.com> writes:
> 
> > This also begs this hypothetical: if Hermes (not hermes.el) currently was compliant, recommending/steering only
> > to LLMs currently GNU acceptable (I'm not arguing ATM that is is or isn't), and then someone on the Hermes team
> > changed it to recommending something unacceptable (or merely objectionable?), is the Emacs team responsible
> > for such ongoing accounting of downstream dependencies?
> 
> As alternative: does it suffice to act if someone actively brings the
> problem to their attention?
> 
> In that case there could be at least four actions to react to a report:
> 
> - investigate the report and find that the problem isn’t as bad as it seems
> - get in contact with Hermes and ask them not to do what’s unacceptable
> - change hermes.el or patch Hermes Agent such that it stops doing it
> - remove hermes.el from elpa

The 2nd and the 3rd alternatives are basically tong-in-cheek: they
will rarely if ever materialize.

Removing a package after it has been on ELPA is IMNSHO out of
question: it leaves such a bad taste with the author that there's a
real risk for that author (and others, perhaps) never again coming to
us.

We really should think some more about the authors of the packages
when we bring up such proposals.  They are not bots, they are real
people with real feelings.  Put yourself in their shoes, then talk.

Eli Zaretskii <eliz@gnu.org> writes:

> The 2nd and the 3rd alternatives are basically tong-in-cheek: they
> will rarely if ever materialize.

They are common practice in fully free distros.

Those may not be Emacs, but they show that patching out problematic
stuff is a real option.

> Removing a package after it has been on ELPA is IMNSHO out of
> question: it leaves such a bad taste with the author that there's a
> real risk for that author (and others, perhaps) never again coming to
> us.

If we cannot remove packages from elpa, we must be much more careful
which packages are accepted in elpa, than when we can remove packages
when their situation changes.

And if elpa includes packages that violate the GNU principles, other
people may leave, because that also leaves a bad taste.

> They are not bots, they are real people with real feelings. Put
> yourself in their shoes, then talk.

I am a package author myself. I=E2=80=99ve also experienced packages being
removed, though not from elpa, but from distros and from melpa.

And I know the consequences of never being able to remove a package.

Best wishes,
Arne

I'm not sure if the PGTK version of this patch is necessary. In my tests on
KDE Plasma the font struct returned by this call in pgtkterm.c

      struct font *font =3D font_for_underline_metrics (s);

always has font->underline_thickness =3D=3D 1. The underline is scaled nice=
ly,
i.e. it is not too thin on my 185 DPI screen. I'm using a system scaling of
150%; I also tried 200%.

I tested on Wayland, XWayland (by setting GDK_BACKEND=3Dx11), and on an X11
session. No difference.

By the way, it would be helpful if the patches you post were complete, i.e.
based on the Git version of the code, and not on top of code including
patches posted earlier in this thread.

Eli Zaretskii <eliz@gnu.org> writes:

>> > The 2nd and the 3rd alternatives are basically tong-in-cheek: they
>> > will rarely if ever materialize.
>>=20
>> They are common practice in fully free distros.
>
> Maybe because they provide both the package and its dependencies.

They also patch out unfree online resources which provide access to
stuff outside the distro.

>> If we cannot remove packages from elpa, we must be much more careful
>> which packages are accepted in elpa, than when we can remove packages
>> when their situation changes.
>
> Yes, and that's my main point.  We must test all those conditions up
> front, and if the conditions can change thereafter, we are screwed.

That then excludes any package that uses an online service whose license
may change.

That=E2=80=99s why I do not think that it=E2=80=99s viable to promise that =
every package
that got into elpa once will stay there forever.

Though I think removing a package should be a measure of last resort. In
the vast majority of cases changes to the package should enable curing
the problem, just like they can if the URL of a service it uses changes.

>> I am a package author myself. I=E2=80=99ve also experienced packages bei=
ng
>> removed, though not from elpa, but from distros and from melpa.
>>=20
>> And I know the consequences of never being able to remove a package.
>
> Well, then I guess our sensitivity levels differ.

Or our view of consequences. I am still annoyed that Debian pushed the
Hurd out of the official debian ports while I was contributing. So it=E2=80=
=99s
not like I don=E2=80=99t know that having a package removed hurts.

I just consider it worse to not be able to trust elpa not to steer me
into dependency on proprietary software.

Which is not just theoretical: I stumbled over that because I looked for
free (as in freedom) LLMs to try their performance, and hermes looked
like it would enable this (the name sounding like it=E2=80=99s independent =
from
the big LLM companies and being mentioned in the emacs lists that it is
compatible with GNU principles). If I hadn=E2=80=99t clicked the website fi=
rst
and then checked the licensing, I would have started to depend on
Hermes=E2=80=99 proprietary platform for trying to find free LLMs.

And that was just from seeing the name in the list here. Seeing it via
elpa (named "gnu" in package-list-packages) would have misled me into
thinking that it=E2=80=99s been vetted by GNU as preserving Software Freedo=
m.

Best wishes,
Arne

ohne es zu merken.

Dear Eli,

I heard you will wait for standards.texi to updated. Maybe it is not 
part of this thread. Yet I was thinking you will first understand what 
should be the policy in order to act.

On 2026-10-02 09:32, Eli Zaretskii wrote:
> Removing a package after it has been on ELPA is IMNSHO out of
> question: it leaves such a bad taste with the author that there's a
> real risk for that author (and others, perhaps) never again coming to
> us.

That author get pissed off is human and understandable. However, it 
would not happen in the first place if author would be reminded of GNU 
coding standards and package evaluated against it.

So it is responsibility of managers of ELPA to do that.

In addition GNU doesn't have policy on accepting LLM generated packages, 
and hermes.el is LLM generated package. And that has not been resolved. 
Together with the other author's package codex-ide as well that is also 
purposefully made for SaaSS.

> We really should think some more about the authors of the packages
> when we bring up such proposals.  They are not bots, they are real
> people with real feelings.  Put yourself in their shoes, then talk.

I agree that people have feelings. That is why I am raising the question 
early, before more packages are accepted, rather than after. The 
question is not whether the author has feelings; it is whether the 
project will apply its own standards. If the standards are applied from 
the beginning, the difficult conversation happens before the package is 
accepted, not after.

Author wish to contributes to GNU and that is commendable. And first 
thing to establish is if such package conforms to GNU standards. GNU did 
not come to author, author came to GNU. That means all contributors are 
welcome within boundaries of GNU standards.

-- 
Jean Louis

> not? is "rendo-shrimp.de" also a URL, and if so, why? what about

> textsec.el currently decides whether it's a URL by looking at the
> return value of url-generic-parse-url.

I use here thing-at-point which also returns nil on such urls, but it
can be tweaked to return such urls with 

    (let ((thing-at-point-beginning-of-url-regexp "www\\."))
        (thing-at-point 'url))

But I am not sure it is the right thing to do (I have reverted this
change for now)

Francesco Potort=C3=AC <pot@potorti.it> writes:

>>[...] "www.rendo-shrimp.de" is an
>>url (even if abbreviated), so in such case why is the link (very) differe=
nt? I mean if
>>"www.rendo-shrimp.de" is a valid (and safe) url why using something else?
>
> If I understand your question correctly, I have observed two cases when p=
eople do that.
>
> One, common in publicity email, newsletters and so on, is gathering
> user statistics: the real url is unique per user, pointing to a
> tracking system which provides user statistics.  This means that the
> user is individually and reliably identified and tracked.
>
> Anopther one, common in istitutional email systems, is security: when
> I write to some university colleague, for examples, and they reply in
> html to me while citing my text-only email, I see that in the cited
> email all plain text links have been converted to links where the text
> of the link is the plain text link that I had written, while the url
> of the link points to a shielding service intended to prevent users
> from following dangerous links.

Thanks for these infos, this reinforce the idea of not clicking blindly
on urls in emails, this is why I want to present the underlying url to
helm users when they C-x C-f on such urls with a textsec warning or not,
see attached screenshot.

 <mailto:emacs-devel-request@gnu.org?subject=subscribe>
X-List-Received-Date: Fri, 02 Oct 2026 19:38:45 -0000

I think emacs could benefit greatly from a PDF writing/export
capability, so I started to write a library to do that. The first user
of the library is a function to export a buffer as PDF.

There are missing things, like CCF fonts or bitmap fonts, and a
drawing API, and many more.

The bulk of the work is the subsetting and embedding of fonts, which
was painful to write and more painful to read, and I don't think is
production ready. In retrospective probably using Cairo or something
for this part would be better, instead of building it on pure lisp as
I did.

The library is not complete, although it can generate documents such
as this, embedding 20 font subsets to display so many beautiful scripts, 
correctly marked to allow text discovery and copy/paste:

https://github.com/cpardotortosa/epdf/blob/28072c60b78416020485d4412ca5bf1b8d52609d/hello.pdf

I find that absolutely gorgeous :)

The concept works, in case someone would like to take it on.

https://github.com/cpardotortosa/epdf

> Of course, since GNU Emacs is built to give users freedom to use,
> modify, and extend it as they see fit, there's nothing we could do to
> prevent someone from integrating LLMs into their Emacs.  However, that
> doesn't mean we need to embrace it ourselves.

The issue I have with this is that it moves the goal from "defend
Free Software" to "defend against generative AI".

The Free Software movement's goals are largely aligned with many other
social movements, yet to avoid fragmenting our community, the FSF has
been very careful to try and stick to software freedom (and let
individual members combine this with any other issue they like).

I'd rather leave the fight against slop to other groups, even if there
might be a lot of overlap between that group and ours.


=== Stefan

> The second question is when the hook should run. If we go with modifying the
> DOM by overwriting :dom in 'eww-data', then we probably want to run the hook
> shortly after we parse the HTML, and (I think) also after we call
> 'eww-readable-dom'. I'd recommend doing this in 'eww-display-html' and
> 'eww-readable', since those are the places we parse the HTML. (You'd have to
> move the '(plist-put eww-data :dom document)' call in 'eww-display-document'
> to those functions too, but I think that's a good idea because it
> consolidates where we write to 'eww-data'.)

Doing it at two places is OK, but as a general rule it's best if we run
such hooks at only a single place.
Also, AFAICT, when `eww-readable` is called, we've already rendered with
`eww-display-html`, so it doesn't seem right.

> It'd also be nice to call this before we display other content
> types. I think the relevant functions are 'eww-display-pdf',
> 'eww-display-image', and 'eww-display-raw'.

But these don't have a DOM on which to work, no?
It might be OK for those functions to run a before-render hook, but it
wouldn't be able to assume it can work on a DOM, so I think it would
naturally be a different hook than the one we're discussing.

IOW, I think I'd add a hook inside `eww-display-document`, run just
after setting the `:dom` property (plus maybe add a `*-before-render-*`
hook to `eww-render`).


=== Stefan

ps-print.el is in Emacs for a very long time, but its significant
disadvantage is that it cannot support non-ASCII text except Latin-1,
not without a lot of non-trivial tinkering, installing specialized
fonts, etc., and even then some characters are impossible to print.
Given that Emacs has all the machinery to lay out and show any text,
using that for producing printable documents is a natural idea.

Hello,


the systemd unit for emacs server (etc/emacs.service) is launched under
any user, including the system users. This means when the emacs.service
is enabled, under the GNOME login screen, there is a running Emacs,
compiling the elisp into native code and storing the objects to
/var/lib/gdm3/.emacs.d .

I think it would be nice to add an ExecCondition=3D option to the unit
file, preventing start of Emacs at least in obviously wrong cases. The
attached patch inhibits the start if $HOME is in /var or /run .

Regards,
--=20
Jindrich Makovicka

--=-c6uApjP45cVedywPkTHW

Stefan Monnier [01/Oct 10:02am -04] wrote:
> Our regexp engine is using a backtracking approach, which has all kinds
> of benefits but means that it does not enjoy the nice linear-time
> complexity that theoretical CS says should apply to the problem of
> regexp matching.
>
> In practice this is usually not a problem: the time is almost always
> linear anyway, and the backtracking approach has a fairly nice constant
> factor, so all is well.  *Except* when it isn't: for those regexps that
> can match the same string in many different ways (e.g. "a*a*a*" or
> "(a*)*"), we hit the non-linear part of our algorithm which is typically
> experienced by the end user as "Emacs froze" (because some font-lock
> regexp bumped into a somewhat unusual line that hit that pathological
> spot so the match takes minutes instead of a fraction of a second).
>
> I have pushed to `scratch/regex-memoize` a patch which purports to fix
> this problem by memoizing the failures during backtracking, so we get
> back the linear-time complexity even for those nasty regexps.
>
> I've been using a similar patch for a few years locally but it had
> a fairly high cost in the "normal" case, so it seemed inappropriate for
> `master`, but I have now refined the patch with enough "fastpath" that
> the normal case is almost as fast as before in my tests:
>
> I have found one test where I still see a 26% slowdown when running on
> an ARM Cortex-A55 (a low-power in-order CPU), but in x86 CPUs the
> slowdown is below 10% on all my tests (and for most tests there is
> simply no measurable performance difference or a slight speed up,
> except of course for those tests that bump into the pathological
> behavior where the new code trounces the old one).
>
> I'd be interested to hear feedback from people out there who may have
> benchmarks of their own.  For the curious I attached the current patch.

Nice work.  ISTM that avoiding those freezes might be worth some
slowdown in other cases.

This might be a na=C3=AFve question, but could we first scan a regexp and s=
ee
if there are any back references, and if not, not use the backtracking
approach at all?

--=20
Sean Whitton

On 10/2/2026 9:05 PM, Stefan Monnier via Emacs development discussions. 
wrote:
> Also, AFAICT, when `eww-readable` is called, we've already rendered with
> `eww-display-html`, so it doesn't seem right.

'eww-readable' reloads the page, re-parsing the cached HTML into a 
s-expr and (by default) adds a new entry in the history (for the 
back/forward commands). The only thing it *doesn't* do is re-fetch the 
document over HTTP. I think we'd need to call the hook in this case, 
unless we make more sweeping changes to how 'eww-readable' works.

>> It'd also be nice to call this before we display other content
>> types. I think the relevant functions are 'eww-display-pdf',
>> 'eww-display-image', and 'eww-display-raw'.
> 
> But these don't have a DOM on which to work, no?
> It might be OK for those functions to run a before-render hook, but it
> wouldn't be able to assume it can work on a DOM, so I think it would
> naturally be a different hook than the one we're discussing.

Right. I'm thinking about how we can add a new hook called at the right 
time that can do more than *just* transform the DOM. That way we don't 
proliferate many special-purpose hooks in EWW.

Like I mentioned though, I don't feel that strongly about this and was 
just trying to pick an option so we could move forward.

> IOW, I think I'd add a hook inside `eww-display-document`, run just
> after setting the `:dom` property (plus maybe add a `*-before-render-*`
> hook to `eww-render`).

If we do this, then we could name the 'eww-display-document' hook (or 
wherever it ends up in the code) 'eww-dom-content-loaded-hook' to match 
the existing Javascript event: 
<https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Document/DOMContentLoaded_event>.

Jindrich Makovicka <makovick@gmail.com> writes:

> Hello,

Hi,

> the systemd unit for emacs server (etc/emacs.service) is launched under
> any user, including the system users. This means when the emacs.service
> is enabled, under the GNOME login screen, there is a running Emacs,
> compiling the elisp into native code and storing the objects to
> /var/lib/gdm3/.emacs.d .

Can you explain why this would occur?  Isn't that a system configuration
mistake if you enable the Emacs deamon for a system service?

> I think it would be nice to add an ExecCondition= option to the unit
> file, preventing start of Emacs at least in obviously wrong cases. The
> attached patch inhibits the start if $HOME is in /var or /run .
>
> Regards,
> -- 
> Jindrich Makovicka
>
> From 4a88ca705456d03b4d3f1e53413dc0e59e1884a6 Mon Sep 17 00:00:00 2001
> From: Jindrich Makovicka <makovick@gmail.com>
> Date: Fri, 18 Sep 2026 19:24:21 +0200
> Subject: [PATCH] emacs.service: Avoid starting emacs server for system users
>
> Systemd does not distinguish between regular users and system users like
> gdm3 under which the GNOME display manager runs. This means emacs
> daemon (including native compilation) runs uselessly under the login
> screen.
>
> Augment the systemd unit with an ExecCondition= sanity check for a home
> directory, excluding /run and /var.
> ---
>  etc/emacs.service | 4 ++++
>  1 file changed, 4 insertions(+)
>
> diff --git a/etc/emacs.service b/etc/emacs.service
> index 809c49cdbc5..91d994eff73 100644
> --- a/etc/emacs.service
> +++ b/etc/emacs.service
> @@ -10,6 +10,10 @@ Documentation=info:emacs man:emacs(1) https://gnu.org/software/emacs/
>  Type=notify
>  ExecStart=emacs --fg-daemon
>  
> +# Do not run emacs for system users with $HOME in /var or /run
> +# Allow /var/home for immutable systems
> +ExecCondition=/bin/sh -c 'case "$1" in /var/home/*) exit 0 ;; /var/*|/run/*) exit 1 ;; esac' -- %h
> +
>  # Emacs will exit with status 15 after having received SIGTERM, which
>  # is the default "KillSignal" value systemd uses to stop services.
>  SuccessExitStatus=15

>     A running Emacs session has a single, privileged point.

I think we're trying too hard: "session" here just gives the wrong
impression (as if that point was the same for the whole session).
IMO, there's nothing really special about point being more unique than the
value of any variable or the current buffer or the selected window,
...

AFAIK "the" point is just the buffer point of the current buffer.

But your change explicitly introduced this "There is only ever one
point" idea, so I assume you had a good reason to insist on it being
unique.  Not knowing that reason, my suggestions probably wouldn't be
very helpful.



=== Stefan

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > If we cannot remove packages from elpa, we must be much more careful
  > which packages are accepted in elpa, than when we can remove packages
  > when their situation changes.

We must be able remove packages if we accepted them based on the wrong
criteria and the problem is grave.  We ought to apologize for such
mistakes -- but we need to correct them.

We should care about contributors' feelings, but
Emacs does not exist mainly for its contributors' feelings.
We all want to make Emacs practically better,
but above all we must make sure Emacs leads users to have freedom
and to value freedom.

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > Of course, since GNU Emacs is built to give users freedom to use, 
  > modify, and extend it as they see fit, there's nothing we could do to 
  > prevent someone from integrating LLMs into their Emacs. However, that 
  > doesn't mean we need to embrace it ourselves.

That is true, of course -- but it slightly mis-states the issue at
hand.  To correct slightly the point Stefan made in his reply, this
text quoted above changes the issue from "stand against nonfree
software" to "stand against LLMs."

We don't reject LLMs on principle.  We do reject freedom-denying LLMs
on principle, along with other freedom-denying computing technology.
Given a useful, free LLM, we would have no a priori objection to it.

We are temporarily rejecting code made by LLMs, but that is not a
moral judgment.  It is because we do not know how that affects
copylefting the code.

Stefan Monnier via "Emacs development discussions." [03/Oct 10:30pm -04] wrote:
>>     A running Emacs session has a single, privileged point.
>
> I think we're trying too hard: "session" here just gives the wrong
> impression (as if that point was the same for the whole session).
> IMO, there's nothing really special about point being more unique than the
> value of any variable or the current buffer or the selected window,
> ...
>
> AFAIK "the" point is just the buffer point of the current buffer.
>
> But your change explicitly introduced this "There is only ever one
> point" idea, so I assume you had a good reason to insist on it being
> unique.  Not knowing that reason, my suggestions probably wouldn't be
> very helpful.

It's now

    A running Emacs session has a single instance of point.

at Eli's suggestion.

I think that the perspective in the e-mail from Richard would be helpful
to new Lisp programmers.  The idea of saying "point" not "the point"
clicked more firmly into place in my own head upon reading it -- it had
seemed like an arbitrary style rule, but now it doesn't.
I wanted to try to capture this somehow.

>From cace1cc48a78630ae715b1bdc0d90defc630be16 Mon Sep 17 00:00:00 2001
From: zdn <zhaodaniu1@gmail.com>

Subject: [PATCH] Support scaling of strike-through, overline, and underline
 for face.

* src/xdisp.c (syms_of_xdisp): Add variable
underline-text-scaling-p, overline-text-scaling-p, and
strike-through-text-scaling-p, to control whether text scale with
text scaling when drawn.

* src/w32term.c (w32_draw_glyph_string, w32_draw_underwave): Use
font->underline_thickness as the scaled thickness for
strike-through, overline, and underlines.

* src/xterm.c (x_draw_underwave): Add new argument 'thickness'.
(x_draw_glyph_string): Rework.

* src/pgtkterm.c (pgtk_draw_underwave): Add new argument 'thickness'.
(pgtk_draw_glyph_string): Rework.

Co-authored-by: Elias Gabriel Perez <eg642616@gmail.com>

>> Also, AFAICT, when `eww-readable` is called, we've already rendered with
>> `eww-display-html`, so it doesn't seem right.
> 'eww-readable' reloads the page, re-parsing the cached HTML into a s-expr
> and (by default) adds a new entry in the history (for the back/forward
> commands).  The only thing it *doesn't* do is re-fetch the document over
> HTTP.  I think we'd need to call the hook in this case, unless we make more
> sweeping changes to how 'eww-readable' works.

I see.  Then we need to be more careful about how we define and document
the hook so it's clear when it should(n't) be run and what data it can
expect to find in which variables.

> Right.  I'm thinking about how we can add a new hook called at the right time
> that can do more than *just* transform the DOM.  That way we don't
> proliferate many special-purpose hooks in EWW.

I get the vague impression that these are two conflicting requirements.

> Like I mentioned though, I don't feel that strongly about this and was
> just trying to pick an option so we could move forward.

FWIW, I don't feel strongly about it either, nor have enough experience
with EWW to have a good intuition for which options would be most useful.

>From 2d6dc2083dcad3603afe8d5f3010a3d5486b13e2 Mon Sep 17 00:00:00 2001
From: Zach Shaftel <zach@shaf.tel>
Date: Mon, 5 Oct 2026 18:18:59 -0400
Subject: [PATCH] Improve comment in lisp-mode-syntax-propertize-rules

* lisp/emacs-lisp/lisp-mode.el
(lisp-mode-syntax-propertize-rules): Describe the purpose of
the first rule.
---
 lisp/emacs-lisp/lisp-mode.el | 5 ++++-
 1 file changed, 4 insertions(+), 1 deletion(-)

diff --git a/lisp/emacs-lisp/lisp-mode.el b/lisp/emacs-lisp/lisp-mode.el
index 2778b7f53cf..8a559c718f6 100644
--- a/lisp/emacs-lisp/lisp-mode.el
+++ b/lisp/emacs-lisp/lisp-mode.el
@@ -87,7 +87,10 @@ lisp-mode-syntax-table
 (eval-and-compile
   (defconst lisp-mode-syntax-propertize-rules
     (syntax-propertize-precompile-rules
-     ;; Give entire |multiple escape| sections symbol syntax.
+     ;; Give entire multiple escape sections symbol syntax.  Without
+     ;; this, `forward-sexp' and co. treat symbols| like |this as three
+     ;; expressions, and `lisp-mode-symbol-regexp' won't capture escape
+     ;; sections at all.
      ((rx "|" (+ (or (seq (syntax escape) "|") (not "|"))) "|")
       (0 (and (not (ppss-comment-or-string-start (syntax-ppss)))
               (string-to-syntax "_"))))

I use vc-annotate a lot to dig into the history of code I'm working on,
typically with vc-annotate-revision-previous-to-line and
vc-annotate-revision-at-line, but often, I go too far and would like to
back up a few jumps.

The patch attached adds to vc-annotate.el:
1. vc-annotate-revision-history -- a buffer local variable holding the
revspecs of the revisions visited.
2. vc-annotate-undo-warp-revision, bound to "C-/", which warps to the car
of the above list
3. vc-annotate-update-history, a function to maintain the above list.

vc-annotate-warp revision is modified to call vc-annotate-update-history
just before the warp happens.

Properly, vc-annotate-revision-history should be cleared when vc-annotate
is invoked on a file, but I haven't dealt with that yet -- I figure there's
time to do that while I get comments from the community.

--Peter
