On 10/4/2026 8:51 PM, Richard Stallman wrote:
> [[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
> [[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
> [[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]
> 
>    > Of course, since GNU Emacs is built to give users freedom to use,
>    > modify, and extend it as they see fit, there's nothing we could do to
>    > prevent someone from integrating LLMs into their Emacs. However, that
>    > doesn't mean we need to embrace it ourselves.
> 
> That is true, of course -- but it slightly mis-states the issue at
> hand.  To correct slightly the point Stefan made in his reply, this
> text quoted above changes the issue from "stand against nonfree
> software" to "stand against LLMs."
> 
> We don't reject LLMs on principle.  We do reject freedom-denying LLMs
> on principle, along with other freedom-denying computing technology.
> Given a useful, free LLM, we would have no a priori objection to it.
> 
> We are temporarily rejecting code made by LLMs, but that is not a
> moral judgment.  It is because we do not know how that affects
> copylefting the code.

My concern isn't exactly a moral one (though I do also have moral 
concerns with LLMs, and am unconvinced that it's possible to resolve 
these while keeping the "Large" in "Large Language Model"). I'm more 
immediately concerned with how LLMs impact the ability to maintain 
communities, which I feel is the most critical piece of Emacs and 
GNU/FSF as a whole. Hence, I see this as mainly a practical problem.

LLMs have unfortunately made it easier for people to produce large 
volumes of plausible output that they don't fully understand, both 
burdening maintainers and undermining LLM users' ability to develop 
their skills. The LLMs of course don't understand anything at all, but 
have been fine-tuned to produce pleasing answers and to function as a 
replacement of human social interaction and expertise.

I've already had to deal with bad behavior brought on by overzealous LLM 
users in other software communities and have seen the beginnings of it 
appear on the Emacs mailing lists. Here and elsewhere, this issue seems 
to be getting worse, not better, which has made me reconsider where we 
ought to draw the line. Are LLM-related packages in ELPA a wise idea? 
I'm not so sure anymore.

I'd hate to see our decisions push away thoughtful contributors who 
value the community built here over the years. I don't feel sure enough 
to stake out a definite position on the immediate issue of ELPA packages 
here, though as mentioned, I'm increasingly worried. I chiefly wanted to 
share my concerns about these second-order harms while the Emacs 
community is still generally healthy.

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > On the other hand, Gmail is so popular that it's not as though we're 
  > *promoting* it to users who might not be aware. For better or worse, 
  > everyone who'd read the Gnus manual already knows about Gmail.

That is true.  "Pretend Gmail does not exist" is not obligatory,
and I would guess it is not a very effective way of fighting back.

  > However, I don't see anything in the manual about 
  > configuring to use OAuth or "less-secure" authentication, so it's not as 
  > helpful for this goal as it could be.

Since (according to your message) configuring that way involves
running some nonfree software, we have to be careful how to present
that.  Perhaps, "There is a way you can run some nonfree software one
last time so as to cut your ties with unjust Gmail authentication."

There is a crucial moral difference between (1) "I choose nasty
practice A because it is not as nasty as practice B", and (2) "I will
do X _once_ to cut the ties that compel me to accept practice Y."  If
you are willing to accept pattern (1) as valid, that willingness can
be used to maneuver you into rationalizing any injustice, simply by
making you choose between that one and something worse.  Not so for
(2).

On Mon, Oct 05, 2026 at 10:28:38PM -0700, Jim Porter wrote:

[...]

> My concern isn't exactly a moral one (though I do also have moral concerns
> with LLMs, and am unconvinced that it's possible to resolve these while
> keeping the "Large" in "Large Language Model"). I'm more immediately
> concerned with how LLMs impact the ability to maintain communities, which=
 I
> feel is the most critical piece of Emacs and GNU/FSF as a whole. Hence, I
> see this as mainly a practical problem.

Thanks for bringing that up. Exactly my thoughts (although I wouldn't have
managed to put it so cleanly in so few words).

Ultimately, I think this /is/ a moral problem, after all, since it targets
the very core of communication, the glue which holds our communities
together.

What else has been software, if not a means of communication? What else
has been the GPL if not the way to enable open communities, communicating
via their copylefted programs, making sure they stay open?

This is about to change. You can't "talk" to a generative LLM. I'm
deeply worried by the current power assymetry as those things are being
deployed large-scale.

Cheers
--=20
t

Peter Mao [05/Oct 10:49pm -07] wrote:
> I use vc-annotate a lot to dig into the history of code I'm working on,
> typically with vc-annotate-revision-previous-to-line and
> vc-annotate-revision-at-line, but often, I go too far and would like to
> back up a few jumps.
>
> The patch attached adds to vc-annotate.el:
> 1. vc-annotate-revision-history -- a buffer local variable holding the
> revspecs of the revisions visited.
> 2. vc-annotate-undo-warp-revision, bound to "C-/", which warps to the car
> of the above list
> 3. vc-annotate-update-history, a function to maintain the above list.
>
> vc-annotate-warp revision is modified to call vc-annotate-update-history
> just before the warp happens.
>
> Properly, vc-annotate-revision-history should be cleared when vc-annotate
> is invoked on a file, but I haven't dealt with that yet -- I figure there's
> time to do that while I get comments from the community.

use 'r' and 'l' to go back and forth in history like Info.

> My concern isn't exactly a moral one (though I do also have moral 
> concerns with LLMs, and am unconvinced that it's possible to resolve 
> these while keeping the "Large" in "Large Language Model"). I'm more 
> immediately concerned with how LLMs impact the ability to maintain 
> communities, which I feel is the most critical piece of Emacs and 
> GNU/FSF as a whole. Hence, I see this as mainly a practical problem.
> 
> LLMs have unfortunately made it easier for people to produce large 
> volumes of plausible output that they don't fully understand, both 
> burdening maintainers and undermining LLM users' ability to develop 
> their skills. The LLMs of course don't understand anything at all, but 
> have been fine-tuned to produce pleasing answers and to function as a 
> replacement of human social interaction and expertise.

IMO, there's nothing to codify here, as far as GNU is concerned.  If
you don't want to accept voluminous output, you can always ask the
author to rewrite it in more concise form, explaining that you cannot
afford reading through such long texts.  It doesn't matter whether the
text was generated manually or with LLM support.

I don't see how this is at all related to the current discussion.  It
isn't even a tangent.

> I've already had to deal with bad behavior brought on by overzealous LLM 
> users in other software communities and have seen the beginnings of it 
> appear on the Emacs mailing lists. Here and elsewhere, this issue seems 
> to be getting worse, not better, which has made me reconsider where we 
> ought to draw the line. Are LLM-related packages in ELPA a wise idea?

Hi martianh,

a while back I proposed an alternative implementation supporting
asynchronous operations.  If you're interested, see

https://lists.gnu.org/archive/html/emacs-devel/2025-11/msg00806.html

I also have some ideas regarding extending auth-source to be async, as
well as using the system "online accounts" service (works well at least
on GNOME):

https://codeberg.org/astoff/minimail/src/branch/main/online-accounts.el

On Wed, 30 Sep 2026, martianh wrote:

> hi emacs,
>
> pls CC me in replies, i'm a non-subscriber.
>
> i am considering using oauth2.el to reduce/simplify the authentication
> code in mastodon.el, which gives me headaches, but i'm having trouble
> understanding some basics.
>
> i have successfully obtained and stored a token with a registered app,
> but i'm unclear on how to fetch the token from the store as needed.
>
> the main entrypoint has client-secret and client-id as mandatory
> parameters, which seems to mean that i have to store them somewhere
> else (presumably in a second encrypted plstore, causing more
> headaches: client-id and client-secret should be treated like
> passwords) in order to be able to fetch the auth token. is this
> correct, or is a package expected to handle tokens in some other way?
>
> mastodon.el also supports multiple accounts, at least for saving auth
> credentials. you set username and host to a different value,
> reauthenticate, and mastodon.el keeps two sets of credentials, so if
> you switch back to the first account you don't have to do the auth
> flow again. i didn't manage to try this out due to the previous
> hurdle, but i'm curious if this would be (easily) supported by
> oath2.el, or does it assume 1 account per service somehow?
>
> finally, mastodon.el also supports storing auth tokens (but not
> client/app data) in auth-sources. i take it oauth2.el doesn't have
> support for storing in auth-sources?

>  Btw, in the future please post patches to the bug tracker.  A

> OK, but it's not a bug, and I was thinking of the patch as more of a conversation starter than a ready-to-ship
> thing.

The debbugs bug tracker is used for discussing and tracking patches
and issues as well, not just bugs.  That's why we have the
submit-emacs-patch command in the first place.  Discussions and
patches on this list are harder to link to and harder to find, so if
in some distant future someone wants to re-read the discussion and
understand how and why we made some decisions, it's much easier when
the commit logs have a bug number.

> that.  Perhaps, "There is a way you can run some nonfree software one
> last time so as to cut your ties with unjust Gmail authentication."
>
> There is a crucial moral difference between (1) "I choose nasty
> practice A because it is not as nasty as practice B", and (2) "I will
> do X _once_ to cut the ties that compel me to accept practice Y."  If
> you are willing to accept pattern (1) as valid, that willingness can
> be used to maneuver you into rationalizing any injustice, simply by
> making you choose between that one and something worse.  Not so for
> (2).

I agree modulo the fact that experience shows that "one last time" is
true only until "the next time", so it's still a rationalization.  🙁

The variable backup-by-copying-when-privileged-mismatch
preserves the ownership of files with low user or group id
(e.g., root-owned system files).  Its current range for
deciding what ids are in the system range is 200 and below.
I think this boundary is too low for modern systems.

Systemd uses ids 1-999 for system services.

Various GNU/Linux/Unix user-creation tools I looked at
(adduser and useradd) create user accounts starting with
id 1000 or 1001.

macOS starts numbering regular users with id 501.

MS Windows starts regular users accounts with id 1000.

Based on these data, I conclude that
backup-by-copying-when-privileged-mismatch
should be increased to this:

  (if (eq system-type 'darwin) 500 999)

Note that backup-by-copying-when-mismatch is t by default
anyway, and backup-by-copying-when-privileged-mismatch
then has no further effect.

What do other people see on their systems?  Does anybody
have regular user or group ids low enough that this change
would break you?

 < Stephen

On Thu,  8 Oct 2026, Johan Myr=C3=A9en wrote:

> On Wed, 7 Oct 2026 at 22:27, Augusto Stoffel <arstoffel@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>  I wonder why it helps using a GTK API for that.  There is `xdg-open' on
>  the free DEs, `open' MacOS, and other OSs surely have a version of that
>  command.
>
> I think this would be a good idea, but only if xdg-open can handle what t=
he
> x-gtk-launch-uri function=E2=80=94which this discussion originally was ab=
out=E2=80=94was created for
> in the first place (in 2023): to raise the browser window. Without this f=
eature, on
> Wayland, the web page is displayed in an already open browser window, but=
 the window
> stays buried under other windows, which is confusing the user.

Okay, indeed calling xgd-open in a subprocess does not raise the browser
window.  I'm pretty sure that's for the same reason why x-gtk-launch-uri
only focuses the browser if called when Emacs's frame itself is focused.

So that would be an argument in favor of changing browse-url-xdg-open to
use x-gtk-launch-uri if possible, with (call-process "xdg-open" ...) as
a fallback.

> 
> The variable backup-by-copying-when-privileged-mismatch
> preserves the ownership of files with low user or group id
> (e.g., root-owned system files).  Its current range for
> deciding what ids are in the system range is 200 and below.
> I think this boundary is too low for modern systems.
> 
> Systemd uses ids 1-999 for system services.
> 
> Various GNU/Linux/Unix user-creation tools I looked at
> (adduser and useradd) create user accounts starting with
> id 1000 or 1001.
> 
> macOS starts numbering regular users with id 501.
> 
> MS Windows starts regular users accounts with id 1000.

Doesn't Administrator have a lower ID on Windows, like 500?  And the
Administrators group (which is frequently used as owner of many files
on Windows) has ID of 544, AFAIR.

> Based on these data, I conclude that
> backup-by-copying-when-privileged-mismatch
> should be increased to this:
> 
>   (if (eq system-type 'darwin) 500 999)
> 
> Note that backup-by-copying-when-mismatch is t by default
> anyway, and backup-by-copying-when-privileged-mismatch
> then has no further effect.
> 
> What do other people see on their systems?  Does anybody
> have regular user or group ids low enough that this change
> would break you?

Adding Paul to this discussion.

backup-by-copying-when-privileged-mismatch is a defcustom, so why do
we need to discuss its default value? just customize it to a different
value if it doesn't fit your needs, and move on.

As for the default value, I think the important question is not where
the "privileged" IDs end, but whether an ID higher than 200 is
frequently enough assigned to privileged accounts, and what are those
accounts.  If exceeding the value of 200 is relatively rare, the
current default is still OK, IMO -- as the default.

Content-Type: text/plain; format=flowed

Hi,

please find attached two Gnus/IMAP/SMTP patches.

The first simply changes the order of ports 25 and 587 to nudge 
users
towards port 587. (Some servers support both, but allow 
authentication only on 587. On those servers the code would 
incorrectly assume that authenticating was pointless or 
impossible, and then fail to send mail unless the user knew more 
than most. On other servers this change makes sending mail 
slightly faster or slower.)

The second patch is much larger, and adds support for RFCs 6530-3, 
9755 and parts of 9051 as a side effect. FWIW 6530 is now 
supported by the servers for 70-80% of internet users, including 
the biggest two, gmail and o365.

I've been using versions of these patches since 2023. The 
attachments are newly rebased to 32.0.50, though.

Thanks in advance for any comments.

Arnt

=46rom 05ca8fec85c88fd4b8ac4f30f2f7d46f07d0c38a Mon Sep 17 00:00:00 2001
From: Arnt Gulbrandsen <arnt@gulbrandsen.priv.no>
Date: Sun, 9 Apr 2023 16:26:17 +0200
Subject: [PATCH 1/2] Prefer port 587 to 25 when querying for an SMTP =
server

If approximately the same software runs on the two ports, or one port
isn't used, then this makes no difference.

If significantly different software runs on the two ports, then 587 may
well be the port to use for submission, but 25 is unlikely to be.

* lisp/mail/smtpmail.el (smtpmail-query-smtp-server): Try port 587
before port 25.

Content-Type: text/x-diff; charset=utf-8

=46rom 7a4a4aa99189ff1b800a7c26a8bd5d3220645e75 Mon Sep 17 00:00:00 2001
From: Arnt Gulbrandsen <arnt@gulbrandsen.priv.no>
Date: Tue, 7 Feb 2023 17:12:17 +0000
Subject: [PATCH 2/2] Add support for unicode email addresses in Gnus/IMAP=
 and
 SMTP.

Send and receive RFC6531/RFC6532 mail and use RFC9755 UTF-8 mailbox
names. The existing IDNA support and usage is preferred in the cases
where that's enough.

If Gnus could read/send a message correctly before this commit, it
behaves identically after. There are a couple of minor related bugfixes
(Sender is now IDNA-encoded like other address fields, etc).

Note that a user who has pinned the charset (e.g. via
gnus-default-charset) will see mojibake when looking at UTF8 addresses
and other new syntax from RFC6532.

Note also a new standards deviation: If message-use-idna is nil (it is t
by default) and the user sends a message to an ASCII@non-ASCII address,
Gnus can choose to send it with the UTF8 address in a header field,
without requiring SMTPUTF8. Sending unencoded UTF8 requires SMTPUTF8
according to RFC6531.

* lisp/gnus/message.el (message-bogus-addresses): Drop the non-ASCII
localpart pattern. Such addresses are no longer bogus.
(message-address-headers): Name the header fields whose contents are
addresses, so SMTPUTF8 and IDNA cannot drift apart.
(message-localpart-uses-smtputf8, message-domain-uses-unicode): New
predicates on a single address.
(message--address-headers-any): New helper.
(message-header-uses-smtputf8, message-header-uses-unicode-addresses):
New predicates on a header.
(message-send-mail, message-send-news): Skip encoded-word encoding, and
the all-Latin-1 assertion, when a header holds a u-label.
(message-idna-to-ascii-rhs): Encode the domains of every address header
rather than six of them, Bcc and the Resent- fields included; leave
them alone when the message needs SMTPUTF8.  Doc fix.

* lisp/mail/smtpmail.el (smtpmail-encode-address-domain): New defun.
(smtpmail--as-characters): New helper.
(smtpmail-address-needs-smtputf8, smtpmail-addresses-need-smtputf8):
New predicates, on localparts only, tolerating a null sender.
(smtpmail-via-smtp): Qualify recipients before deciding anything, then
decide once for the whole transaction: either SMTPUTF8 with u-labels
throughout, or a-labels throughout and an ASCII envelope.  Recognise
the SMTPUTF8 extension in the EHLO response, send the SMTPUTF8 and
BODY=3D8BITMIME parameters when they are called for, and signal an error
rather than sending raw UTF-8 to a server that offers neither.  Take
care to follow the caller's choice of unibyte/multibyte as well as
encoding.
(smtpmail-send-it): Fix the case where the caller already converted
multibyte/unibyte, so RFC2047 encoding is no longer appropriate.

* lisp/gnus/nnimap.el (nnimap): New ENABLED slot.
(nnimap-open-connection-1): Send ENABLE QRESYNC UTF8=3DACCEPT and record
what the server enabled.
(nnimap-token-to-string, nnimap-enabled-utf8): New defuns.
(nnimap-group-to-imap): Send the mailbox name as UTF-8 when UTF8=3DACCEPT
is in force, and apply the namespace either way.
(nnimap-imap-to-group): New defun, split out of 'nnimap-get-groups'
for roundtrip testing.
(nnimap-get-groups): Use it.
(nnimap-send-command): Encode the command as UTF-8; the connection is
binary.
(nnimap-unfold-quoted-lines): Handle arriving mailbox names as strings
even if they arrive as IMAP literals.

* lisp/gnus/gnus-search.el (gnus-search-imap-search-command): Omit the
charset from SEARCH once UTF8=3DACCEPT is enabled, per RFC9755 5.

* test/lisp/gnus/message-tests.el (message-tests--with-headers): New
helper.
(message-address-predicates,
message-idna-encodes-domains-only-without-smtputf8): Add tests.
(message-detect-smtputf-usage): Remove, subsumed by the above.

* test/lisp/gnus/nnimap-tests.el: New file, testing the mailbox name
encodings in both directions, including names that look like modified
UTF-7 and must not be mistaken for it, and proper handling of non-ASCII
mailbox names from the server.

* test/lisp/mail/smtpmail-tests.el: New file, testing the SMTPUTF8
decision and the envelope encoding.

* test/lisp/mail/ietf-drums-tests.el (ietf-drums-tests):
* test/lisp/mail/mail-extr-tests.el (mail-extract-test-cases): Add
unicode addresses.

+(defconst message-address-headers
+  '("From" "Sender" "To" "Cc" "Bcc" "Reply-To" "Mail-Reply-To"
+    "Mail-Followup-To" "Resent-From" "Resent-To" "Resent-Cc" "Resent-Bcc=

+  "Header fields whose contents are addresses.
+A non-ASCII localpart in any of these forces SMTPUTF8, since nothing can
+encode one. If the message does not use SMTPUTF8, a non-ASCII domain in
+any of them may become an a-label (xn--...).  The Resent- fields matter
+to the envelope as well: `smtpmail-deduce-address-list' uses them for =
RCPT
+TO in place of To, Cc and Bcc whenever one of them is present.")

+(defun message-localpart-uses-smtputf8 (address)
+  "Return non-nil if ADDRESS has a non-ASCII localpart.
+See `message-address-headers'."
+  (string-match "[^[:ascii:]][^@ \t<]*@" address))
+
+(defun message--address-headers-any (predicate)
+  "Return non-nil if PREDICATE holds for an address in an address =
header.
+The buffer is expected to be narrowed to the headers; see
+`message-narrow-to-headers'."
+  (seq-some (lambda (header)
+              (let ((field (message-fetch-field header)))
+                (and field
+                     (seq-find predicate
+                               (mail-header-parse-addresses field t)))))
+            message-address-headers))
+
+(defun message-header-uses-smtputf8 ()
+  "Return non-nil if the current buffer needs SMTPUTF8, and nil if not.
+Only localparts count here; see `message-localpart-uses-smtputf8'."
+  (message--address-headers-any #'message-localpart-uses-smtputf8))
+
+(defun message-domain-uses-unicode (address)
+  "Return non-nil if ADDRESS has a non-ASCII domain.
+This thoroughly ignores display name and localpart."
+  (string-match "@[^@ \t<>,;]*[^[:ascii:]]" address))
+
+(defun message-header-uses-unicode-addresses ()
+  "Return non-nil if an address header holds a non-ASCII address.
+Domains matter here, unlike in `message-header-uses-smtputf8', because
+this is used to decide whether to apply RFC2047 encoding, which would
+break domains, while `message-header-uses-smtputf8' is used for
+transport-related decisions."
+  (message--address-headers-any
+   (lambda (address)
+     (or (message-localpart-uses-smtputf8 address)
+         (message-domain-uses-unicode address)))))

+(defun smtpmail--as-characters (string)
+  "Return STRING as characters, decoding raw UTF-8 bytes if that is what
+it holds."
+  (if (and (multibyte-string-p string)
+           (not (seq-some (lambda (char) (eq (char-charset char) =
'eight-bit))
+                          string)))
+      string
+    (decode-coding-string (encode-coding-string string 'raw-text) =
'utf-8)))

+(defun smtpmail-encode-address-domain (address)
+  "Return ADDRESS with its domain as an a-label.
+(Return the localpart as provided.)"
+  (if (string-match "\\`\\(.*\\)@\\([^@]+\\)\\'" address)
+      (concat (match-string 1 address) "@"
+              (puny-encode-domain
+               (smtpmail--as-characters (match-string 2 address))))
+    address))
+
+(defun smtpmail-address-needs-smtputf8 (address)
+  "Return non-nil if ADDRESS has a non-ASCII localpart.
+A non-ASCII domain does not count, since it has an a-label to fall back
+on.  A localpart has no plan b, so it alone forces use of SMTPUTF8."
+  (string-match "\\`[^@]*[^[:ascii:]]" address))

+(defun message-tests--with-headers (headers function)
+  "Call FUNCTION in a buffer holding HEADERS, narrowed to them."
+  (with-temp-buffer
+    (insert headers "Subject: hei\n\n--text follows this line--\nHello.\=
n")
+    (save-restriction
+      (message-narrow-to-headers)
+      (funcall function))))
+
+
+;;; Internationalised addresses.
+;;
+;; There are eight possible combinations of `message-use-idna` being
+;; set, the localpart using non-ASCII and the domain using non-ASCII.
+;; In some of those eight cases, we have to decide whether to use
+;; u-labels (UTF8) or a-labels (xn--) in the header fields and in
+;; the SMTP transaction. This table shows the intended decisions:
+;;
+;;   message-use-idna  localpart  domain   | header domain  transport
+;;   -------------------------------------------------------------------
+;;   t                 ASCII      ASCII    | --             plain SMTP
+;;   nil               ASCII      ASCII    | --             plain SMTP
+;;   t                 ASCII      Unicode  | a-label        plain SMTP
+;;   nil               ASCII      Unicode  | u-label        plain SMTP =
(*)
+;;   t                 Unicode    ASCII    | --             SMTPUTF8
+;;   nil               Unicode    ASCII    | --             SMTPUTF8
+;;   t                 Unicode    Unicode  | u-label        SMTPUTF8
+;;   nil               Unicode    Unicode  | u-label        SMTPUTF8
+;;
+;; A Unicode localpart cannot be encoded in any way, so it forces
+;; SMTPUTF8 and `message-use-idna' has nothing left to decide. In the =
top half
+;; the domain has an a-label to fall back on, so `message-use-idna' =
chooses.
+;;
+;; (*) deliberately breaks the rules in RFC6531 3.4, which would have us
+;; require SMTPUTF8 for any non-ASCII header content.  A u-label in a =
header
+;; under an ASCII envelope is not permitted, but it is widely supported,
+;; and it is much better to show the reader UTF8 than xn--. smtpmail =
sends
+;; the envelope as a-labels in that row; see
+;; `smtpmail-encode-address-domain'.
+
+(ert-deftest message-address-predicates ()
+  (pcase-dolist (`(,headers ,smtputf8 ,unicode)
+                 '(("To: gunnar@example.com\n"       nil nil)
+                   ("To: Ren=C3=A9 <rene@example.com>\n"  nil nil)
+                   ("To: arnt@gr=C3=A5.org\n"             nil t)
+                   ("To: G=C3=B8ril <goeril@gr=C3=A5.org>\n"   nil t)
+                   ("Resent-To: info@gr=C3=A5.org\n"      nil t)
+                   ("To: gr=C3=A5@example.com\n"          t   t)
+                   ("To: gr=C3=A5@gr=C3=A5.org\n"              t   t)
+                   ("To: Ren=C3=A9 <ren=C3=A9@gr=C3=A5.org>\n"      t   =
t)
+                   ("Sender: g=C3=B8ril@example.com\n"    t   t)
+                   ("Bcc: =E0=A4=89=E0=A4=A6=E0=A4=BE=E0=A4=B9=E0=A4=B0=E0=
=A4=A3@=E0=A4=89=E0=A4=A6=E0=A4=BE=E0=A4=B9=E0=A4=B0=E0=A4=A3.=E0=A4=AD=E0=

+  (declare (indent 1))
+  `(let ((nnimap-object (make-nnimap
+                         :enabled (and ,enabled '("QRESYNC" "UTF8=3DACCE=
PT")))))
+     ,@body))
+
+(ert-deftest nnimap-enabled-utf8 ()
+  (should (nnimap-tests--with-utf8 t (nnimap-enabled-utf8)))
+  (should-not (nnimap-tests--with-utf8 nil (nnimap-enabled-utf8)))
+  ;; The server may answer in any case, and does not have to name
+  ;; everything we asked it to enable.
+  (let ((nnimap-object (make-nnimap
+                        :enabled (mapcar #'nnimap-token-to-string
+                                         '(qresync "utf8=3Daccept")))))
+    (should (nnimap-enabled-utf8))))
+
+(ert-deftest nnimap-group-to-imap-utf8 ()
+  (let ((nnimap-namespace nil))
+    ;; UTF8=3DACCEPT means the mailbox name travels as a u-label.
+    (should (equal (nnimap-tests--with-utf8 t
+                     (nnimap-group-to-imap "Gel=C3=B6scht"))
+                   "Gel=C3=B6scht"))
+    ;; Without it, the modified UTF-7 of RFC3501 5.1.3 is all we have.
+    (should (equal (nnimap-tests--with-utf8 nil
+                     (nnimap-group-to-imap "Gel=C3=B6scht"))
+                   "Gel&APY-scht"))
+    (should (equal (nnimap-tests--with-utf8 t (nnimap-group-to-imap =
"INBOX"))
+                   "INBOX"))))
+
+(ert-deftest nnimap-group-to-imap-namespace ()
+  ;; The namespace prefix applies either way; only the encoding differs.
+  (let ((nnimap-namespace "INBOX."))
+    (should (equal (nnimap-tests--with-utf8 t
+                     (nnimap-group-to-imap "Gel=C3=B6scht"))
+                   "INBOX.Gel=C3=B6scht"))
+    (should (equal (nnimap-tests--with-utf8 nil
+                     (nnimap-group-to-imap "Gel=C3=B6scht"))
+                   "INBOX.Gel&APY-scht"))
+    (should (equal (nnimap-tests--with-utf8 t (nnimap-group-to-imap =
"INBOX"))
+                   "INBOX"))
+    (should (equal (nnimap-tests--with-utf8 t (nnimap-group-to-imap =
"#Shared"))
+                   "Shared"))))
+
+(ert-deftest nnimap-group-to-imap-escapes-ampersand ()
+  ;; A Gnus name that already looks like modified UTF-7 must come back
+  ;; escaped, or it would name a different mailbox on the server.
+  (let ((nnimap-namespace nil))
+    (should (equal (nnimap-tests--with-utf8 nil
+                     (nnimap-group-to-imap "A&-B"))
+                   "A&--B"))
+    (should (equal (nnimap-tests--with-utf8 nil
+                     (nnimap-group-to-imap "A&AOU-B"))
+                   "A&-AOU-B"))
+    ;; With UTF8=3DACCEPT the ampersand means nothing and is left alone.
+    (should (equal (nnimap-tests--with-utf8 t
+                     (nnimap-group-to-imap "A&-B"))
+                   "A&-B"))))
+
+(ert-deftest nnimap-group-name-round-trip ()
+  ;; `nnimap-group-to-imap' and `nnimap-imap-to-group' are inverses, for
+  ;; both encodings and whether or not a namespace is in the way.
+  (dolist (namespace '(nil "INBOX."))
+    (dolist (enabled '(nil t))
+      (let ((nnimap-namespace namespace))
+        (dolist (group '("plain" "INBOX" "#Shared" "Gel=C3=B6scht" =
"Gel=C3=B6scht&Co"
+                         "A&-B" "A&=3DB" "A&AOU-B" "=E4=BE=8B=E5=AD=90")=
)
+          (should
+           (equal group
+                  (nnimap-tests--with-utf8 enabled
+                    (nnimap-imap-to-group
+                     (encode-coding-string (nnimap-group-to-imap group)
+                                           'utf-8))))))))))
+
+(ert-deftest nnimap-unfold-quoted-lines-keeps-bytes ()
+  ;; A UTF-8 mailbox name can arrive either as a quoted string or as a
+  ;; literal. This tests that the literal form ends up being readable,
+  ;; instead of showing backslashed octal.
+  (let ((bytes (encode-coding-string "=D0=98=D1=81=D1=85=D0=BE=D0=B4=D1=8F=
=D1=89=D0=B8=D0=B5" 'utf-8)))
+    (should (eq (length bytes) 18))
+    (with-temp-buffer
+      (mm-disable-multibyte)
+      (insert "* LIST (\\hasnochildren) \"/\" {18}\r\n" bytes "\r\n")
+      (goto-char (point-min))
+      (nnimap-unfold-quoted-lines)
+      (should (equal (buffer-string)
+                     (concat "* LIST (\\hasnochildren) \"/\" \"" bytes =
"\"\r\n"))))))
+
+(provide 'nnimap-tests)
+
+;;; nnimap-tests.el ends here

+;;; smtpmail-tests.el --- tests for smtpmail.el  -*- lexical-binding:t =
-*-
+
+;; Copyright (C) 2026 Free Software Foundation, Inc.
+
+;; This file is part of GNU Emacs.
+
+;; GNU Emacs is free software: you can redistribute it and/or modify
+;; it under the terms of the GNU General Public License as published by
+;; the Free Software Foundation, either version 3 of the License, or
+;; (at your option) any later version.
+
+;; GNU Emacs is distributed in the hope that it will be useful,
+;; but WITHOUT ANY WARRANTY; without even the implied warranty of
+;; MERCHANTABILITY or FITNESS FOR A PARTICULAR PURPOSE.  See the
+;; GNU General Public License for more details.
+
+;; You should have received a copy of the GNU General Public License
+;; along with GNU Emacs.  If not, see <https://www.gnu.org/licenses/>.
+
+;;; Code:
+
+(require 'ert)
+(require 'smtpmail)
+
+(ert-deftest smtpmail-detect-smtputf8 ()
+  ;; A domain has an a-label to fall back on, so it decides nothing =
here.
+  (should (smtpmail-address-needs-smtputf8 "gr=C3=A5@gr=C3=A5.org"))
+  (should (smtpmail-address-needs-smtputf8 "g=C3=B8ril@example.com"))
+  (should (smtpmail-address-needs-smtputf8 "=E9=98=BFQ@=E4=BE=8B=E5=AD=90=
.=E4=B8=AD=E5=9B=BD"))
+  (should-not (smtpmail-address-needs-smtputf8 "arnt@gr=C3=A5.org"))
+  (should-not (smtpmail-address-needs-smtputf8 "info@m=C3=BCnchen.de"))
+  (should-not (smtpmail-address-needs-smtputf8 "arnt@xn--gr-zia.org"))
+  (should-not (smtpmail-address-needs-smtputf8 "gunnar@example.com")))
+
+(ert-deftest smtpmail-detect-smtputf8-unibyte ()
+  ;; By the time smtpmail sees an address it may have been through a
+  ;; unibyte send buffer, so both spellings have to answer alike.
+  (let ((address "g=C3=B8ril@example.com"))
+    (should (eq (not (smtpmail-address-needs-smtputf8 address))
+                (not (smtpmail-address-needs-smtputf8
+                      (encode-coding-string address 'utf-8)))))))
+
+(ert-deftest smtpmail-detect-smtputf8-envelope ()
+  ;; The question is asked of the transaction, not of each address, so
+  ;; that one Unicode localpart settles it for every recipient.
+  (should (smtpmail-addresses-need-smtputf8
+           "arnt@example.com" '("m=C3=BCller@m=C3=BCller.de" "info@g=C3=B6=
rtz.de")))
+  (should (smtpmail-addresses-need-smtputf8
+           "arnt@example.com" '("gunnar@example.com" "=E0=A4=89=E0=A4=A6=
=E0=A4=BE=E0=A4=B9=E0=A4=B0=E0=A4=A3@=E0=A4=89=E0=A4=A6=E0=A4=BE=E0=A4=B9=
=E0=A4=B0=E0=A4=A3.=E0=A4=AD=E0=A4=BE=E0=A4=B0=E0=A4=A4")))
+  (should (smtpmail-addresses-need-smtputf8
+           "ren=C3=A9@example.com" '("gunnar@example.com")))
+  ;; A domain alone never does, however many of them there are.
+  (should-not (smtpmail-addresses-need-smtputf8
+               "arnt@example.com" '("arnt@gr=C3=A5.org" "info@g=C3=B6rtz=
.de")))
+  (should-not (smtpmail-addresses-need-smtputf8 "arnt@example.com" nil))
+  ;; The null sender is a legal MAIL FROM, so nil must not signal.
+  (should-not (smtpmail-addresses-need-smtputf8 nil '("gunnar@example.co=
m"))))
+
+(ert-deftest smtpmail-encode-address-domain ()
+  (should (equal (smtpmail-encode-address-domain "arnt@gr=C3=A5.org")
+                 "arnt@xn--gr-zia.org"))
+  (should (equal (smtpmail-encode-address-domain "info@g=C3=B6rtz.de")
+                 "info@xn--grtz-5qa.de"))
+  ;; It encodes what it is handed; deciding whether to is the caller's =
job.
+  (should (equal (smtpmail-encode-address-domain "gr=C3=A5@gr=C3=A5.org"=
)
+                 "gr=C3=A5@xn--gr-zia.org"))
+  (should (equal (smtpmail-encode-address-domain "gunnar@example.com")
+                 "gunnar@example.com"))
+  ;; Idempotent, which matters because `smtpmail-via-smtp' retries.
+  (should (equal (smtpmail-encode-address-domain "arnt@xn--gr-zia.org")
+                 "arnt@xn--gr-zia.org"))
+  ;; An address taken from an already-encoded message buffer arrives as
+  ;; bytes, either as a unibyte string or, once it has been through a
+  ;; multibyte buffer, as eight-bit characters.  Encoding those one by =
one
+  ;; would give xn--gr-ci583hoda.org.  Both spellings are asserted to be
+  ;; what they claim first: without that, rewriting either into a plain
+  ;; literal would leave a test that passes without testing anything.
+  (let ((unibyte (encode-coding-string "arnt@gr=C3=A5.org" 'utf-8))
+        (eight-bit (with-temp-buffer
+                     (insert (encode-coding-string "arnt@gr=C3=A5.org" =
'utf-8))
+                     (buffer-string))))
+    (should-not (multibyte-string-p unibyte))
+    (should (seq-some (lambda (char) (eq (char-charset char) 'eight-bit)=
)
+                      eight-bit))
+    (should (equal (smtpmail-encode-address-domain unibyte)
+                   "arnt@xn--gr-zia.org"))
+    (should (equal (smtpmail-encode-address-domain eight-bit)
+                   "arnt@xn--gr-zia.org")))
+  ;; A local address has no domain to encode.
+  (should (equal (smtpmail-encode-address-domain "gr=C3=A5") "gr=C3=A5")=
)
+  (should (smtpmail-address-needs-smtputf8 "gr=C3=A5")))
+
+(provide 'smtpmail-tests)
+
+;;; smtpmail-tests.el ends here
=2D-=20

On 2026-10-08 23:36, Eli Zaretskii wrote:
> backup-by-copying-when-privileged-mismatch is a defcustom, so why do
> we need to discuss its default value? just customize it to a different
> value if it doesn't fit your needs, and move on.

Sure, but if this problem happens over and over, and is typical for GNU/Linux etc., it's better if the default matches the platform rather than to ask Emacs users to figure out the value for their respective platforms.

>I think the important question is not where
> the "privileged" IDs end, but whether an ID higher than 200 is
> frequently enough assigned to privileged accounts, and what are those
> accounts.

On GNU/Linux at least it's common. My Fedora 44 workstation at UCLA has 25 such UIDs. They're assigned dynamically as packages are installed, starting at 999 (on my platform, "systemd-oom") and growing down. This assignment is done automatically by systemd-sysusers. Other platforms do something similar with the useradd program.

Arnt,

Hi there! Yes, comments are welcome.

When you review, please keep in mind that, as of right now, only
IMAP4rev1 + UTF8=ACCEPT is supported. No support for IMAP4rev1 +
UTF8=ONLY and IMAP4rev2 yet. Those will be coming soon. The user still
gets the benefits of using non-ASCII characters in search queries.

In the next release, I plan on making the ASCII-encoding of articles'
headers optional when posting. In the release after that, I will change
the login mechanism to match RFC 9051. Then I will mostly finalize the
rev2 support. I say "mostly" because I am still not sure how I could
test for non-ASCII e-mail addresses. I will sort that out later. This is
my roadmap for now.

Nickolai Dobrynin <ndobrynin@gmail.com> writes:
> Hi there! Yes, comments are welcome.

I love that you used 9755 rather than 6855 ;)

> When you review, please keep in mind that, as of right now, only 
> IMAP4rev1 + UTF8=ACCEPT is supported. No support for IMAP4rev1 + 
> UTF8=ONLY and IMAP4rev2 yet. Those will be coming soon. The user 
> still gets the benefits of using non-ASCII characters in search 
> queries. 

UTF8=ONLY is basically unnecessary, I'd say. If you want to be 
historical about it, one of the last pre-RFC drafts of 6855 added 
this when an implementer suggested that UTF8=ONLY was too much 
work:

   The "UTF8=ONLY" capability, described in Section 6, implies the 
   "UTF8=ACCEPT" capability.  A server is said to support 
   "UTF8=ACCEPT" if it advertises either "UTF8=ACCEPT" or 
   "UTF8=ONLY". 
 
   A client MUST use the "ENABLE" command [RFC5161] with the 
   "UTF8=ACCEPT" option (defined in Section 4 below) to indicate 
   to the 
... 
 
> In the next release, I plan on making the ASCII-encoding of 
> articles' headers optional when posting. In the release after 
> that, I will change the login mechanism to match RFC 9051. Then 
> I will mostly finalize the rev2 support. I say "mostly" because 
> I am still not sure how I could test for non-ASCII e-mail 
> addresses. I will sort that out later. This is my roadmap for 
> now.

Sounds okay. I would guess that you get better interop by using 
e.g. AUTHENTICATE PLAIN than by 9051 LOGIN, though. The LOGIN 
command only added UTF8 support in 9051, but the AUTHENTICATE 
command has supported UTF8 for decades, and it's simple for a 
client.

I'll read through 
https://debbugs.gnu.org/cgi/bugreport.cgi?bug=81684 and comment 
there. 

Arnt

> Sounds okay. I would guess that you get better interop by using
> e.g. AUTHENTICATE PLAIN than by 9051 LOGIN, though.

Without a doubt. Per RFC 9051: "The LOGIN command SHOULD NOT be used
except as a last resort (after attempting and failing to authenticate
using the AUTHENTICATE command one or more times), and it is recommended
that client implementations have a means to disable any automatic use of
the LOGIN command."

There needs to be a server-level (defvoo) variable to regulate this.

> I'll read through https://debbugs.gnu.org/cgi/bugreport.cgi?bug=81684
> and comment there. Arnt

OK.

> On 2026-10-08 23:36, Eli Zaretskii wrote:
> > backup-by-copying-when-privileged-mismatch is a defcustom, so why do
> > we need to discuss its default value? just customize it to a different
> > value if it doesn't fit your needs, and move on.
> 
> Sure, but if this problem happens over and over, and is typical for GNU/Linux etc., it's better if the default matches the platform rather than to ask Emacs users to figure out the value for their respective platforms.

Agreed.  So we need to find out whether this is common enough.

> >I think the important question is not where
> > the "privileged" IDs end, but whether an ID higher than 200 is
> > frequently enough assigned to privileged accounts, and what are those
> > accounts.
> 
> On GNU/Linux at least it's common. My Fedora 44 workstation at UCLA has 25 such UIDs. They're assigned dynamically as packages are installed, starting at 999 (on my platform, "systemd-oom") and growing down. This assignment is done automatically by systemd-sysusers. Other platforms do something similar with the useradd program.

OK, then I guess we will need to modify the default value depending on
the OS.

The question is what to do on MS-Windows, where the low-value user IDs
are a mix of privileged and non-privileged accounts.  For example ID
500 is the local Administrator (the moral equivalent of root on Posix
systems), but 501 is Guest, which has the less-than-normal privileges.
I guess we will need to do something sub-optimal on Windows, because
its use of user IDs doesn't match the Posix model.

The font-lock-*-face variables have been made obsolete with commit
3d3c1094604c, end of 2024.

However, they are still used in many places in Emacs. For example,
font-lock-compile-keyword returns an unquoted symbol:

   (font-lock-compile-keyword "foobar")
      =E2=87=92 ("foobar" (0 font-lock-keyword-face))
   (font-lock-compile-keyword '("foobar" . 0))
      =E2=87=92 ("foobar" (0 font-lock-keyword-face))

Or, font-lock-default-fontify-syntactically refers to one of the
variables for a face property:

   (put-text-property beg (match-end 0) 'face
                      font-lock-comment-delimiter-face)

Are these variable references retained intentionally, so that users
can continue customizing the variables for some transition time?
On the other hand, NEWS.31 says this:

   "If you have been using these variables in Lisp code (for example,
   in font-lock rules), simply quote the symbol, to use the face
   directly instead of its now-obsolete variable."

from which I would conclude that all remaining uses should be
eliminated?

So, what is the roadmap for this?

>       =E2=87=92 ("foobar" (0 font-lock-keyword-face))

>       =E2=87=92 ("foobar" (0 font-lock-keyword-face))
>
> Or, font-lock-default-fontify-syntactically refers to one of the
> variables for a face property:
>
>    (put-text-property beg (match-end 0) 'face
>                       font-lock-comment-delimiter-face)
>
> Are these variable references retained intentionally, so that users
> can continue customizing the variables for some transition time?
> On the other hand, NEWS.31 says this:
>
>    "If you have been using these variables in Lisp code (for example,
>    in font-lock rules), simply quote the symbol, to use the face
>    directly instead of its now-obsolete variable."
>
> from which I would conclude that all remaining uses should be
> eliminated?
>
> So, what is the roadmap for this?

Patches welcome to fix the remaining cases.

>>>>> On Sat, 10 Oct 2026, Sean Whitton wrote:

> Ulrich M=C3=BCller [10/Oct 11:10am +02] wrote:
>> The font-lock-*-face variables have been made obsolete with commit
>> 3d3c1094604c, end of 2024.
>>=20
>> However, they are still used in many places in Emacs. For example,
>> font-lock-compile-keyword returns an unquoted symbol:
>>=20
>> (font-lock-compile-keyword "foobar")
>> =E2=87=92 ("foobar" (0 font-lock-keyword-face))
>> (font-lock-compile-keyword '("foobar" . 0))
>> =E2=87=92 ("foobar" (0 font-lock-keyword-face))
>>=20
>> Or, font-lock-default-fontify-syntactically refers to one of the
>> variables for a face property:
>>=20
>> (put-text-property beg (match-end 0) 'face
>> font-lock-comment-delimiter-face)
>>=20
>> Are these variable references retained intentionally, so that users
>> can continue customizing the variables for some transition time?
>> On the other hand, NEWS.31 says this:
>>=20
>> "If you have been using these variables in Lisp code (for example,
>> in font-lock rules), simply quote the symbol, to use the face
>> directly instead of its now-obsolete variable."
>>=20
>> from which I would conclude that all remaining uses should be
>> eliminated?
>>=20
>> So, what is the roadmap for this?

> Patches welcome to fix the remaining cases.

AFAICS there are several hundred instances.

Fixing them should be mostly a mechanical task. However, not entirely
trivial because one must count how often the symbol must be quoted.
And of course, the starting point is inconsistent; currently one can
evaluate the variable any number of times, and the result will still
be correct.

Let's start with some low-hanging fruit. Patch for font-lock.el itself
is included below.

Hi Philip,

I apologize for the slow reply. I have been busy, and thank you for your
patience.

Thank you for the review. I have made the changes you suggested:

- The redundant, non-uniform whitespace between entries is gone.
- The unicode section headers now follow outline-minor-mode conventions,
for example ";;;; font-lock (syntax)".
- Package-Requires now says Emacs 24.1. You were right that nothing in the
theme needs 27. The tab-bar and tab-line faces are simply ignored on older
Emacs, and I have noted that in the README.

The file still byte-compiles cleanly with byte-compile-error-on-warn.

One thing got cut off in your message. It reads "I would also add" and then
stops. Could you tell me what you meant to suggest?

Thank you for taking care of the elpa-packages entry. I will read
https://www.google.com/url?q=3Dhttps://elpa.gnu.org/contributing.html&sourc=
e=3Dgmail&ust=3D1791753489882000&sa=3DE
now and let you know if anything there needs action from me.

Thanks again,

Greg

> Finally, I wonder why you depend on Emacs 27?  This is a pretty vanilla

>
> > nightpanel is a dark theme modelled on a Saab instrument cluster seen a=
t
> > night. The canvas is pure black, body text is an instrument-scale
> > green, and amber is reserved for the things that would be a needle or a
> > warning lamp on a real dashboard: search matches, strings, constants,
> > TODO keywords. Red appears only for genuine errors. Comments and
> > inactive chrome recede to a dim green, so the code itself is the
> > brightest thing on screen.
> >
> > License: GPL-3.0-or-later, notice in the file header
> > Contents: one file, nightpanel-theme.el, 155 lines
> > Requires: Emacs 27.1, no package dependencies
> > Author: me, and I am the only contributor so far
> > Version: 0.1.0, tagged v0.1.0 in git
> >
> > The repository has an .elpaignore that excludes screenshot.png, so the
> > release tarball carries the theme file, the README and the license.
> >
> > package-lint, checkdoc, and byte-compilation with
> > byte-compile-error-on-warn are all clean on Emacs 30.1. I am the author
> > and maintainer, and I am glad to maintain the NonGNU ELPA version and t=
o
> > coordinate on any changes you would like.
> >
> > One disclosure, since it is visible in the file. The header carries an
> > "Assisted-by: Claude:claude-opus-5" line, which follows the MELPA
> > convention for this. The palette and the face definitions are my own
> > work. An AI assistant helped with the packaging around them: the header
> > block, the license boilerplate, the autoload cookie and the commentary.
> > I read and checked all of it, and the file is short enough to review in
> > one sitting. Please tell me if NonGNU ELPA would prefer that line
> > worded differently or dropped.
>
> FYI you could also use the `auto-insert' command for this.  But I also
> don't think AI is that concerning here, since the meat of the package is
> just ... a list of faces, which as you say are your own work.
> Generating the formalities using AI is about as problematic as copying

> This patch adds two Gnulib modules localtime and tzsanitize to Emacs, and emacs/admin/merge-gnulib said I should fix nt/gnulib-cfg.mk or notify emacs-devel. I'm doing the latter in this email's cc. Though I'm no NT expert I guess no change to nt/gnulib-cfg.mk is needed.

Actually, this broke the MS-Windows build, because Emacs on MS-Windows
has its own replacement for localtime in w32.c.  When fixing this, I
realized that omitting the localtime module via nt/gnulib-cfg.mk is
not enough, because Gnulib's time.h forcibly redirects localtime to
rpl_localtime on MS-Windows.  I fixed that by a kludge: I added a
trivial rpl_localtime to both lib-src programs and to Emacs itself,
but I hope the Gnulib folks will add something to Gnulib to allow
omitting the localtime module in a cleaner fashion.

Btw, why does tzsanitize call SetEnvironmentVariable only in the UCRT
build, leaving the MSVCRT build with an invalid TZ=$ setting?  The
comments in the code don't explain this part of the implementation, or
what did I miss?

  > > There is a crucial moral difference between (1) "I choose nasty
  > > practice A because it is not as nasty as practice B", and (2) "I will
  > > do X _once_ to cut the ties that compel me to accept practice Y."

  > I agree modulo the fact that experience shows that "one last time" is
  > true only until "the next time", so it's still a rationalization.  🙁

You've oversimplified my point so that it becomes a straw man.

The nature of life is that new problems arise and need to be
addressed.  After we get out of practice Y, some day we may find
practice Z has become a problem that we need to solve somehow or
other.  That doesn't mean the same problem has come back.

> From: Bruno Haible <bruno@clisp.org>

> Eli Zaretskii wrote:
> > I hope the Gnulib folks will add something to Gnulib to allow
> > omitting the localtime module in a cleaner fashion.
> 
> Does '--avoid=localtime' not work?

Where should one do that? if during merge-gnulib, then we don't want
Paul (or anyone else from the Gnulib developers) to do something that
is specific to MS-Windows.  The other platforms don't have their
emulation of 'localtime', so they need to use what Gnulib does.

The selective (and relatively rare) disabling of Gnulib features and
modules is done on nt/gnulib-cfg.mk (where we omit some modules) and
nt/mingw-cfg.site (where we set some configure-time variables so as to
disable certain tests whose results we know in advance).  I hoped that
some combination of these techniques could work in this case as well.

> > Btw, why does tzsanitize call SetEnvironmentVariable only in the UCRT
> > build
> 
> Because in my testing with different versions of mingw+msvcrt, the
> SetEnvironmentVariable invocation is not needed: The 3 unit tests
> pass without it.
> 
> > leaving the MSVCRT build with an invalid TZ=$ setting?
> 
> That's not what the code does. The code creates a '$Z=something'
> string, thereby eliminating the 'TZ=something' setting.

Thanks for explaining this.

> of the library is a function to export a buffer as PDF.

> I did.

On 2026-10-11 03:56, Eli Zaretskii wrote:
> Let me rephrase: I don't want to ask Paul to do this, and I'd like to
> avoid the need to run gnulib-tool myself.  Would you (or someone else
> on the Gnulib team) please kindly tell how to produce the effect of
> "--avoid=localtime" without actually running the script?

Yes: install the attached patch. Quite possibly it will work as-is; perhaps we'll need to fiddle with it a bit. Either way, it's heading in the right direction.

This patch follows Bruno's suggestion of avoiding the Gnulib localtime module because Emacs doesn't need it. It goes further by also avoiding Gnulib's tzsanitize module, as I assume Emacs doesn't need that either. If my assumption is incorrect I can create another patch that avoids localtime but not tzsanitize.

Although one can incorporate Gnulib code without running gnulib-tool, it's such an error-prone process that I don't recommend it. I generated the attached patch by running Emacs's admin/merge-gnulib script, which ran gnulib-tool for me.

Jean Louis <bugs@gnu.support> writes:

> I was thinking you were using some kind of agent written in Elisp. But=20
> that is not what `gptel` is. `gptel` is located on GNU servers, and it=20
> was made with the primary purpose of accessing SaaSS. Its own page says=20
> so:
> ...

Yet, it is also an agent. And you can implement more complex agents
using gptel (or with its extension - gptel-agent).

>> The services ChatGPT, Azure, Gemini, Anthropic AI, Together.ai,=20
>> Perplexity, AI/ML API, Anyscale, OpenRouter, Groq, PrivateGPT,=20
>> DeepSeek, Cerebras, GitHub Copilot chat, AWS Bedrock, Novita AI, xAI,=20
>> Sambanova, Mistral Le Chat and Kagi (FastGPT & Summarizer).
>
> That is a list of SaaSS services. The package also supports local models=
=20
> via Ollama, Llama.cpp, Llamafiles, and GPT4All, but the description=20
> begins with ChatGPT, and the default configuration is ChatGPT:
>
>> "ChatGPT is configured out of the box."

> It is a client for SaaSS services, with a local option that the user=20
> must configure manually.

You must configure everything manually, including ChatGPT, where you
need to provide api key. For local servers, it is similar - need to put
a short snippet to configure.

> The package uses the word "LLM" throughout, but it never interacts with=20
> an LLM. An LLM is the model itself =E2=80=94 the weights on disk, run loc=
ally by=20
> an inference engine. What `gptel` interacts with is a remote API on a=20
> web server. That is SaaSS, not an LLM. The terminology is inaccurate,=20
> and the inaccuracy hides what the package actually does.

API on server is not necessarily saas.
I get it that you have different views on terminology, but people use
these words differently, alas.

> The remaining modules =E2=80=94 `gptel-ollama.el`, `gptel-context.el`,=20
> `gptel-integrations.el`, `gptel-oauth.el`, `gptel-org.el`,=20
> `gptel-request.el`, `gptel-rewrite.el`, `gptel-transient.el`, and the=20
> core `gptel.el` =E2=80=94 are not dedicated SaaSS clients. `gptel-ollama.=
el` is=20
> the local option. The others are infrastructure that does not itself=20
> connect to a service.

Yes, the others are building blocks you can use for agents, among other
things. That's what I was talking about. gptel-context is how you can
control what to send to LLMs from Emacs. gptel-request contains API to
build agents (see gptel-request, for example).

> So my request is not to remove the whole package. My request is...

We are not discussing requests about changing gptel here.
We are talking about agents in Elisp.

On 2026-10-11 21:20, Ihor Radchenko wrote:
> Jean Louis <bugs@gnu.support> writes:
> 
>> Yet, running it locally is currently not possible with free software.
>> One needs at least proprietary kernel blobs as firmware for GPU cards
>> and there is no LLM that is fully free.
> 
> No. You can run certain things in CPU nowadays (I do it myself).
> I expect more to be available in future.
> Also, technically, you can run any inference on CPU. It is just not
> practical. But doable.

Yes, it is possible to run it on CPU, and that can be done with free 
software, correction!

I was thinking you were using some kind of agent written in Elisp. But 
that is not what `gptel` is. `gptel` is located on GNU servers, and it 
was made with the primary purpose of accessing SaaSS. Its own page says 
so:

> The services ChatGPT, Azure, Gemini, Anthropic AI, Together.ai, 
> Perplexity, AI/ML API, Anyscale, OpenRouter, Groq, PrivateGPT, 
> DeepSeek, Cerebras, GitHub Copilot chat, AWS Bedrock, Novita AI, xAI, 
> Sambanova, Mistral Le Chat and Kagi (FastGPT & Summarizer).

That is a list of SaaSS services. The package also supports local models 
via Ollama, Llama.cpp, Llamafiles, and GPT4All, but the description 
begins with ChatGPT, and the default configuration is ChatGPT:

> "ChatGPT is configured out of the box."

It is a client for SaaSS services, with a local option that the user 
must configure manually.

The package uses the word "LLM" throughout, but it never interacts with 
an LLM. An LLM is the model itself — the weights on disk, run locally by 
an inference engine. What `gptel` interacts with is a remote API on a 
web server. That is SaaSS, not an LLM. The terminology is inaccurate, 
and the inaccuracy hides what the package actually does.

The package is not a single client. It is a collection of modules, and 
most of them exist to connect Emacs to one specific SaaSS service. The 
modules dedicated to SaaSS are `gptel-openai.el`, 
`gptel-openai-extras.el`, `gptel-openai-oauth.el`, 
`gptel-openai-responses.el`, `gptel-anthropic.el`, `gptel-bedrock.el`, 
`gptel-gemini.el`, `gptel-gh.el`, and `gptel-kagi.el`. Each of these 
modules is a dedicated client for one SaaSS service. None of them can 
work with a free alternative and each one falls under the criterion 
Stallman stated in this thread: "a comparable interface package that 
could only work with various SaaSS packages would be a different kind of 
issue."

The remaining modules — `gptel-ollama.el`, `gptel-context.el`, 
`gptel-integrations.el`, `gptel-oauth.el`, `gptel-org.el`, 
`gptel-request.el`, `gptel-rewrite.el`, `gptel-transient.el`, and the 
core `gptel.el` — are not dedicated SaaSS clients. `gptel-ollama.el` is 
the local option. The others are infrastructure that does not itself 
connect to a service.

So my request is not to remove the whole package. My request is that the 
modules whose only purpose is SaaSS access be removed, so that what 
remains is a package that does not recommend SaaSS. The modules to be 
removed are the nine listed above: the OpenAI modules, the Anthropic 
module, the Bedrock module, the Gemini module, the GitHub Copilot 
module, and the Kagi module.

I am also asking that this be applied consistently. If `gptel` is 
permitted to keep dedicated SaaSS modules, then the same standard 
applies to `llm`, `hermes.el`, `codex-ide`, `aidermacs`, `ellama`, 
`minuet`, and any other package on GNU servers with the same structure.

--
Jean Louis

On 2026-10-11 23:00, Cecilio Pardo wrote:
>> Jean Louis <bugs@gnu.support> writes:
>> 
>>> Yet, running it locally is currently not possible with free software.
>>> One needs at least proprietary kernel blobs as firmware for GPU cards
>>> and there is no LLM that is fully free.
> 
> What do you think of the olmo LLMs, Jean Louis?

I think that efforts of the Allen AI company are commendable considering 
how much evil Microsoft did over the time to humanity. Yet the dataasets 
are not fully free by GNU standards, they may be full "open" by AI2 as 
model weights are Apache 2.0 license, the Dolma set ODC-BY, and there 
are training codes. It gives good knowledge on how to actually make the 
fully free model in the future, yet now it is not. The OLMo 2 paper 
describes its pretraining mix as derived from Dolma, and Dolma is 
explicitly documented as containing Common Crawl data.

So OLMo 2 is "fully open" in the sense that AI2 has published 
everything. It is not "fully free" for GNU in the sense that all the 
training data is under free licenses.

That distinction matters for this GNU discussion.

When I say "LLM," I mean the weights — the model on your own machine. I 
do not mean a remote service reached through an API. Calling that an 
"LLM" hides the real problem: the computing is not yours, and the 
software is not yours to run, study, modify, or share. An API client 
accessing not your computer is a SaaSS client, not an LLM interface.

-- 
Jean Louis

> Yes: install the attached patch. Quite possibly it will work as-is; perhaps we'll need to fiddle with it a bit. Either way, it's heading in the right direction.
> 
> This patch follows Bruno's suggestion of avoiding the Gnulib localtime module because Emacs doesn't need it. It goes further by also avoiding Gnulib's tzsanitize module, as I assume Emacs doesn't need that either. If my assumption is incorrect I can create another patch that avoids localtime but not tzsanitize.

Yes, let's do the latter, please.  The tzsanitize module is beneficial
to Emacs on MS-Windows, since I've seen enough packages and Lisp
programs which set TZ to the likes of Europe/Amsterdam or
EST5EDT,M3.2.0/2,M11.1.0/2.  That's why I added the call to tzsanitize
in the w32 wrapper for the libc 'localtime'.

> Although one can incorporate Gnulib code without running gnulib-tool, it's such an error-prone process that I don't recommend it. I generated the attached patch by running Emacs's admin/merge-gnulib script, which ran gnulib-tool for me.

Thanks.

> Em 11 de outubro de 2026 23:28:10 BRT, Jean Louis <bugs@gnu.support> 
> escreveu:
>> So my request is not to remove the whole package. My request is that 
>> the modules whose only purpose is SaaSS access be removed, so that 
>> what remains is a package that does not recommend SaaSS. The modules 
>> to be removed are the nine listed above: the OpenAI modules, the 
>> Anthropic module, the Bedrock module, the Gemini module, the GitHub 
>> Copilot module, and the Kagi module.
> If this were to be done, gptel's userbase would drop by like 98%.

Emacs packages are all over the place, and GNU project doesn't control 
where packages are distributed from. Every person has freedom to 
distribute free software anywhere.

Just that distribution of SaaSS packages should not be from GNU servers.

I am personally for the adoption of LLMs with Emacs, but not adoption of 
services as software substitute, which obviously so many users mistake 
for "LLM". They call it LLM, while Emacs doesn't interact with any LLM 
at all. It interacts with APIs.

So I would like that we have free firmware, and free GPU drivers, and 
free GPUs, yet now we don't have it.

I would like there is truly free LLM, yet it is not there.

So yes, I would like Emacs to interact with the LLMs in the sense of 
users' own computing. Not in the sense of interacting with remote SaaSS. 
Why did I buy my own computer? To use a rented computer? Ah, no.

Jean Louis

> Reduced the main implementation to about 1,400 lines. It still
> covers three responsibilities:
>
> revealing source at point
>
> additional Markdown rendering
>
> MathJax-based math previews
>
> After considering the trade-offs, I chose to retain all three.
>
> markdown-ts-mode provides basic rendering, but not the additional
> treatments I wanted for Wiki links, quote markers, GitHub-style
> callouts, table borders, and code fences. Source revelation needs
> to coordinate with those decorations, so separating them would
> still require an integration layer. For now, I have kept them
> together.
>
> I also tried latex-to-svg. In my testing, its source-reveal
> behavior overlapped with mine, and I encountered conflicts and
> asynchronous update issues. I therefore retained the MathJax-based
> implementation.
>
> I understand that 1,400 lines is still substantial, and that
> reducing the line count alone does not make the code easier to
> maintain. There may still be rough edges, but I intend to maintain
> the package and keep improving its readability.

It still sounds a lot better.  If you want to I can take another look at
it sometime soon.

> I am open to renaming the package from appear to reveal. I
> personally prefer the current name, but would welcome your
> recommendation if you think reveal communicates its purpose more
> clearly.

I would defer this question to the maintainers of markdown-ts-mode,
since they are the most affected by any namespace grabbing.  If they are
fine with the name, we can at least add the package to the archive with
the promise of future cleanups.

> Thysrael

I think Rahul will agree, markdown-ts-appear is fine.  I did not realize
there was an equivalent package called org-appear that might make discovery
easier for people already familiar with that package.  I still think reveal
is the more correct and more common terminology, however, see WordStar
reveal codes, Microsoft Word's reveal formatting, et. al., functions.

I'm not sure precisely what we will be adding to the mode itself and there
is a list of things we've held back for Emacs 32 (and a potential interim
ELPA release) that may include some similar features.  I see no harm in
having an extra third-party package, but keep to the public
markdown-ts-mode API if you depend on any functions from the mode.

> I would like there is truly free LLM, yet it is not there.

But it could be. You "only" need to replace Olmo training data with 
something free, for example the "Common Pile". It can be found using Google.

Then you can add all the GPL licensed code out there, because Common 
Pile doesn't include it.

Then you need to do some things with the data, all with free software, 
and do the training, all with free software. The free software is there 
already.

This is something users themselves should be able to do on their normal 
machines. Am I right? Could the model be considered free if it cannot be 
_built_, only _used_, on that computer that you bought?

The good news it that it can be built! A normal computer would complete 
in an small amount of centuries.

More updates from feedback.

2026-10-12  Brad Howes  <bradhowes@mac.com <mailto:bradhowes@mac.com>>

	Ignore .dir-locals.el and .dir-locals-2.el when byte compiling

	* lisp/files.el (dir-locals=E2=80=94-file-names): New function =
that returns
	the two `dir-locals' file names, `.dir-locals.el=E2=80=99 and =
`.dir-locals-2.el=E2=80=99.
	* lisp/files.el (dir-locals-file-p): New function, returns true =
if given
	file that matches a `dir-locals' name.
	* lisp/files.el (dir-locals=E2=80=94-all-files): Updated to use=20=

	`dir-locals=E2=80=94-file-names=E2=80=99.
	* test/lisp/files-tests.el (dir-locals--file-names, =
dir-locals-file-p)
	(dir-locals--all-files, dir-locals--all-files-base-only): New =
tests.

	* lisp/emacs-lisp/bytecomp.el (byte-compile-file): Call
	`dir-locals-file-p=E2=80=99 with file path and when true act as
	if file contains `no-byte-compile' file variable set true.
	* test/lisp/emacs-lisp/bytecomp-tests.el
	(byte-compile-file/no-byte-compile-dir-locals)
	(byte-compile-file/no-byte-compile-dir-locals-2): New tests.

	* lisp/emacs-lisp/comp.el (comp--native-compile): Call
	`dir-locals-file-p=E2=80=99 with file path and when true skip =
native
	compilation on file.
	* test/lisp/emacs-lisp/comp-tests.el
	(test-native-compile-ignores-dir-locals): New test.

search engines just because search engines are deemed necessary. You 
provide your search term, and your IP, and whatever the web page can get 
from you. Then nonfree software, which runs as SaaS, use your search 
term to return to you a page with some links, and a couple of ads maybe. 
You don't "examine" the database. That's is a misrepresentation, made 
just to rationalize accepting the use of search engines. Because search 
engines are convenient. Convenience over freedom.

> When you send a prompt to an API of new generative LLMs, you are asking

On 2026-10-12 22:12, Cecilio Pardo wrote:
> On 10/12/2026 8:01 PM, Jean Louis wrote:
> 
>> So yes, I would like Emacs to interact with the LLMs in the sense of 
>> users' own computing. Not in the sense of interacting with remote 
>> SaaSS. Why did I buy my own computer? To use a rented computer? Ah, 
>> no.
> 
> Do you use google or search? Or DuckDuckGo? Why? You only need a couple 
> exabytes of disk an a free web indexer.

Search engine is not SaaSS as such a server doesn't take your data to 
compute it for you.

The essay says:

"Services such as search engines collect data from around the web and 
let you examine it. Looking through their collection of data isn't your 
own computing in the usual sense — you didn't provide that collection — 
so using such a service to search the web is not SaaSS." -- read here to 
understand better: 
https://www.gnu.org/philosophy/who-does-that-server-really-serve.html

When you send a prompt to an API of new generative LLMs, you are asking 
the remote computer to make computation for you, to write a code or 
translate the text, to summarize documents, to prepare your notes, so 
that is computing as a service which you could eventually do it with 
your own computer. That is why it is service as a software substitute.

The technology as such is good, yet not free. The solution is to build 
or get free hardware to create those LLMs, without depending on 
proprietary companies which control users. Yes, training on CPU would 
take looong time. But that is a problem to solve.

The free alternative requires free hardware (not available), free 
drivers (not available for most GPUs), free firmware (not available) and 
free training data (the Common Pile is a step, but the models trained on 
it are not yet competitive) and compute to train (not available to 
individuals).

So what should GNU project do when there is no free alternative? The 
answer is not to use SaaSS and to work on the free replacement. The 
right answer is not to drive users to SaaSS in the meantime because the 
free alternative is hard. Making GNU was hard enough itself, yet we have 
it, so people can build free replacement hardware and software.

-- 
Jean Louis

On 2026-10-13 01:59, Cecilio Pardo wrote:
> I understand it. The thing is that I disagree. An exception is made for 
> search engines just because search engines are deemed necessary. You 
> provide your search term, and your IP, and whatever the web page can 
> get from you. Then nonfree software, which runs as SaaS, use your 
> search term to return to you a page with some links, and a couple of 
> ads maybe. You don't "examine" the database. That's is a 
> misrepresentation, made just to rationalize accepting the use of search 
> engines. Because search engines are convenient. Convenience over 
> freedom.

It is okay to disagree. Let me just correct you that SaaSS is SaaSS no 
matter if it runs free software or non-free software. When user uses 
service as a software substitute, that is SaaSS.

Many websites in general are running software, they are just computed, 
but user receives it as information, yet website isn't static. That 
doesn't make it service as a software substitute.

If you can do your spreadsheet work at your computer, but you do it on 
Google Spreadsheets, that is service as a software substitute.

I also think that using Gmail is harmful, as service is deceitfully 
"free" because user is a product to sell him advertising parsing his 
private information.

Search engine? That is really searching the database, like a library, 
you can go there and search for books, yet there is no computing 
substitute involved.

Stallman would be last person in the world to rationalize over the 
principle.

The point is not that search engines are accepted because they are 
convenient but because the computing is not the user's. If a service did 
the user's computing, it would be SaaSS regardless of how convenient it 
was.

>> When you send a prompt to an API of new generative LLMs, you are 
>> asking the remote computer to make computation for you, to write a 
>> code or translate the text, to summarize documents, to prepare your 
>> notes, so that is computing as a service which you could eventually do 
>> it with your own computer. That is why it is service as a software 
>> substitute.
> 
> This is not fundamentally different from using your search term in 
> combination with google's data to return a search result. Don't you 
> think they may use some kind of AI model, not necessarily an LLM?

That computers on Internet run some software that is common and usual. 
It doesn't need to be a search engine, millions of websites run some 
software.

The distinction is not whether a remote computer is involved. Both 
involve a remote computer. The distinction is whose computing it is.

Google searhc engine is data Google collected and controls, it is not 
yours and is not built from your data you would be computing at home, it 
is not substituting your computing. For an LLM API: you send your 
prompt, and the service generates a result from it produced from your 
input. If you had the model weights and an inference engine, you could 
produce the same result on your own computer and the computing would be 
yours. That is why it is SaaSS, when computing is not yours.

Just as it empowers users to have their own computer and their own 
operating system like GNU, it also empowers users to have their own 
computing. Users giving away their computing to third parties start 
being controlled by those third parties as power is given to third 
parties.

It does not matter what technology the search engine uses internally (as 
you said "AI") but what matters is the nature of the activity.

> Whatever technology google uses to build the result is nonfree either, 
> and is not just a lookup in their database. It could be ANYTHING. How 
> can you deny that? Do you really thing google.com is no the front for a 
> proprietary company that controls users?

Those are other issues and I personally think Google has too many dark 
patterns, it would be best it be dissolved into smaller companies and 
examined against the laws in all jurisdictions. It does break many laws 
and is each in a while punished by courts.

>> The free alternative requires free hardware (not available), free 
>> drivers (not available for most GPUs), free firmware (not available) 
>> and free training data (the Common Pile is a step, but the models 
>> trained on it are not yet competitive) and compute to train (not 
>> available to individuals).
> 
> The free alternative to google requires building a monstrosity too. But 
> that we accept, because we like search engines, but don't like Bullshit 
> generators.

Please do not mistake my rejection of SaaSS to rejection of bullshit 
generators, as I create on this computer too many blueprints for 
manufacturing using local models, so   there is great wish and passion 
from my side to find truly free LLM solutions. You mentioned yesterday 
Common Pile and I hoped that the model Comma that used Common Pile could 
be free by definition of GNU project. But then I found out they use 
"openly licensed" information which for example ingests CC-BY-SA which 
is good for information but basically makes the output again legally 
questionable. I find that effort to make free LLMs good, yet just not 
well thought of. Authors do not have profound knowledge of licensing. 
But it will come soon. We have to talk and communicate and explain what 
really makes LLM free and good thing is that many authors do respond.

>> So what should GNU project do when there is no free alternative? The 
>> answer is not to use SaaSS and to work on the free replacement. The 
>> right answer is not to drive users to SaaSS in the meantime because 
>> the free alternative is hard. Making GNU was hard enough itself, yet 
>> we have it, so people can build free replacement hardware and 
>> software.
> 
> Certainly. The answer is not to use it at all and wait. They will 
> probably evaporate. So the Free Software movement hands non-technical 
> users to the corporations, at everylevel. Not the first time.

True, some users may go to proprietary software and SaaSS, everybody has 
a choice. Though GNU has to set examples for others. In fact, would 
there be no free software philosophy I don't believe huggingface.co as 
such would exist today. So think about wider and future influence. The 
choice is not to promote to use SaaSS or hand non-technical users to 
corporations but to work on the free solution while declining to 
recommend SaaSS solution.

Opinions on topics differ, it is very much on the topic, as topic is 
promoting SaaSS from GNU project, and exchanging opinions is important.

-- 
Jean Louis

This list is for discussing Emacs development.  The aspects of Emacs
development related to LLMs and their sites cannot be usefully
discussed until the GCS is updated and we understand what these
updates mean for Emacs.

More general discussions about LLMs and their servers, such as what
was going on in this thread for the last couple of days, are off-topic
here, so please take them elsewhere.

It is not enough to understand my position.  You are requested to
comply.

You were asked nicely and kindly to comply, several times, but you
didn't, and neither did others.  So now it's time to ask less nicely:
please don't post anymore on this sub-topic, or your messages will be
rejected as inappropriate.

Likewise everyone else: please don't continue posting on these
aspects.  Anyone who will ignore the request and will keep posting
will have his/her moderation flag set, and messages from them about
these aspects will be also rejected.

I'm sorry to have to use these drastic measures, but it's becoming
impossible to do useful work here due to an impossibly high level of
noise, and ignoring explicit requests to stop off-topic discussions is
considered extremely rude.

Today if emacs is built --with-pgtk and started with no arguments and no
wayland or X server reachable, it will exit 1 after complaining about the
inability to reach a display (this is the subject of at least debbugs 63555,
65886, 72303, and the PROBLEMS entry the latter spawned in
commit 309d0a718).

Quoting PROBLEMS: "This is a byproduct of GTK's not providing any
means of probing
for a display connection before committing to opening one, and cannot be
addressed by Emacs."
It seems to me that we could work around the lack of the above means by
fork'ing and gtk_init'ing in the child (and then _exit(0)'ing), and using
the exit status of the child as an indication of whether gtk_init is
likely[*] to fail and so we should inhibit_window_system=1 in the parent.

Would a patch implementing this approach be welcome, or has this approach
already been considered & rejected?
(apologies if the latter; searching emacs-devel for pgtk
<https://lists.gnu.org/archive/cgi-bin/namazu.cgi?query=pgtk&submit=Search%21&idxname=emacs-devel&max=100&result=normal&sort=date%3Aearly>
shows nothing newer than 2021)

Cheers,
-Ami

[*] "likely" is weaker than I'd like, but the proposed test can also fail
due to fork() failing for reasons that wouldn't prevent gtk_init from
succeeding, in which case it's more nuanced to decide whether to
inhibit_window_system; a tty-less GUI executor would probably rather fall
back to GTK while a display-less terminal executor would probably rather
fall back to tty. Either way, this seems more corner-case than the main
thing being fixed here.
