;;; elisp-refactor.el --- Toy Emacs Lisp backend for refactor.el  -*- lexic=
al-binding: t; -*-

;; Author: Jo=C3=A3o T=C3=A1vora <joaotavora@gmail.com>
;; Version: 0.1
;; Package-Requires: ((emacs "29.1") (refactor "0.1"))
;; Keywords: languages, lisp

;;; Commentary:

;; A deliberately dumb Emacs Lisp backend for refactor.el, meant to
;; show how to USE refactor.el's API, not how to analyse Elisp.  Turn
;; it on with
;;
;;   (add-hook 'emacs-lisp-mode-hook #'elisp-refactor-mode)
;;
;; The parts of the API exercised, by section:
;;
;; - Setup: a backend is any value returned from a function in
;;   `refactor-backend-functions'; here, the symbol `elisp-refactor',
;;   on which all the `refactor-backend-*' methods dispatch.
;;
;; - Rename: `refactor-backend-rename-bounds' claims the symbol at
;;   point, `refactor-backend-rename' returns a changeset renaming it
;;   textually within the current defun.
;;
;; - Actions: `refactor-backend-actions' offers `refactor-action's
;;   only where they make sense ("Convert `if' to `cond'" on an `if'
;;   form, "Expand macro" on a macro call), honoring the RKIND filter,
;;   and `refactor-backend-execute' later carries the chosen one out.
;;   A new kind, `macroexpand', is defined with `refactor-defkind'.
;;
;; - Diagnostics: `refactor-backend-actions' also offers quick fixes
;;   for the byte compiler's "Unused lexical variable" warnings, as
;;   reported to Flymake by `elisp-flymake-byte-compile'.

;;; Code:

(require 'cl-lib)
(require 'refactor)
(require 'flymake)
(require 'pp)

;;;; Setup

(defun elisp-refactor-backend ()
  "Return the Elisp refactor backend.
For `refactor-backend-functions'."
  'elisp-refactor)

;;;###autoload
(define-minor-mode elisp-refactor-mode
  "Toy refactorings for Emacs Lisp."
  :lighter nil
  (cond (elisp-refactor-mode
         (add-hook 'refactor-backend-functions #'elisp-refactor-backend nil=
 t)
         (refactor-suggestion-mode 1))
        (t
         (remove-hook 'refactor-backend-functions #'elisp-refactor-backend =
t)
         (refactor-suggestion-mode -1))))

(cl-defmethod refactor-backend-name ((_backend (eql elisp-refactor)))
  "Elisp (toy)")

(refactor-defkind macroexpand inline
  "Replace a macro call with its expansion.")

;;;; Rename

(cl-defmethod refactor-backend-rename-bounds ((_backend (eql elisp-refactor=
)))
  (and (bounds-of-thing-at-point 'defun)
       (bounds-of-thing-at-point 'symbol)))

(cl-defmethod refactor-backend-rename ((_backend (eql elisp-refactor)) newn=
ame)
  ;; refactor.el's changesets only know about files.
  (unless buffer-file-name
    (user-error "Can only rename in file-visiting buffers"))
  (let ((regexp (concat "\\_<" (regexp-quote (thing-at-point 'symbol t)) "\=
\_>"))
        (defun (bounds-of-thing-at-point 'defun))
        (case-fold-search nil)
        (edits '()))
    (save-excursion
      (goto-char (car defun))
      (while (re-search-forward regexp (cdr defun) t)
        (push (list (match-beginning 0) (match-end 0) newname) edits)))
    (list (make-instance 'refactor-file-edit
                         :file buffer-file-name :edits edits))))

;;;; Actions

(defun elisp-refactor--form-at (pos)
  "Return (OPEN . FORM) if POS is on the paren or head of a non-top-level l=
ist."
  (save-excursion
    (goto-char pos)
    (when (and (eq (char-before) ?\() (looking-at "\\_<"))
      (backward-char))
    (let ((ppss (syntax-ppss)))
      (when (and (eq (char-after) ?\()
                 (cl-plusp (car ppss))
                 (not (nth 8 ppss)))
        (ignore-errors (cons (point) (read (current-buffer))))))))

(defun elisp-refactor--unused (&optional beg end)
  "Return (POS . NAME) for unused variables diagnosed between BEG and END."
  (cl-loop for d in (flymake-diagnostics beg end)
           for msg =3D (flymake-diagnostic-text d '(message))
           when (string-match "\\`Unused lexical \\(?:variable\\|argument\\=
) \
[`=E2=80=98']\\([^'=E2=80=99]+\\)" msg)
           collect (cons (flymake-diagnostic-beg d) (match-string 1 msg))))

(cl-defmethod refactor-backend-actions
    ((_backend (eql elisp-refactor)) beg _end &key rkind trigger-kind
     &allow-other-keys)
  ;; This runs every time point moves in `refactor-suggestion-mode', so
  ;; keep it cheap: actions only record what `refactor-backend-execute'
  ;; needs to do the actual work.
  (let ((actions '())
        (form-at (elisp-refactor--form-at beg)))
    (cl-flet ((offer (kind title &rest data)
                (when (refactor-kind-matches-p kind rkind)
                  (push (make-instance 'refactor-action
                                       :title title :kind kind
                                       :preferred (eq kind 'quickfix)
                                       :backend 'elisp-refactor
                                       :data data)
                        actions))))
      (pcase-dolist (`(,pos . ,name) (elisp-refactor--unused beg))
        (offer 'quickfix (format "Prefix `%s' with underscore" name)
               :positions (list pos)))
      ;; Whole-file actions apply anywhere, so offer them only when
      ;; explicitly asked, not when `refactor-suggestion-mode' asks
      ;; with TRIGGER-KIND 2, lest its indicator show up everywhere.
      (when-let* (((not (eql trigger-kind 2)))
                  (all (elisp-refactor--unused)))
        (offer 'fix-all "Prefix all unused variables with underscore"
               :positions (mapcar #'car all)))
      (pcase-let ((`(,open . ,form) form-at))
        (pcase form
          (`(if ,_ ,_ . ,_)
           (offer 'rewrite "Convert `if' to `cond'"
                  :open open :fn #'elisp-refactor--if-to-cond))
          (`(,(and head (pred macrop)) . ,_)
           (offer 'macroexpand (format "Expand `%s' once" head)
                  :open open :fn #'macroexpand-1)
           (offer 'macroexpand (format "Expand `%s' fully" head)
                  :open open :fn #'macroexpand-all)))))
    (nreverse actions)))

(defun elisp-refactor--if-to-cond (form)
  "Rewrite FORM, an `if', as a `cond', flattening nested else `if's."
  (pcase-let ((`(if ,test ,then . ,else) form))
    `(cond (,test ,then)
           ,@(pcase else
               ('() nil)
               (`((if . ,_)) (cdr (elisp-refactor--if-to-cond (car else))))
               (_ `((t ,@else)))))))

(defun elisp-refactor--rewrite (open fn)
  "Return edits replacing the form at OPEN with FN's rewrite of it.
Comments inside the form are lost."
  (save-excursion
    (goto-char open)
    (let* ((column (current-column))
           (form (read (current-buffer)))
           (text (string-trim-right (pp-to-string (funcall fn form)))))
      `((,open ,(point) ,(string-replace "\n" (concat "\n" (make-string col=
umn ?\s))
                                         text))))))

(cl-defmethod refactor-backend-execute ((_backend (eql elisp-refactor)) act=
ion)
  (let* ((data (oref action data))
         (edits (if-let* ((positions (plist-get data :positions)))
                    (mapcar (lambda (pos) (list pos pos "_")) positions)
                  (elisp-refactor--rewrite (plist-get data :open)
                                           (plist-get data :fn)))))
    (if buffer-file-name
        (refactor-apply-changeset
         (list (make-instance 'refactor-file-edit
                              :file buffer-file-name :edits edits))
         :origin this-command)
      ;; Changesets can't target non-file buffers, but we can still use
      ;; refactor's machinery for applying edits.
      (refactor-apply-text-edits edits))))

(provide 'elisp-refactor)
;;; elisp-refactor.el ends here

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > I understand it. The thing is that I disagree. An exception is made for 
  > search engines just because search engines are deemed necessary.

As the one who established these policies, I know what the reasons were.
I did not make an "exception for search engines".  They are not SaaSS
because they do not fit the definition.

The term SaaSS, "Service as a Software Substitute", looks a lot like
"SaaS", "Software as a service."  That is no coincidence.  I chose the
term "SaaSS" to mock "SaaS".

But SaaSS is something rather specific, and it is unjust for a
specific reason.

As for SaaS (Software as a Service), that is a very broad term.  Not
all kinds of SaaS are unjust.  For instance, renting a server (real or
virtual) on which you control the software load is not a bad thing.
An unenshittified search engine is basically ok -- it does not need an
"exception".  Google's Smirch is another story.  (Look at meaning 2 of
"smirch" in Wiktionary.)

I chose "SaaSS" to mock "SaaS", but later I came to the conclusion
that the terms are too similar.  A couple of years ago I held a
discussion looking for a new term to replace "SaaSS".  But the
discussion did not converge on a term to use.

> From: João Távora <joaotavora@gmail.com>
> Date: Wed, 14 Oct 2026 22:03:40 +0100
> 
> For the past two months or so I've been slowly working on pulling
> Eglot's code actions machinery out into a new library,
> lisp/progmodes/refactor.el, so that it's not tied to LSP anymore.  The
> attached patch is the result of that work.
> 
> It's a :core package that's setup as an Eglot dependency, just like
> Flymake, ElDoc, Xref and others.
> 
> This fell partially out of an old request from Eli to work on something
> like this (or so I seem to remember) and, more recently, from some
> discussion with Eshel Yaron about Flymake having "quickfix" commands,
> where he and I disagreed on how to implement it.  Quickfixes are
> supported of course, and they're just another kind of action.

Yes, I think having refactoring capabilities in Emacs is a very
important improvement.  Thank you for working on this.

> The working concept of actions came from LSP, obviously.  I and probably
> most Eglot users have been using them for many years now.  It's very
> useful, I use rename hundreds of times a day, and other actions also
> quite frequently.  So IMO it's a battle-tested architecture to adopt in
> refactor.el.
> 
> Roughly, refactor.el has:
> 
> - No manual yet, but the Commentary section is decently fleshed out and
>   could be the start of a manual.
> 
> - Some Elisp entry points for backend authors:
>   refactor-backend-functions, a hook much like xref-backend-functions,
>   except every backend contributes.  Backends implement a few generics:
>   refactor-backend-actions, refactor-backend-execute,
>   refactor-backend-rename-bounds and refactor-backend-rename.
> 
> - Commands: M-x refactor, refactor-rename, refactor-quickfix,
>   refactor-fix-all, refactor-extract, refactor-inline, refactor-rewrite
>   and refactor-organize-imports.
> 
> - A small hierarchy of action kinds (quickfix, rewrite, extract...),
>   extensible with refactor-defkind.
> 
> - Changesets: lists of operations (file edits, creations, renames,
>   deletions) that refactor-apply-changeset carries out, honoring
>   refactor-confirmation (summary, diff, etc.).  That's what used to be
>   eglot-confirm-server-edits.
> 
> - refactor-suggestion-mode: the ElDoc-based "actions available here"
>   indicator Eglot had.
> 
> Eglot is now just one backend, and its old commands and variables are
> obsolete aliases that point to the new commands.  I've been daily
> driving this in Eglot for some weeks now.  The only visible backward
> incompatibility I've noticed is that the keybinding I had for
> eglot-code-actions doesn't show up in the ElDoc suggestion anymore, so
> instead of my clangd saying '[f4]: Swap operands to ==' it now says 'M-x
> refactor: Swap operands to =='.  That's just because I haven't bothered
> to bind f4 to M-x refactor.  The binding itself still works fine.

If you think refactor.el is already in good shape, feel free to add it
to Emacs (with a NEWS item announcing that).  Adding documentation is
always welcome, but we can always do this later, and in any case it
might be wise to wait with user-level documentation until we have more
than just one backend in the tree.

On 10/15/2026 5:15 AM, Richard Stallman wrote:
> [[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
> [[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
> [[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]
> 
>    > I understand it. The thing is that I disagree. An exception is made for
>    > search engines just because search engines are deemed necessary.
> 
> As the one who established these policies, I know what the reasons were.
> I did not make an "exception for search engines".  They are not SaaSS
> because they do not fit the definition.
> 
> The term SaaSS, "Service as a Software Substitute", looks a lot like
> "SaaS", "Software as a service."  That is no coincidence.  I chose the
> term "SaaSS" to mock "SaaS".
> 
> But SaaSS is something rather specific, and it is unjust for a
> specific reason.
> 
> As for SaaS (Software as a Service), that is a very broad term.  Not
> all kinds of SaaS are unjust.  For instance, renting a server (real or
> virtual) on which you control the software load is not a bad thing.
> An unenshittified search engine is basically ok -- it does not need an
> "exception".  Google's Smirch is another story.  (Look at meaning 2 of
> "smirch" in Wiktionary.)

By your definition, SaaSS is computing I could do with a program on my 
own computer.

For web search, that program exists: YaCy, LPGL. Crawls, indexes and 
ranks on the user's own computer.

So web search is my own computing, and a search engine doing it for me 
is SaaSS by your own test.

> 
> Understood. I am fine with that. But I want to ask, if their changes can be compressed to be within 15LOC, can it be acceptable without revert? I am afraid if we revert builds for more than Windows might break and we'll have to redo it differently to get it to build. 

Actually, the MinGW related changes look strange to me.  Linking
against a DLL on Windows doesn't need to tell the linker to look in
the bin/ subdirectory where the DLL lives.  The linker should look at
the import library, which should live in the lib/ subdirectory, where
the linker looks on all platforms.

To explain this in more detail: when a DLL is built on Windows, the
build should produce 2 files: FOO.dll and FOO.dll.a.  The former is
the DLL, which will be loaded at run time; the latter is the import
library which the linker will find if the link command says -lFOO, as
it does on Unix.

So if the import library is generated when mupdf is built on Windows,
then the changes in the first patch above should not be necessary.
And if the import library is NOT generated (or included in the mupdf
installation), then it's a bug in mupdf, not in your module.

Maybe I'm missing something, in which case the person who contributed
those changes is kindly asked to explain why those changes were
needed.

Thanks.

Eli Zaretskii <eliz@gnu.org> writes:

>> >> https://codeberg.org/MonadicSheep/emacs-reader/commit/43b23e19e7a6e0c8ba07a7cd8e276d5e5c86dcf8
>> >>
>> >> https://codeberg.org/MonadicSheep/emacs-reader/commit/873cb28a6d9ea1be7dba7f926c7ede961049e9ae
>> >
>> > I think we do need copyright assignment for these.  I think your only
>> > option if you can't get it is to revert and wait until someone else who
>> > hasn't seen the old code happens to come along and implement it.
>> 
>> Understood. I am fine with that. But I want to ask, if their changes
>> can be compressed to be within 15LOC, can it be acceptable without
>> revert? I am afraid if we revert builds for more than Windows might
>> break and we'll have to redo it differently to get it to build.
>
> Actually, the MinGW related changes look strange to me.  Linking
> against a DLL on Windows doesn't need to tell the linker to look in
> the bin/ subdirectory where the DLL lives.  The linker should look at
> the import library, which should live in the lib/ subdirectory, where
> the linker looks on all platforms.

I suspect the patch author's environment was not configured correctly
and somehow endend linking directly against the .dll instead of the
.dll.a, which is supported.

So the changes related to that part are unneeded.

Then, the changes to the README are obsolete: MSYS2 already has a new
mupdf package, the referenced PR was merged and, more importantly, the
MINGW64 is deprecated and on its way to removal. Actually, mupdf is not
available on MINGW64, only on the officially supported environments:
UCRT64, CLANG64 and CLANGARM64. So that part of the patch can be
discarded and rewritten with current information.

The changes to .gitignore can be also left out, although they are
trivial.

So it seems that only the changes to Makefile are really required, which
looks like they are below the 15 LOC threshold, moreover when one patch
partly modifies the previous one.

Thank you for your engagement on this issue.  Here are
my thoughts on the unresolved issues raised so far.

MS-Windows Guest account: even though this account, with low
id 501, is *less* privileged, it still falls under the case of
a special id that should continue to own its files, even when
they are edited by an administrator with a different id.

Should there be an upper limit: no, I don't think we need one.
IDs above the historic upper limit for regular users (60000)
are used for dynamic users that are unlikely to own any
persistent files that anyone would edit.

 < Stephen

[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

When you are reading a document using emacs-reader,
how does that document appear to Emacs Lisp programs?
Is it possible for programs to access the contents of a document
by calling functions from Lisp code?  Is the document something like a buffer?
If you call `buffer-string' on it, do you get Lisp data representing
its contents?  That would be truly Emacs-like integration.

Likewise, when the document is displayed, how does its screen image
relate to windows and buffers?  Is it smoothly integrated with
the rest of Emacs display?

Looks good to me, thanks.  Nice improvement.
Some comments below.


=== Stefan


> +(defvar refactor-mouse-map
> +  (let ((map (make-sparse-keymap)))
> +    (define-key map [mouse-2] #'refactor-at-mouse)
> +    (define-key map [left-margin mouse-1] #'refactor-at-mouse)
> +    map)
> +  "Keymap active on action indicators and clickable diagnostics.")
[...]
> +            (setq indicator
> +                  (propertize refactor-indicator
> +                              'face 'refactor-indicator-face
> +                              'help-echo "mouse-1: execute actions at point"
> +                              'mouse-face 'highlight
> +                              'keymap refactor-mouse-map))

The code binds `mouse-2` rather than `mouse-1`.  IIRC the default value
of `mouse-1-click-follows-link` will make `mouse-1` also work, but IIRC
that same machinery should take care of changing the help-echo
accordingly, so the help-echo should say `mouse-2`.

> +(defalias 'refactor-at-mouse (refactor--mouse-call 'refactor)
> +  "Like `refactor', but intended for mouse events.")
> [...]
> +    (define-key map [mode-line mouse-1]
> +                (refactor--mouse-call 'refactor-at-mouse t))

AFAICT, `refactor--mouse-call` takes a function as argument, so I'd use
`#'` to quote its argument.  More importantly, this seems to wrap
`refactor` in two layers of `refactor--mouse-call`.

Also, why does the `mode-line mouse-1` binding need `update-mode-line`
while the other bindings don't?

> +(defun refactor--mouse-call (what &optional update-mode-line)
> +  "Make an interactive lambda for calling WHAT with the mouse."
> +  (lambda (event)
> +    (interactive "e")
> +    (let ((start (event-start event)))
> +      (with-selected-window (posn-window start)
> +        (save-excursion
> +          (unless (posn-area start)
> +            (goto-char (posn-point start)))
> +          (call-interactively what)
> +          (when update-mode-line
> +            (force-mode-line-update t)))))))

I think it's usually best to use a single command that works both for mouse
events and for other events (the above code should work fine with plain
old key events), so that `where-is` gives more informative results.
So I'd recommend renaming `refactor` to `refactor--1` and
`refactor-at-mouse` to `refactor`.

Also this probably deserves a comment explaining why we don't use
`posn-set-point`.

I'd want a comment explaining why we need to call
`force-mode-line-update` and especially why we need to do it with
a non-nil arg.

IIUC when we use `refactor(-at-mouse)` binding in the mode-line it will
operate "at point" (rather than at the mouse-click), which sounds fair,
but when using the binding in the left-margin it will also operate "at
point" whereas I'd expect it to operate at a place related to where
I clicked in the margin.

Admittedly, I haven't tried it out yet, so
maybe I just misunderstand some aspect of the UI.
Oh wait, I guess the event for margin clicks give as `posn-point` the
position of the buffer text that has the `display` property (and
doesn't have a `posn-area`)?  Yeah, that's probably it.

> +;;;###autoload
> +(define-minor-mode refactor-suggestion-mode
> +  "Minor mode for showing refactoring suggestions at point.
> +Add `refactor-suggestion' to `eldoc-documentation-functions' and
> +show `refactor-mode-line-indicator' while actions are available."
> +  :init-value nil
> +  :lighter refactor-mode-line-indicator
> +  (if refactor-suggestion-mode
> +      (add-hook 'eldoc-documentation-functions #'refactor-suggestion nil t)
> +    (remove-hook 'eldoc-documentation-functions #'refactor-suggestion t)
> +    (when (overlay-buffer refactor--suggestion-overlay)
> +      (delete-overlay refactor--suggestion-overlay))))

Maybe this should come with a globalized version that's enabled as soon
as there are `refactor-backend-functions` (so Eglot doesn't need
to enable the mode explicitly)?  Or maybe even a plain old global mode?

Richard Stallman <rms@gnu.org> writes:

> [[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
> [[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
> [[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]
>
> When you are reading a document using emacs-reader,
> how does that document appear to Emacs Lisp programs?
> Is it possible for programs to access the contents of a document
> by calling functions from Lisp code?  Is the document something like a buffer?
> If you call `buffer-string' on it, do you get Lisp data representing
> its contents?  That would be truly Emacs-like integration.

Right now in the `master` branch, a document for Emacs is a buffer with an overlay that has specific :display, :window and other properties. Right now `buffer-string' will simply give the binary PDF data from the buffer, which is pretty much useless.

So the issue is, a PDF document has two forms:
1. binary data
2. rendered image of the binary data

The binary data itself is, in my opinion, unusable. We /must/ first render the data into an image. But the issue then is how to interact with the document when it is shown as an image?

I think there are a few avenues to us. With the dynamic module, we basically have the entirety of libmupdf available to us. Which means, any operation libmupdf can do (which is a lot), we can also do via emacs-reader. Examples of this would be: say, you want to write a lisp program that takes all the text of the current page and do some operation on it. That would be very much possible (and is indeed via another branch that hasn't been merged yet) by simply writing a thin wrapper around a module function that calls a libmupdf function which gives us the page's text as a UTF-8 string. All of this can be made available to Emacs Lisp.

Similarly, various other data can be fetched via libmupdf such as images, embedded media, annotations, signatures, etc. We can also get every bit of metadata. And of course we can operate on each of this data in manipulating the document, say for redacting some text, or removing annotations. And now that we have canvas image type, we do not have any limitations on graphical operations either.

To reiterate: anything that libmupdf allows, can be done to a PDF or any supported document format, as long as we have an Elisp function that wraps a module funcall and uses the appropriate libmupdf functions. Using this, one can programmatically call such primitive functions and use their returned data within Emacs for any purpose. What Emacs needs to provide are: the coordinates in the rendered image where it wants the data. We can then ask mupdf to give us any kind of data for these given coordinates. We can do this at any level of granularity: coordinates, pages, or entire document.

A few things we've taken in this direction in another branch is to have 'embedded cursors', i.e., a cursor /inside/ the rendered image showing the document. This cursor duplicates Emacs' buffer notions of point, mark and region allowing you to move /within/ the text via C-f/b/n/p, mark, yank, etc. It is a rudimentary implementation as a proof of concept. But by allowing such navigation, we can then allow Emacs to operate on a given region programmatically. Of course, this can also be done by simply selecting a region with the mouse. We plan to later use this to integrate Emacspeak and make documents accessible for visually impaired users.

> Likewise, when the document is displayed, how does its screen image
> relate to windows and buffers?  Is it smoothly integrated with
> the rest of Emacs display?

Each window holds its own overlay which gets updated separately. We have certain metadata that is buffer-local. Since it is just an overlay, it integrates fine and can be manipulated in any manner.

Regards,
-- 
Divya Ranjan Pattanaik,
Philosophy, Mathematics, Libre Software.

>From 5d238b9739dbc5f57f43e3f124ca627fade9e4b9 Mon Sep 17 00:00:00 2001
From: Arash Esbati <arash@gnu.org>
Date: Fri, 16 Oct 2026 14:19:19 +0200
Subject: [PATCH] Add updated instructions for Windows build

* README.org (Windows): Add updated instructions for building the
package on Windows.  Mention also that Emacs must be built for the
UCRT64 environment as well.
---
 README.org | 16 ++++++++++++++++
 1 file changed, 16 insertions(+)

diff --git a/README.org b/README.org
index 78fb672..5ff550e 100644
--- a/README.org
+++ b/README.org
@@ -118,6 +118,22 @@ And then use the straight or package-vc recipe from the [[* GNU/Linux][GNU/Linux
 
 Find more information [[https://codeberg.org/divyaranjan/emacs-reader/issues/142#issuecomment-8854941][here]].
 
+** Windows
+Install the needed files in a working MSYS2 environment.  Open a
+=UCRT64= shell and insert:
+#+begin_src shell
+  pacman -S --needed base-devel   \
+  mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-toolchain \
+  mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-git       \
+  mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-libmupdf
+#+end_src
+
+Note that the MSYS2 project doesn't provide =libmupdf= for the
+=MINGW64= environment.  Hence, your Emacs must be built for the
+=UCRT64= environment as well.
+
+Now proceed with the steps described in [[* GNU/Linux][GNU/Linux]] section.
+
 ** Manual
 *** User lisp directory (recommended)
 1. Clone the repository into ~~/.emacs.d/user-lisp/~,
--

Divya Ranjan Pattanaik <divya@dialetheia.xyz> writes:

> Lastly, we would greatly appreciate a thorough review and any feedback
> on the package.

Many thanks for working on this and congratulations.  I didn't install
the package, but had a brief look at the Makefile (while preparing the
patch for Windows).  I have some comments reg. build on macOS:

In the Makefile, you have:

  CC := gcc

On macOS, gcc is actually Apple Clang:

  $ gcc --version
  Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.3.34.2)
  Target: arm64-apple-darwin25.6.0
  Thread model: posix
  InstalledDir: /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools/usr/bin

  $ which gcc
  /usr/bin/gcc

If you install gcc via Homebrew, the binary has the version attached to
gcc, e.g.:

  $ gcc-16 --version
  gcc-16 (Homebrew GCC 16.2.0) 16.2.0
  Copyright (C) 2026 Free Software Foundation, Inc.
  This is free software; see the source for copying conditions.  There is NO
  warranty; not even for MERCHANTABILITY or FITNESS FOR A PARTICULAR
  PURPOS

  $ which gcc-16
  /opt/homebrew/bin/gcc-16

I'm not sure what's the best way forward is since I didn't try to build
the package.  IIUC, the compilation will break if users do:

  $ brew install gcc

as described in the README.org.

Another thing is the mupdf detection via brew in the Makefile:

  # macOS manual detection via brew
  BREW_PREFIX := $(shell brew --prefix mupdf 2>/dev/null)

which returns for me:

  /opt/homebrew/opt/mupdf

but I don't have mupdf installed.

  $ ls `brew --prefix mupdf`
  ls: cannot access '/opt/homebrew/opt/mupdf': No such file or directory

Maybe the Makefile should check if the directory actually exists.

Finally, Homebrew provides two packages (Formulae in Homebrew parlance):
mupdf and mupdf-tools.  I have mupdf-tools installed:

  $ brew --prefix mupdf-tools
  /opt/homebrew/opt/mupdf-tools

  $ ls `brew --prefix mupdf-tools`
  /opt/homebrew/opt/mupdf-tools@

which is a symlink to ../Cellar/mupdf-tools/1.28.5/.  Maybe the Makefile
could also check if mupdf-tools is installed which provides the files
Reader needs to build.

Again, I didn't try to build the package.  Feel free to ignore the above
if my comments are off.

HTH.  Best, Arash

> Furthermore, the next major version (0.5.0) is planned to be based on
> the canvas image type .

> Lastly, we would greatly appreciate a thorough review and any feedback
> on the package. The Emacs Lisp files are in the root directory, while
> the C files live in render/ directory.

Would it make sense to postpone the inclusion of your package
until version 0.5 is released? It seems like a major rewrite to
me, which would obsolete most of the reviews from here.

~~

I'd also like to revisit our discussion [1] about the naming of
your package. On the one side, I acknowledge that names of
Emacs-Lisp packages should be self-explanatory and discoverable.
On the other side, I think it is bad for the community and the
diversity of packages, when a package is named in a way that
suggests that it is the default, standard, one-and-only package to
solve the problem at hand.

In marketing and branding, this strategy is called =E2=80=9Ccategory
ownership=E2=80=9D, I think. From the perspective of maximizing the number
of users of your package, this is likely good. But for Emacs
users, it is often confusing and misleading; and for authors of
similar document-viewing Emacs-Lisp packages, it might feel
unfair.

We already have this problem with packages like =E2=80=9Clsp-mode=E2=80=9D =
[2]
where a lot of Emacs users assume it is the one and only way to
use LSP in Emacs and don't even consider that Emacs might have a
built-in LSP client.

Of course, it still is as trade-off between the mentioned two
sides, meaning no naming can be ideal. But personally, I'm
convinced that =E2=80=9CThe Emacs Reader=E2=80=9D / =E2=80=9CEmacs Reader=
=E2=80=9D / =E2=80=9CReader=E2=80=9D is
too generic in mentioned regards.

~~

Kind regards
Mekeor

[1] https://codeberg.org/MonadicSheep/emacs-reader/issues/65

[2] https://github.com/emacs-lsp/lsp-mode

>
> as described in the README.org.
>
> Another thing is the mupdf detection via brew in the Makefile:
>
>   # macOS manual detection via brew

>
> which returns for me:
>

>

>   ls: cannot access '/opt/homebrew/opt/mupdf': No such file or directory

>

>
> which is a symlink to ../Cellar/mupdf-tools/1.28.5/.  Maybe the Makefile

> >   ls: cannot access '/opt/homebrew/opt/mupdf': No such file or director=
y
> >
> > Maybe the Makefile should check if the directory actually exists.

> > Finally, Homebrew provides two packages (Formulae in Homebrew parlance)=
:

$ brew ls --versions mupdf # zero exit status indicates installed
$ brew --prefix # query the ambient homebrew prefix; returns, e.g.,
/opt/homebrew
$ brew --prefix --installed mupdf # ditto on zero exit status and combines
both above into one

>From there you can tell make what's what.

--8<---------------cut here---------------start------------->8---
(progn
  (add-to-list 'load-path
               (directory-file-name "~/.emacs.d/lisp/emacs-reader/")
               t)

  (byte-recompile-directory (expand-file-name "~/.emacs.d/lisp/emacs-reader/")
                            0 t)
  
  (loaddefs-generate
   (expand-file-name "~/.emacs.d/lisp/emacs-reader/")
   (expand-file-name "~/.emacs.d/lisp/emacs-reader/reader-autoloads.el"))

  (load "~/.emacs.d/lisp/emacs-reader/reader-autoloads.el" nil t t) )
--8<---------------cut here---------------end--------------->8---

>>
>> We already have this problem with packages like =E2=80=9Clsp-mode=E2=80=
=9D [2]

I'd like to make another argument: In context of Emacs, the term
=E2=80=9Creader=E2=80=9D is already used for many other things: The lisp re=
ader,

al.

=80=9D
will have a negative effect on searchability for users.

Mekeor Melire <mekeor@posteo.de> writes:
>
>> But, if others here have any suggestions on a change of name,
>> I'm all ears :)
>
> Before searching for new names, we should discuss with arguments
> whether renaming is appropriate.

Sure, I'm open to hear others' opinions on this. My arguments have been made an year ago, so I don't wish to repeat them in deail again. In short, I don't think it is /necessary/ to change the name. A brief scroll through elpa.gnu.org would show several packages with very generic names. To name a few: bluetooth.el, chess, djvu, scaner, typewriter, web-server, etc.

So, yes, it is a generic name, but I have not seen genericity being considered a negative indicator when considering the package names for ELPA submission.

I understand that some people have the opinion that generic names should be avoided, but I differ from such an opinion. For me, the name should first and foremost signify the goal of the program. In this case, it does. It's a program to read documents.

Let's hear what others have to say on this. That said, if Emacs or ELPA maintainers consider it absolutely necessary for the package to be renamed to be considered for inclusion in ELPA, I will comply.

Divya Ranjan Pattanaik <divya@dialetheia.xyz> writes:

> Mekeor Melire <mekeor@posteo.de> writes:
>>
>>> But, if others here have any suggestions on a change of name,
>>> I'm all ears :)
>>
>> Before searching for new names, we should discuss with arguments
>> whether renaming is appropriate.
>
> Sure, I'm open to hear others' opinions on this. My arguments have
> been made an year ago, so I don't wish to repeat them in deail
> again. In short, I don't think it is /necessary/ to change the name. A
> brief scroll through elpa.gnu.org would show several packages with
> very generic names. To name a few: bluetooth.el, chess, djvu, scaner,
> typewriter, web-server, etc.

I guess in all these examples, the names are generic but just generic
enough to describe their use-cases.  I think that Mekeor has a point
that "Reader" as a description is a broader term that could create
confusion.

> So, yes, it is a generic name, but I have not seen genericity being considered a negative indicator when considering the package names for ELPA submission.

There have been differences of opinions here, usually more along the
lines that packages have obscure references, jokes or cultural
connotations that don't hint what a package is about.  Rarely have we
had the opposite case like here, that a package is non-specific enough.

> I understand that some people have the opinion that generic names
> should be avoided, but I differ from such an opinion. For me, the name
> should first and foremost signify the goal of the program. In this
> case, it does. It's a program to read documents.

What would your opinion be on "doc-reader" or "doc-read"?  You could use
shorthands within the development the abbreviate the symbols, if you are
concerned about that.  The user will probably not care much either way,
since the major mode will be enabled via auto-mode-alist and IIRC the
relevant commands were all bound and not invoked using M-x.  Also it
would be a nice parallel to doc-view.

> Let's hear what others have to say on this. That said, if Emacs or
> ELPA maintainers consider it absolutely necessary for the package to
> be renamed to be considered for inclusion in ELPA, I will comply.

For my part, I wouldn't say that it is necessary if you and the other
maintainers of the package insist.  In the contribution guidelines, we
list our preferences about package names under the list of soft
criteria[0], that we do not enforce but would like you to still take
seriously.  I know that Stefan is never a fan of these kinds of
discussions (but as I said, they are usually in favor of making a
package name more generic), so you can wait for him to give an opinion
or ping him directly; other than that it is up to you.

[0] https://elpa.gnu.org/contributing.html#check-name

> Regards,

Stefan Monnier <monnier@iro.umontreal.ca> writes:

> Looks good to me, thanks.  Nice improvement.
> Some comments below.

Thanks for the careful read.  Most of the thing you found are real
problems and they came from Eglot directly.

>> +(defvar refactor-mouse-map
>> +  (let ((map (make-sparse-keymap)))
>> +    (define-key map [mouse-2] #'refactor-at-mouse)
>> +    (define-key map [left-margin mouse-1] #'refactor-at-mouse)
>> +    map)
>> +  "Keymap active on action indicators and clickable diagnostics.")
> [...]
>> +            (setq indicator
>> +                  (propertize refactor-indicator
>> +                              'face 'refactor-indicator-face
>> +                              'help-echo "mouse-1: execute actions at p=
oint"
>> +                              'mouse-face 'highlight
>> +                              'keymap refactor-mouse-map))
>
> The code binds `mouse-2` rather than `mouse-1`.  IIRC the default value
> of `mouse-1-click-follows-link` will make `mouse-1` also work, but IIRC
> that same machinery should take care of changing the help-echo
> accordingly, so the help-echo should say `mouse-2`.

Right, the help-echo is wrong and already broken in Eglot (and nobody
complained, hehe). Does mouse-1 really work there?  I think
`mouse-1-click-follows-link` only kicks in if a some of property on the
text.  I can't add that to the shared refactor-mouse-map anyway, because
a plain mouse-1 click in a diagnostic span would start executing
actions, and we want it to set point.

>> +(defalias 'refactor-at-mouse (refactor--mouse-call 'refactor)
>> +  "Like `refactor', but intended for mouse events.")
>> [...]
>> +    (define-key map [mode-line mouse-1]
>> +                (refactor--mouse-call 'refactor-at-mouse t))
>
> AFAICT, `refactor--mouse-call` takes a function as argument, so I'd use
> `#'` to quote its argument.  More importantly, this seems to wrap
> `refactor` in two layers of `refactor--mouse-call`.

Indeed the double wrapping was a brain fart.  Though I'm happy if we can
get rid of it, see below.

> Also, why does the `mode-line mouse-1` binding need `update-mode-line`
> while the other bindings don't?

It doesn't.  That's inherited from Eglot's mode-line menus, where
commands change server state and the mode-line must catch up.  It
doesn't apply here, so I've removed the UPDATE-MODE-LINE arg
altogether, which also answers your `force-mode-line-update` question
below.

>> +(defun refactor--mouse-call (what &optional update-mode-line)
>> +  "Make an interactive lambda for calling WHAT with the mouse."
>> +  (lambda (event)
>> +    (interactive "e")
>> +    (let ((start (event-start event)))
>> +      (with-selected-window (posn-window start)
>> +        (save-excursion
>> +          (unless (posn-area start)
>> +            (goto-char (posn-point start)))
>> +          (call-interactively what)
>> +          (when update-mode-line
>> +            (force-mode-line-update t)))))))
>
> I think it's usually best to use a single command that works both for mou=
se
> events and for other events (the above code should work fine with plain
> old key events), so that `where-is` gives more informative results.
> So I'd recommend renaming `refactor` to `refactor--1` and
> `refactor-at-mouse` to `refactor`.

Very reasonable goal, and I never liked the Eglot solution anyway.  I've
actually made two versions, but the one I've pushed to the branch is, I
think, the one you suggest: `refactor--1` + a new `refactor` command
takes an optional EVENT, defaulting to `last-nonmenu-event`, and
dispatches on `mouse-event-p`.

(There is another one version which keeps `refactor`'s (BEG END RKIND
INTERACTIVE) signature and teaches its interactive spec about mouse
events: it computes the bounds where the click happened.  Looked more
complicated.)

> Also this probably deserves a comment explaining why we don't use
> `posn-set-point`.

Added: it would move point and select the window permanently, whereas we
just want to run the command there and put things back.  Though I'm not
super-sure this comment is that essential...

> I'd want a comment explaining why we need to call
> `force-mode-line-update` and especially why we need to do it with
> a non-nil arg.

Gone, see above.

> IIUC when we use `refactor(-at-mouse)` binding in the mode-line it will
> operate "at point" (rather than at the mouse-click), which sounds fair,
> but when using the binding in the left-margin it will also operate "at
> point" whereas I'd expect it to operate at a place related to where
> I clicked in the margin.
>
> Admittedly, I haven't tried it out yet, so
> maybe I just misunderstand some aspect of the UI.
> Oh wait, I guess the event for margin clicks give as `posn-point` the
> position of the buffer text that has the `display` property (and
> doesn't have a `posn-area`)?  Yeah, that's probably it.

You made me bring all this into the brain cache, but I think have it
now: your first reading is right: for a margin click `posn-area` is
`left-margin` and `posn-point` is just the beginning of the clicked
line, so it operates at point.  But that's by design: the indicator only
ever appears on point's line, standing for the actions at point, so a
click on it means "point".  It isn't as simple as going to `posn-point`
anyway, the diagnostic is often not there.  The comment should clarify.

Thinking about this did turn up a real bug, though: the indicator
showed in every window displaying the buffer, but it stands for point
in just one of them.  Clicking it in another window, with point
elsewhere, ran actions at the wrong place.  This was already the case
in Eglot since the margin binding went in (852d50ecfcf), and nobody
reported it.  Now the overlay has a `window` property, and the
mode-line indicator also shows only in that window.

>> +;;;###autoload
>> +(define-minor-mode refactor-suggestion-mode
>> +  "Minor mode for showing refactoring suggestions at point.
>> +Add `refactor-suggestion' to `eldoc-documentation-functions' and
>> +show `refactor-mode-line-indicator' while actions are available."
>> +  :init-value nil
>> +  :lighter refactor-mode-line-indicator
>> +  (if refactor-suggestion-mode
>> +      (add-hook 'eldoc-documentation-functions #'refactor-suggestion ni=
l t)
>> +    (remove-hook 'eldoc-documentation-functions #'refactor-suggestion t)
>> +    (when (overlay-buffer refactor--suggestion-overlay)
>> +      (delete-overlay refactor--suggestion-overlay))))
>
> Maybe this should come with a globalized version that's enabled as soon
> as there are `refactor-backend-functions` (so Eglot doesn't need
> to enable the mode explicitly)?  Or maybe even a plain old global mode?

I don't really see the point, to be honest.  Eglot enables
`refactor-suggestion-mode` exactly like it handles Flymake, ElDoc, Xref
and friends: buffer-locally, when it starts managing a buffer, and not
at all if the user said `eglot-stay-out-of`.  A global mode would lose
that consistency and make `eglot-stay-out-of` awkward, for little gain:
it's one line in Eglot, and other backends can do the same.  Major modes
providing a backend might as well enable it.  Also the mode's lighter
_is_ the indicator.

Also, I'm not sure a globalized mode turns on at the right time, maybe
it does so before Eglot or anyone else has had a chance to add to
`refactor-backend-functions`, so "enabled as soon as there are backends"
would possibly need extra machinery that I don't find justified.

Jo=C3=A3o

>
> > So, yes, it is a generic name, but I have not seen genericity being

PA
> submission.
>
> There have been differences of opinions here, usually more along the
> lines that packages have obscure references, jokes or cultural
> connotations that don't hint what a package is about.  Rarely have we
> had the opposite case like here, that a package is non-specific enough.
>
> > I understand that some people have the opinion that generic names
> > should be avoided, but I differ from such an opinion. For me, the name
> > should first and foremost signify the goal of the program. In this
> > case, it does. It's a program to read documents.
>
> What would your opinion be on "doc-reader" or "doc-read"?  You could use
> shorthands within the development the abbreviate the symbols, if you are
> concerned about that.  The user will probably not care much either way,
> since the major mode will be enabled via auto-mode-alist and IIRC the
> relevant commands were all bound and not invoked using M-x.  Also it
> would be a nice parallel to doc-view.
>
> > Let's hear what others have to say on this. That said, if Emacs or
> > ELPA maintainers consider it absolutely necessary for the package to
> > be renamed to be considered for inclusion in ELPA, I will comply.
>
> For my part, I wouldn't say that it is necessary if you and the other
> maintainers of the package insist.  In the contribution guidelines, we
> list our preferences about package names under the list of soft
> criteria[0], that we do not enforce but would like you to still take
> seriously.  I know that Stefan is never a fan of these kinds of
> discussions (but as I said, they are usually in favor of making a
> package name more generic), so you can wait for him to give an opinion
> or ping him directly; other than that it is up to you.
>
> [0] https://elpa.gnu.org/contributing.html#check-name


To the degree it could be considered a replacement for doc-view, it could

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > By your definition, SaaSS is computing I could do with a program on my 
  > own computer.

I think you have altered it in restating it.  The crucial point of
SaaSS is that the job doesn't inherently involve anyone but you.  That
implies the job could be done in private on your computer.

Any kind of internet or web search inherently needs to look at the
servers of many others -- it can't be done in private on your computer.
So it is not SaaSS.

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > > I think it is better if I do not take that bait.  If there is a valid
  > > serious point here, someone will make it non-sarcastically.

  > I agree I was sarcastic, more than I intended to.

Thank you.  I forgive you.

                                                      But the point is clear:
  > Is a piece of software that you can run but not rebuild free?

That software certainly has a practical problem.  But we shouldn't try to
squeeze the question into a yes-or-no answer.

There was a somewhat similar situation 25 years ago with programs
written in Java, because no free Java compiler or interpreter existed.
What could we say to describe Java programs whose sources carried free
licenses.

We concluded that Java programs were free but "trapped".  When we made
a free Java implementation, that released those free programs from the
trap.  See https://gnu.org/philosophy/java-trap.html.

The GPU trap is not precisely equivalent to that, but the basic idea fits.

various use cases and report back.)

On 10/17/2026 6:13 AM, Richard Stallman wrote:

>    > Is a piece of software that you can run but not rebuild free?
> 
> That software certainly has a practical problem.  But we shouldn't try to
> squeeze the question into a yes-or-no answer.
> 
> There was a somewhat similar situation 25 years ago with programs
> written in Java, because no free Java compiler or interpreter existed.
> What could we say to describe Java programs whose sources carried free
> licenses.
> 
> We concluded that Java programs were free but "trapped".  When we made
> a free Java implementation, that released those free programs from the
> trap.  See https://gnu.org/philosophy/java-trap.html.
> 
> The GPU trap is not precisely equivalent to that, but the basic idea fits.

I don't think so. Renouncing Java until a free compiler was available 
was possible. Rewritting the programas in another language was possible. 
Having a friend build them for you was possible.

Here, the solution is not getting closer, on the contrary. Also, the 
impact of Java is not comparable to the impact of this thing.

Have you considered using and possibly modifying my program paps,
https://github.com/dov/paps? It renders pango markup to pdf through pango.
The simplest solution would be to turn emacs buffers into pango markup and
then render it with paps. Of course it only supports a subset of emacs
buffer capabilities, e.g. embedded images are not supported. But we could
extend pango markup, and perhaps call it paps markup, that would support
whatever is missing. Or add markdown support to paps.

In any case, let me know if this is a route that interests you.

On 10/17/2026 7:19 PM, Dov Grobgeld wrote:

> Have you considered using and possibly modifying my program paps, 
> https://github.com/dov/paps <https://github.com/dov/paps>? It renders 
> pango markup to pdf through pango. The simplest solution would be to 
> turn emacs buffers into pango markup and then render it with paps. Of 
> course it only supports a subset of emacs buffer capabilities, e.g. 
> embedded images are not supported. But we could extend pango markup, and 
> perhaps call it paps markup, that would support whatever is missing. Or 
> add markdown support to paps.
> 
> In any case, let me know if this is a route that interests you.
I probably should have gone the cairo-pango route instead. The good 
thing about this implementation is that it just lisp, and doesn't need 
any modification to emacs C core, and would be a library that lisp 
programas could use to build pdfs, not only with text, but with 
graphics. The bad thing is that it has to do everything from scratch.

paps seems like a good way. Requires only an external tool, and building 
pango markup should be straightforward from buffer text and properties. 
Also pango markup can do paragraph formatting, can't it? That would be 
really nice.

paps with an emacs package would be useful. I don't think epdf would add 
anything to it.

On 2026-10-16 22:39, Eli Zaretskii wrote:
> This change causes the following new warnings with GCC 9.2.0 on
> MS-Windows when compiling the latest master branch:
> 
>    In file included from getopt.c:44:
>    gettext.h: In function 'dcpgettext_expr':
>    gettext.h:471:3: warning: ISO C90 forbids variable length array 'msg_ctxt_id' [-Wvla]
>      471 |   char msg_ctxt_id[msgctxt_len + msgid_len];
> 	|   ^~~~
>    gettext.h: In function 'dcnpgettext_expr':
>    gettext.h:516:3: warning: ISO C90 forbids variable length array 'msg_ctxt_id' [-Wvla]
>      516 |   char msg_ctxt_id[msgctxt_len + msgid_len];
> 	|   ^~~~

I installed the 3rd attached patch to fix that. This shouldn't affect performance.

>    movemail.c: In function 'movemail_strftime':
>    movemail.c:810:3: warning: ISO C90 forbids variable length array 'fmt' [-Wvla]
>      810 |   char fmt[size + 6], *q;
> 	|   ^~~~

Fixed via the 2nd attached patch, which simplifies the code back to the way it was in 2016 (and makes it run a bit faster). Though the simpler code is less general, it still implements its spec and is good enough for movemail. And the more-general "char fmt[size + 6]" was confusing anyway, as "size" is the size of the destination, not of the incoming format.

>    w32console.c: In function 'turn_on_face':
>    w32console.c:874:3: warning: ISO C90 forbids variable length array 'seq' [-Wvla]
>      874 |   char seq[sz];
> 	|   ^~~~

Fixed by the 1st attached patch, which simplifies the code a tiny bit.

> are we now
> supposed to get rid of all the variable-length arrays in Emacs? why?
Although it's not essential to remove VLAs, it improves portability and makes static analyzers less nervous. VLAs are a notorious source of low-level attacks on C programs, and I suspect that's why Microsoft pushed back on them and got them removed (OK, well, made them optional) in recent editions of the C standard. Even platforms that support VLAs often look askance at them.

For the abovementioned warnings, VLAs were not particularly useful or efficient, and were easy to remove.

Stefan Monnier <monnier@iro.umontreal.ca> writes:

> Sounds good (tho I'm not sure why you need `mouse-event-p`, since the
> `event-start/end` and `posn-*` functions have been designed such that
> you usually don't need to treat mouse events more specially).

You're right `mouse-event-p` isn't needed, but I do like the clarity of
"if this is a mouse-event, we may need to temporarily move point".  And
ctually, I changed my mind and went with a simpler version I found in
the meantime: no shady `refactor--1` internal interactive, and no
"call-at-mouse" wrapper.  `refactor` keeps its (BEG END RKIND
INTERACTIVE) signature and its interactive spec deals with mouse events.
That spec turned out quite short, since margin and mode-line clicks just
mean "point":

  (interactive
   (let ((posn (and (mouse-event-p last-nonmenu-event)
                    (event-start last-nonmenu-event))))
     (when posn (select-window (posn-window posn)))
     `(,@(save-excursion
           ;; Non-text-area clicks (`posn-area' non-nil) already assume
           ;; correct point, but text area clicks are likely on Flymake
           ;; some diagnostic and need moving before `refactor--bounds'.
           (when (and posn (null (posn-area posn)))
             (goto-char (posn-point posn)))
           (refactor--bounds))
       ,(and current-prefix-arg ...)
       t)))

I like that `refactor` is now one function, one name. (refactor BEG END)
stays a usable Lisp entry point returning the actions.  Tests and
backend authors can use that. Also the kind-specific commands have the
same signature again and `eglot-code-actions` can be a plain obsolete
alias again.

>>> Also this probably deserves a comment explaining why we don't use
>>> `posn-set-point`.
>> Added: it would move point and select the window permanently, whereas we
>> just want to run the command there and put things back.  Though I'm not
>> super-sure this comment is that essential...
>
> It could be useful to motivate changes to `posn-set-point` or the
> introduction of some alternative.  IIRC some commands use
> `save-window-excursion` around `posn-set-point`, but indeed
> `with-selected-window` is preferable.  So maybe we should have
> a `with-point-as-posn` or some such.

Could make sense, though with the change above refactor.el no longer has
a use for it.

> Ah, so it's like `cursor-sensor-mode`: it's auto-enabled but never
> auto-disabled.  I suspect we'll eventually want some better way to
> control what sub-feature is activated from which package, but yeah... we
> don't know yet what that should look like.  We'll first have to see
> concrete needs.

Agree.

Jo=C3=A3o

Qiang Sheng <qiangsheng@sjtu.edu.cn> writes:

> Thanks for pointing this out. I've removed the markdown-table-wrap
> dependency and implemented the required table layout directly in
> markdown-ts-appear. Wrapped tables remain available by default.

IMO it isn't really necessary to re-implement the functionality
yourself.  I assume this was done using AI?  As pointed out in the
initial review, one of the main annoyances for humans reading AI code is
that it is much too verbose and more difficult to handle since LLMs
apparently are not trained to be concise (why would they after all if
the business model is pay-per-token).

My advice would really just be to handle this feature as a soft
dependency that your package can enable and integrate if the
markdown-table-wrap is installed, and otherwise gracefully handle the
absence -- that is unless I have misunderstood that this functionality
is essential to the package?

Thanks for the suggestion! Yes, the code was AI-generated, but the =
decision to implement it ourselves was deliberate.

First, I'm not entirely satisfied with an optional dependency. I want =
wrapping to work out of the box as the default, without requiring users =
to install another package. Otherwise, they might never discover it, =
even if it offers a better experience.

Second, this isn't simply a copy of markdown-table-wrap. I've adapted =
the implementation to use Tree-sitter, simplifying the processing logic =
and improving performance.

Finally, the implementation is only about 130 lines. I've reviewed it =
and removed some redundancy, though I may have missed things due to my =
limited experience. I'm happy to hear suggestions for further =
simplification.

I appreciate the feedback, but I think keeping this functionality built =
in is a reasonable choice.

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > Right now in the `master` branch, a document for Emacs is a buffer
  > with an overlay that has specific :display, :window and other
  > properties. Right now `buffer-string' will simply give the binary PDF
  > data from the buffer, which is pretty much useless.

  > So the issue is, a PDF document has two forms: 1. binary data
  > 2. rendered image of the binary data

  > The binary data itself is, in my opinion, unusable. We /must/ first
  > render the data into an image. But the issue then is how to interact
  > with the document when it is shown as an image?

I see the dilemma.  With the current functionality of emacs-reader, is
there an advantage in using a package such as emacs-reader, rather
than launching a free PDF reader program in its own window and
switching between that window and Emacs's frames?

  > I think there are a few avenues to us. With the dynamic module, we
  > basically have the entirety of libmupdf available to us. Which means,
  > any operation libmupdf can do (which is a lot), we can also do via
  > emacs-reader. Examples of this would be: say, you want to write a lisp
  > program that takes all the text of the current page and do some
  > operation on it. That would be very much possible (and is indeed via
  > another branch that hasn't been merged yet) by simply writing a thin
  > wrapper around a module function that calls a libmupdf function which
  > gives us the page's text as a UTF-8 string. All of this can be made
  > available to Emacs Lisp.

This would give emacs-reader a real advantage compared with separate
PDF reader programs.  But we need to verify that the license of
libmupdf is compatible with future versions of the GNU AGPL, not solely
with AGPL version 3.

  > A few things we've taken in this direction in another branch is to
  > have 'embedded cursors', i.e., a cursor /inside/ the rendered image
  > showing the document. This cursor duplicates Emacs' buffer notions of
  > point, mark and region allowing you to move /within/ the text via
  > C-f/b/n/p, mark, yank, etc. It is a rudimentary implementation as a
  > proof of concept. But by allowing such navigation, we can then allow
  > Emacs to operate on a given region programmatically. Of course, this
  > can also be done by simply selecting a region with the mouse. We plan
  > to later use this to integrate Emacspeak and make documents accessible
  > for visually impaired users.

That sounds good, too.

Does this depend on libmupdf, or is it implemented separately?

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

There are many package names (and older file names from before we
called them packages) that mean nothing to users, or that users will
find hard to remember.  Often they spread into command names, too.

For instance, the command to put a mime attachment into an email is in
the file `mml.el' and its name is M-x mml-attach-file.  attach-file is
the natural name for this command, but sometimes I have to strain to
recall the prefix, `mml'.  The file's comments suggest that "MML"
means something related to mime, but I can't find why those three letters.

The command to list the GPG public keys I have is `epa-list-keys'
because it is in a file named `epa.el'.  Sometimes I have to strain to
recall the prefix, "epa".  It is an acronym for Easy PGP Assistant,
which could help me remember it, but not reliably.

Over the decades, lots of Lisp files installed with names that were
not chosen to be helpful to users add up to a major obstacle for using Emacs.

It seems to me that we should try to avoid adding to this obstacle.
To have a standard practice of choosing new, helpful names for packages
when we add them is a natural way to do this.

In other words, keeping the old name is not a good default policy
if we want to help the users.

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > > We concluded that Java programs were free but "trapped".  When we made
  > > a free Java implementation, that released those free programs from the
  > > trap.  See https://gnu.org/philosophy/java-trap.html.
  > > 
  > > The GPU trap is not precisely equivalent to that, but the basic idea fits.

  > I don't think so. Renouncing Java until a free compiler was available 
  > was possible.

That is what we did.  It took a decade.

  > Having a friend build them for you was possible.

That was not a solution.  It would have meant that each of us would
have to send each version of our Java program to the "friend" with the
compiler, to get it compiled.  Basically, that "friend" would be a
SaaSS service (a server that compiles code on demand).

  > Here, the solution is not getting closer, on the contrary.

That is speculation, and vague.  You can't convince the GNU Project to
change its moral standards with handwaving.

Remember, these moral standards are about what is legitimate
for the GNU Project to say and do.  We don't try to dictate
to the users.

                                                               Also, the 
  > impact of Java is not comparable to the impact of this thing.

That is a rather vague statement.  It may be true to some extent, but
it is too vague to imply a specific conclusion.

Divya Ranjan Pattanaik [16/Oct  6:50pm GMT] wrote:
> Mekeor Melire <mekeor@posteo.de> writes:
>>
>>> But, if others here have any suggestions on a change of name,
>>> I'm all ears :)
>>
>> Before searching for new names, we should discuss with arguments
>> whether renaming is appropriate.
>
> Sure, I'm open to hear others' opinions on this. My arguments have
> been made an year ago, so I don't wish to repeat them in deail
> again. In short, I don't think it is /necessary/ to change the name. A
> brief scroll through elpa.gnu.org would show several packages with
> very generic names. To name a few: bluetooth.el, chess, djvu, scaner,
> typewriter, web-server, etc.
>
> So, yes, it is a generic name, but I have not seen genericity being
> considered a negative indicator when considering the package names for
> ELPA submission.
>
> I understand that some people have the opinion that generic names
> should be avoided, but I differ from such an opinion. For me, the name
> should first and foremost signify the goal of the program. In this
> case, it does. It's a program to read documents.
>
> Let's hear what others have to say on this. That said, if Emacs or
> ELPA maintainers consider it absolutely necessary for the package to
> be renamed to be considered for inclusion in ELPA, I will comply.

Genericity of names for packages that aren't general solutions to
problems is, in fact, a negative indicator when considering package
names for ELPA submission.

However, arguably this package is a very general solution to the problem
of reading documents in Emacs, so perhaps it deserves the name.

My main concern here is that this is a complex package, and if the
current maintainers move on at some point, it might fall into disrepair
with no-one willing to dive into the complexity that would be required
to keep it from bitrotting.  One has to be humble about one's own
motivation and spare some thought for this future situation, even if it
seems far off to you at present.

(I also think that Mekeor raises a good point about "reader" clashing
directly with the Lisp reader that's a part of core Emacs, but maybe we
just have to accept this part.  Would you give some thought to renaming
it to "emacs-doc-reader", perhaps?)

-- 
Sean Whitton

Hello ELPA maintainers,

I maintain Clutch, an interactive database client for Emacs, and would
like to request its inclusion in NonGNU ELPA.

Repository: https://github.com/LuciusChen/clutch
License: GPL-3.0-or-later
Current release: 0.7.0
Minimum Emacs version: 29.1
Declared package dependencies: Emacs 29.1 and Transient 0.3.7

Clutch provides SQL editing buffers, an interactive result grid,
schema discovery and completion, and staged row edits that can be
previewed before execution. Its SQLite path uses Emacs's built-in
SQLite support, without additional protocol packages or Java. Other
database backends use optional protocol libraries or a separately
installed JDBC agent.

I would like to clarify the code-provenance policy before proceeding
further. Development includes code generated with OpenAI Codex and
Claude Code, which is disclosed in the package's Assisted-by headers.
Could you confirm whether a package with this development history is
eligible for NonGNU ELPA under the current policy?

The main Lisp file is clutch.el, and the Lisp sources are in the
repository root on the default main branch. Release notes are in
CHANGELOG.md. There is no special build step for the Lisp package.

If the package is eligible, I would appreciate any review comments and
packaging changes needed for inclusion.

Thank you for your guidance and consideration.

Lucius Chen
chenyh572@gmail.com

On 10/19/2026 6:24 AM, Richard Stallman wrote:

>    > Having a friend build them for you was possible.
> 
> That was not a solution.  It would have meant that each of us would
> have to send each version of our Java program to the "friend" with the
> compiler, to get it compiled.  Basically, that "friend" would be a
> SaaSS service (a server that compiles code on demand).

Agreed. I withdraw that.

> 
>    > Here, the solution is not getting closer, on the contrary.
> 
> That is speculation, and vague.  You can't convince the GNU Project to
> change its moral standards with handwaving.
On “the solution is not getting closer,” here is something
specific. Epoch AI estimates that the cost of training frontier models
has grown about 2.4 times per year since 2016, and that the largest
models could cost over a billion dollars to train by 2027. The compute
used grows even faster, 4 to 5 times per year.

That’s the difference with the Java trap. There, one free program,
written once, freed every free Java program. Here, each model needs
its own training, and each new one costs more than the last. Waiting a
decade made the Java trap disappear. With current trends, waiting a
decade makes this one much deeper.

I don't think I proposed any concrete change in the GNU project
standards. Maybe I did and I don't remember.

This things are new. Is only normal that no standards are prepared for
anythin new that could come. That's all I have.

Hello,

I wanted to advise a command to change its interactive form. However,
that means the advice function must have an interactive form as well. As
such, it shows up in, for instance, 'M-x'. I wonder if there is a way to
explicitly mark such a function as non-command? Thanks!

Regards,
Pengji

PS here is an example to reproduce the problem I have (note that
':interactive-only' requires Emacs>=31):

  (define-advice find-file (:interative-only (&rest _) advice)
    (interactive (lambda (spec) (advice-eval-interactive-spec spec)))
    nil)

Then a 'find-file@advice' will show up in 'M-x', which I do not want.

On Mon, Oct 19, 2026 at 8:28=E2=80=AFAM Pengji Zhang <me@pengjiz.com> wrote=

> Hello,
>
> I wanted to advise a command to change its interactive form. However,
> that means the advice function must have an interactive form as well. As
> such, it shows up in, for instance, 'M-x'. I wonder if there is a way to
> explicitly mark such a function as non-command? Thanks!
>
> Regards,
> Pengji
>
> PS here is an example to reproduce the problem I have (note that
> ':interactive-only' requires Emacs>=3D31):
>
>   (define-advice find-file (:interative-only (&rest _) advice)
>     (interactive (lambda (spec) (advice-eval-interactive-spec spec)))
>     nil)
>
> Then a 'find-file@advice' will show up in 'M-x', which I do not want.
>

One way is:

(put 'your-advice-symbol-name 'completion-predicate #'ignore)

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > > If we cannot remove packages from elpa, we must be much more careful
  > > which packages are accepted in elpa, than when we can remove packages
  > > when their situation changes.

  > Yes, and that's my main point.  We must test all those conditions up
  > front, and if the conditions can change thereafter, we are screwed.

Indeed, we need to check that a package meets all our conditions, at
the outset.  That is why I intend to set up a new, careful procedure
for evaluating ELPA packages -- to make sure we notice any problems.

However, if we are stuck with a choice between (1) hurting a
contributor's feelings and (2) violating our principles in what we
distribute to users, the second alternative is far worse.  If we have
fallen into that situation, we must get ourselves out of it.

Hi Joao

A user report for refactor.el.

I'm generally satisfied with it, and it gets getting better the more I 
use it.

There are some points that need might polishing, though.

My ELisp experience (*scatch* and .el files): I'm a bit confused about 
refacctor-suggestion-mode here. It would be nice for a user to know what 
this means.

For example:
I'm quite used to seeing the "old"

defun: ARGS DOCSTRING...

In the mini-buffer when programming. It helps me know where I am and I'd 
be disappointed (and a bit confused) if I lost that. I have found out 
that I get my desried behaviour by disabling refactor-suggestion-mode 
for both. I even disable elisp-refactor-mode in *scratch* completely.

Then, I'm using LSP for LaTeX and Python

- Python (python-lsp-server + ruff) works nicely


- LaTeX: neither Digestif nor TexLab seem to work as expected

[eglot] Connected! Server 'TexLab' now managing '(latex-mode)' buffers 
in project 'fragmentation'.
refactor: backend eglot failed: ("[eglot] Unsupported or ignored LSP 
capability ':codeActionProvider'")

This happens both with and without refactor-suggestion-mode and even 
when I add :codeActionProvider to eglot-ignored-server-capabilities.

- Finally, a quirk <blush> (my fingers, surely) </blush>: if it were 
possible to remove spaces and tabs from the end of the new variable name

But in general, it is an improvement :-)

The Kitty Keyboard Protocol[1] is a new way for terminal emulators to
communicate user input to text mode applications, like xterm's
modifyOtherKeys that we already support, but with several more
enhancements such as distinguishing between key-down and key-up events,
and disambiguating more possible key chord presses.

It's also already widely implemented in terminal emulators (alacritty,
foot, ghostty are some big names on GNU; on non-free platforms, macOS's
iTerm2 and Microsoft's terminal application implement it) as compared
with just Xterm for modifyOtherKeys.

I'm planning to implement KKP for Emacs.  I'll work from the
implementation of modifyOtherKeys, so I don't expect anything to be
difficult or controversial, except for one thing: KKP means that C-g
arrives as a multi-byte sequence, and that means we can't register it as
the controlling tty's VINTR and VQUIT like we do at present.

Essentially this means that with KKP enabled, C-g in a 'emacs -nw' frame
will be like C-g in an 'emacsclient -t' frame: it can still interrupt
Emacs, but only at the next maybe_quit, via the SIGIO route.
The (info "(emacs)Emergency Escape") mechanism would become unavailable.

I think this trade-off is acceptable and KKP should be turned on by
default.  We can document the issue, and users can always turn off KKP
support in favour of keeping emergency escape.  I predict that most
people would prefer to have C-. and C-, work without any specific
configuration in their text mode frames.

I did try asking about extending KKP so that it doesn't rule out use of
VINTR etc. but this did not receive a warm reception.[2]

[1]  https://sw.kovidgoyal.net/kitty/keyboard-protocol/
[2]  https://github.com/kovidgoyal/kitty/issues/10704
     (non-free javascript only, unfortunately)

-- 
Sean Whitton

>>
>>   (define-advice find-file (:interative-only (&rest _) advice)
>>     (interactive (lambda (spec) (advice-eval-interactive-spec spec)))
>>     nil)
>>
>> Then a 'find-file@advice' will show up in 'M-x', which I do not want.
>>
>
> One way is:
>
> (put 'your-advice-symbol-name 'completion-predicate #'ignore)
>

Another way is to do the above "in line" as in:

  (define-advice find-file (:interactive-only (&rest _) advice)
    (declare (completion ignore)) ; tags the symbol for you
    (interactive (lambda (spec) (advice-eval-interactive-spec spec)))
    nil)

> From: Sean Whitton <spwhitton@spwhitton.name>
> Date: Tue, 20 Oct 2026 09:58:28 +0100
> 
> The Kitty Keyboard Protocol[1] is a new way for terminal emulators to
> communicate user input to text mode applications, like xterm's
> modifyOtherKeys that we already support, but with several more
> enhancements such as distinguishing between key-down and key-up events,
> and disambiguating more possible key chord presses.
> 
> It's also already widely implemented in terminal emulators (alacritty,
> foot, ghostty are some big names on GNU; on non-free platforms, macOS's
> iTerm2 and Microsoft's terminal application implement it) as compared
> with just Xterm for modifyOtherKeys.
> 
> I'm planning to implement KKP for Emacs.  I'll work from the
> implementation of modifyOtherKeys, so I don't expect anything to be
> difficult or controversial, except for one thing: KKP means that C-g
> arrives as a multi-byte sequence, and that means we can't register it as
> the controlling tty's VINTR and VQUIT like we do at present.
> 
> Essentially this means that with KKP enabled, C-g in a 'emacs -nw' frame
> will be like C-g in an 'emacsclient -t' frame: it can still interrupt
> Emacs, but only at the next maybe_quit, via the SIGIO route.
> The (info "(emacs)Emergency Escape") mechanism would become unavailable.
> 
> I think this trade-off is acceptable and KKP should be turned on by
> default.  We can document the issue, and users can always turn off KKP
> support in favour of keeping emergency escape.  I predict that most
> people would prefer to have C-. and C-, work without any specific
> configuration in their text mode frames.

How do you envision this to be integrated into Emacs?
Terminal-specific functionality is currently implemented in lisp/term/
packages, and a suitable package is loaded at startup by looking at
the value of TERM.  Will this implementation do the same?  If yes, how
can a terminal other than Kitty request this functionality early
enough to be used throughout the session?  If that's not how you plan
on integrating the protocol, what are your current thoughts on this?

Eli Zaretskii [20/Oct  2:58pm +03] wrote:
>> From: Sean Whitton <spwhitton@spwhitton.name>
>> Date: Tue, 20 Oct 2026 09:58:28 +0100
>>
>> The Kitty Keyboard Protocol[1] is a new way for terminal emulators to
>> communicate user input to text mode applications, like xterm's
>> modifyOtherKeys that we already support, but with several more
>> enhancements such as distinguishing between key-down and key-up events,
>> and disambiguating more possible key chord presses.
>>
>> It's also already widely implemented in terminal emulators (alacritty,
>> foot, ghostty are some big names on GNU; on non-free platforms, macOS's
>> iTerm2 and Microsoft's terminal application implement it) as compared
>> with just Xterm for modifyOtherKeys.
>>
>> I'm planning to implement KKP for Emacs.  I'll work from the
>> implementation of modifyOtherKeys, so I don't expect anything to be
>> difficult or controversial, except for one thing: KKP means that C-g
>> arrives as a multi-byte sequence, and that means we can't register it as
>> the controlling tty's VINTR and VQUIT like we do at present.
>>
>> Essentially this means that with KKP enabled, C-g in a 'emacs -nw' frame
>> will be like C-g in an 'emacsclient -t' frame: it can still interrupt
>> Emacs, but only at the next maybe_quit, via the SIGIO route.
>> The (info "(emacs)Emergency Escape") mechanism would become unavailable.
>>
>> I think this trade-off is acceptable and KKP should be turned on by
>> default.  We can document the issue, and users can always turn off KKP
>> support in favour of keeping emergency escape.  I predict that most
>> people would prefer to have C-. and C-, work without any specific
>> configuration in their text mode frames.
>
> How do you envision this to be integrated into Emacs?
> Terminal-specific functionality is currently implemented in lisp/term/
> packages, and a suitable package is loaded at startup by looking at
> the value of TERM.  Will this implementation do the same?  If yes, how
> can a terminal other than Kitty request this functionality early
> enough to be used throughout the session?  If that's not how you plan
> on integrating the protocol, what are your current thoughts on this?

Almost all the implementation will be in lisp/term/xterm.el.  The query
for whether KKP is supported just goes in alongside the autodetection
that we already do there.  All the existing terminals that support KKP
already use lisp/term/xterm.el, so far as I can tell.

-- 
Sean Whitton
