Sorry for the late reply.

This program is a dumb-ish I/O forwarder, essentially.  You send it JSON
requests like 'send me the contents of this file' or 'run the LSP server to
look up this symbol' or 'run this git command.'.  It executes the request
and sends the response back as json.

Clearly you can do each via individual ssh commands.  But I've worked in a
few places where ssh connections - even with a control channel - are slow
enough to establish where using emacs is unpleasantly slow.  So, I've found
that this helps speed things up.

I used claude code to do a lot of the programming.  Generally, due to time
constraints w.r.t. my day job & family responsibilities.

> License: GPL-3.0-or-later
> Current release: 0.7.0
> Minimum Emacs version: 29.1
> Declared package dependencies: Emacs 29.1 and Transient 0.3.7
>
> Clutch provides SQL editing buffers, an interactive result grid,
> schema discovery and completion, and staged row edits that can be
> previewed before execution. Its SQLite path uses Emacs's built-in
> SQLite support, without additional protocol packages or Java. Other
> database backends use optional protocol libraries or a separately
> installed JDBC agent.
>
> I would like to clarify the code-provenance policy before proceeding
> further. Development includes code generated with OpenAI Codex and
> Claude Code, which is disclosed in the package's Assisted-by headers.
> Could you confirm whether a package with this development history is
> eligible for NonGNU ELPA under the current policy?

If anything, we would have to add it to NonGNU ELPA, since LLM generated
code cannot be covered by the copyright assignment required for GNU ELPA.

> The main Lisp file is clutch.el, and the Lisp sources are in the
> repository root on the default main branch. Release notes are in
> CHANGELOG.md. There is no special build step for the Lisp package.
>
> If the package is eligible, I would appreciate any review comments and
> packaging changes needed for inclusion.

I hope to get around to reviewing the package in the coming days, but
for now I'd be curious to hear from you if you find yourself comfortable
in understanding the code without LLM assistance, whether you have a
real long-term interest in maintaining the package and if you think that
the code is generated in a way that is still human usable (I haven't
even checked out your code yet so I have no idea).

If you haven't already, I would recommend taking a look at
https://elpa.gnu.org/contributing.html.

> Thank you for your guidance and consideration.
>
> Lucius Chen

Hello,

I would like to submit ekp for NonGNU ELPA.

  Package:    ekp
  Repository: https://github.com/emacs-taf/ekp
  Maintainer: Kinney Zhang <vhkdzszh@gmail.com>
  License:    GPL-3.0-or-later
  Requires:   Emacs 29.1

ekp implements Knuth-Plass optimal line breaking for Emacs buffers.
Paragraphs are split into boxes, a globally optimal break sequence is
chosen, and lines are justified to the pixel.  It supports mixed CJK and
Latin text, kinsoku rules, discretionary hyphenation, and per-region
break policies for URLs, paths and identifiers.

Points the submission guidelines ask about:

- The Lisp implementation lives in lisp/, not in the repository root;
  ekp.el at the root is the entry file and adds that directory itself.
- CHANGELOG.md is the changelog.
- There is no Texinfo manual.
- native/ holds an optional C accelerator that the user builds on
  request with make; the package is fully functional without it.
- dictionaries/ carries 84 hyphenation patterns taken from LibreOffice.
  MANIFEST.tsv pins the upstream commit and records the licence evidence
  for each file; LICENSES.md explains the scheme.
- The repository ships 59 acceptance tests, run with make check.

The package passes package-lint with no issues, checkdoc on every file,
and byte compilation with warnings treated as errors.  It also loads
correctly when installed as a package and loaded from its native-
compiled output, with only the package root on load-path.

For the C-h P description, please use the Commentary of ekp.el: the
README is Markdown, and the Commentary opens with the package summary.

One question: should tests/, scripts/ and benchmarks/ stay in the
package tarball?  They are not needed at runtime, and dictionaries/ is
6 MB on its own.

Regards,
Kinney

Hello Sean,

> How does the name "ekp" relate to this synopsis?
> I think the package needs a much more descriptive name.

"ekp" is short for Emacs Knuth-Plass, which indeed says nothing about
what the package does.  It is a paragraph typesetting engine: optimal
line breaking, mixed CJK and Latin text, kinsoku rules, discretionary
hyphenation, and pixel-accurate justification.

I would rename it to "typeset", which describes the whole thing rather
than one algorithm.  Would that work?

Kinney

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > In my estimation, that is sadly a problem with dynamic modules that we
  > are not in a good position to solve.  It is possible, like you are
  > doing, to have a Makefile with a few common package managers, but that
  > is never really portable :/

This mention of "a few common package managers" makes me worried.  In
general, we can't trust package managers not to pull in nonfree
modules.  Whether there might really be a problem depends
on what job is being done with those package managers; of course,
the words above don't say.

Can you explain what job is being done here with those package
managers?  Perhaps show the pertinent part of the makefile?

We may need someone to study that code carefully and verify that _with
each package manager_ it avoids linking with anything nonfree, unless
that thing fits into the "system library" exception in GPLv3.

Are these the "package managers" such as dpkg, used by system distros?
Or are these the "package managers" such as NPM that will often link
your code with nonfree code by default?  Or is it some other kind of
"package manager"?  Whichever it is, why does Emacs need to deal with
them in order to build and use a dynamic module?

  > I would like to clarify the code-provenance policy before proceeding
  > further. Development includes code generated with OpenAI Codex and

Sorry, but our current policy is not to include LLM-generated code.

NonGNU ELPA packages are not strictly speaking part of Emacs, but they
are closely associated with Emacs, so we want them to follow the same
legal policies as GNU packages.

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > "doc-reader" is good, "reader" is even better.

In my opinion, `reader' is too vague and general.  One can imagine
programs that would do totally different jobs that would be a kind
of "reading".

`doc-reader' is better because avoids that problem.  `doc' makes the
purpose less vague.

But "doc" refers primarily to a Microsoft format, and we would rather
not name a whole category of formats after that.  There is probably a
better word, but I can't think of one now.

Would people please try to look for one?  We might find a better one,
and if not, "doc" will still be available.

Hello Sean,

I would like to go with `ekp-wrap`, which Alexander Adolf proposed.
"Wrap" is the term Emacs already uses for breaking text at line
boundaries (word-wrap, visual-line-mode), so it says what the package
does, and the prefix stays short enough to read.

His other idea was `ekp-fill`.  I prefer "wrap" because the package also
handles CJK text, where there is nothing to fill between.

If you would rather avoid the "ekp" abbreviation altogether, I can use
`knuth-plass-typeset`; I only worry that the longer prefix makes every
public symbol heavier.

Kinney

> Hello Sean,
>
> I would like to go with `ekp-wrap`, which Alexander Adolf proposed.
> "Wrap" is the term Emacs already uses for breaking text at line
> boundaries (word-wrap, visual-line-mode), so it says what the package
> does, and the prefix stays short enough to read.
>
> His other idea was `ekp-fill`.  I prefer "wrap" because the package also
> handles CJK text, where there is nothing to fill between.

Thank you for considering the feedback.  It's true that fill is the
usual Emacs term for this, even for CJK text, so ekp-fill is probably
more useful.

> public symbol heavier.

You could consider using the symbol shorthands feature of Emacs.

Thanks.  The package grew inside a rendering framework where line
breaking had to be pluggable, so it started life outside the core.  I
would be glad to see it in core eventually; I assumed a core change
needs copyright assignment and a much slower review, so I began with a
package.

One thing you may not have seen yet: I wrote earlier in this thread that
two merged pull requests came from Copilot, and recent fixes were
prepared with an LLM-assisted editor.  If the policy also applies to
core contributions, then this is a dead end until those parts are
rewritten.  I am willing to rewrite them either way.

Kinney

vhkdzszh@gmail.com writes:

> Sorry, that sentence was muddled.  What I meant was simpler: the two

> policy, and I am prepared to rewrite those parts.  The "if" was not
> meant to suggest the policy is about something else.
>
> So the question is only whether rewriting the affected code is enough
> for you, or whether the history itself makes the submission
> unacceptable.  Either answer is fine; I would rather know than guess.

LLM generated code is a copyright issue for us.  If the changes are
undone and rewritten (ideally by someone not familiar with the initial
implementation) then it shouldn't be an issue.

Regarding NonGNU ELPA:  I do recall Richard mentioning that LLM
generated code shouldn't be added to NonGNU ELPA, but this policy was
never agreed on.  Before the fact, it was already the case that we had
LLM generated code, which is not an issue from the copyright assignment
perspective, since packages in NonGNU ELPA don't have to have the
copyright assigned to the FSF.

So the question is up to you, if you want to have the package in NonGNU
ELPA or in GNU ELPA/core Emacs as Eli suggested.
